title: Prognostic Value of Vestibular Symptoms on the Vestibular Ocular Motor Screening for Return-to-play After Sport-related Concussion: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) contributes to gaze stabilization after head movement, but its independent prognostic value for return-to-play (RTP) after sport-related concussion (SRC) is unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined associations between early vestibular-ocular motor screening (VOMS) assessment and RTP duration following SRC.
METHODS: Searches of PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, PEDro, and Cochrane Library to March 2025 identified studies assessing within 14 days of SRC and reporting RTP outcomes. Two reviewers extracted data and assessed the risk of bias. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed for studies reporting prolonged recovery (≥28-30 days).
RESULTS: Twelve studies (N = 3297 athletes) met inclusion criteria. Meta-analysis of four studies (n = 968) found a positive VOMS screen was associated with increased odds of prolonged recovery (odds ratio 2.39; 95% confidence interval, 1.82-3.13; P < 0.00001; I2=0%). Among nine studies of isolated VOR gain, eight reported significant univariate associations with longer RTP, but only two retained significance after multivariable adjustment. VOMS reliably identifies athletes at risk for protracted recovery, but isolated VOR measures show inconsistent independent predictive value after adjustment.
DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS: Objective VOR gain quantification (eg, vHIT, caloric) is needed to clarify whether physiological VOR dysfunction independently affects recovery. Clinicians should interpret VOR findings within a multimodal assessment.

title: Sex-related differences after ACL reconstruction differ between early functional recovery and 5-year outcomes.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare early functional recovery and 5-year clinical, sports and psychological outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) according to sex.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients who underwent primary ACLR between January 2017 and December 2019, with standardized 6-month functional and psychological assessment and available 5-year follow-up. Patients were analyzed according to sex. Baseline characteristics, 6-month quadriceps strength and hop-test performance, and 5-year patient-reported and sports outcomes were compared between groups. The primary outcome was recovery of preinjury activity level at 5 years, defined as a post-operative Tegner score greater than or equal to the preoperative Tegner score. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors independently associated with the primary outcome.
RESULTS: A total of 479 patients were included, comprising 173 women (36.1%) and 306 men (63.9%). At 6 months, men demonstrated higher quadriceps limb symmetry and lower hop-test deficits than women, whereas anterior cruciate ligament return to sport after injury (ACL-RSI) did not differ significantly between groups. At 5 years, overall return-to-sport rates were similar between sexes (187 [61.2%] men vs. 103 [59.5%] women, p = 0.85), but men had higher post-operative Tegner (6 [5-7] vs. 5 [4-7], p < 0.001), IKDC (82.5 [75.7-87.3] vs. 79.5 [72.8-86.3], p = 0.02) and ACL-RSI scores (77.5 [55.8-92.5] vs. 69.2 [53.3-85.8], p = 0.02) and were more likely to recover their preinjury activity level (137 [45.1%] vs. 48 [28.1%], p < 0.001). In the baseline-adjusted multivariable model, male sex was independently associated with recovery of preinjury activity level (odds ratio [OR] = 2.16, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.40-3.39; p < 0.001). This association persisted after inclusion of 6-month recovery variables (OR = 1.93, 95% CI = 1.20-3.15; p = 0.007), while lower single-hop deficit was also independently associated with the outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: Men and women did not demonstrate the same recovery profile after ACLR. Early differences were mainly functional, whereas 5-year differences involved recovery of preinjury activity level, subjective knee function and psychological readiness, despite similar overall return-to-sport rates. These findings suggest that return to sport should not be interpreted as equivalent recovery quality after ACLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Low graft failure after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in professional soccer players: A retrospective cohort study of 232 knees from the SANTI Study Group.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study aimed to determine graft failure rates after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) in professional soccer players and to evaluate factors associated with graft failure, including lateral extra-articular augmentation.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study included 232 primary ACLRs in 215 professional soccer players: isolated ACLR (n = 31) and ACLR combined with a lateral extra-articular procedure (LEAP) (n = 201). The primary endpoint was graft failure, defined as symptomatic rupture confirmed clinically and by imaging or revision surgery. Time-to-event analyses accounted for variable follow-up. Contralateral ACL injury was recorded descriptively.
RESULTS: At a mean follow-up of 100 months, 13 graft failures occurred (5.6%). Unadjusted failure rates were lower in ACLR + LEAP versus isolated ACLR (4.5% vs. 12.9%), but survival analysis showed no significant difference (hazard ratio [HR] 2.48; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.49-9.87; p = 0.246). Multivariable Cox regression identified no independent predictors of graft failure. Mean time to graft failure was longer in the ACLR + LEAP group than in the isolated ACLR group (54.8 ± 52.0 vs. 36.6 ± 38.2 months). Reoperations occurred in 32 knees (17.7%), with rates of 15.2% in the ACLR + LEAP group and 30.0% in the isolated ACLR group (p = 0.0528). Increased preoperative laxity (≥7 mm; HR 2.72; 95% CI 1.23-6.17; p = 0.014) and bone-patellar tendon-bone graft use (HR 3.14; 95% CI 1.26-7.20; p = 0.037) were independent risk factors for reoperation. Contralateral ACL injury occurred in 27.1% of knees, more frequently in female athletes (48.7% vs. 22.8%). Among patients who experienced graft failure, 53.8% also had a contralateral ACL injury.
CONCLUSION: Primary ACL reconstruction in professional soccer players was associated with durable long-term graft survival. Although ACLR combined with an LEAP was associated with fewer graft failures than isolated ACLR, an independent protective effect was not confirmed. The high rate of contralateral ACL injury highlights the multifactorial nature of reinjury risk in this elite population.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Neuromuscular Electric Stimulation Improves Early Isometric Knee Strength After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction and Repair: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To assess the effectiveness of neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) on quadriceps strength and knee function after anterior cruciate ligament surgery.
METHODS: A comprehensive search of PubMed, Ovid MEDLINE, and Embase from inception until February 2025 was conducted. Randomized controlled trials on adults undergoing anterior cruciate ligament surgery with NMES as an intervention and standard rehabilitation as a control were included. Study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool were performed independently by 2 reviewers. Meta-analysis including subgroup and heterogeneity analysis was conducted using Cochrane RevMan 10.0.1.
RESULTS: Twenty-one randomized controlled trial studies met our inclusion criteria (n = 687 patients, 314 control and 373 NMES patients). The frequency-weighted mean age of included patients across all studies was 27.0 years. Mean follow-up time was 18.4 weeks (4-54). Pooled analysis for isometric knee extension strength showed statistically significant improvements in absolute strength between NMES (n = 54 patients) and control (n = 55 patients) groups (n = 109 patients, mean difference 0.24; 95% confidence interval 0.2-0.27; P < .01, I2 = 9%) and strength as a percentage of the uninvolved limb between NMES (n = 131) and control (n = 133 patients) groups (n = 264 patients, standardized mean difference 0.87; 95% confidence interval 0.11-1.64; P = .03, I2 = 87%) in the early (6-12 weeks) but not late postoperative period (>12 weeks). Similar statistical significance was noted with improvements in knee flexion (P = .01), thigh circumference (P = .04), and Lysholm scores (P = .02) but not International Knee Documentation Committee scores. Four studies reporting isokinetic muscle strength were pooled, and no statistically significant difference was found.
CONCLUSIONS: The use of NMES as an adjunct to a standard physical therapy program after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction appears to modestly improve isometric strength at a faster rate than standard rehabilitation alone. No conclusion can be made regarding the functional recovery or improvements in knee strength beyond the 3-month postoperative period.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, meta-analysis of randomized controlled trial studies.

title: Effectiveness of aerobic exercise on motor function and functional capacity in children and adolescents with neuromuscular diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the effectiveness of aerobic exercise, alone or combined with other modalities, on motor function and functional capacity in children and adolescents with neuromuscular diseases (NMDs).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted (CRD420251110784). Five databases were searched up to September 2025. Randomized and non-randomized trials assessing aerobic exercise in children/adolescents with NMDs were included. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using RoB2, ROBINS-I, and GRADE. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated standardized mean differences (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI).
RESULTS: Eleven studies (227 participants) were included. Aerobic exercise showed no significant effect on motor function (SMD = 0.15, 95% CI: -0.10 to 0.40, I2=0%) but produced moderate improvements in functional capacity (SMD = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.99, I2=78%). Subgroup analyses suggested non-significant effects for sessions <40 min (SMD = 0.83) and combined aerobic plus strength training (SMD = 0.74). Sensitivity analyses showed one study disproportionately influenced results; excluding high-risk studies yielded SMD = 0.36 (I2=0%). GRADE indicated low certainty for motor function and very low certainty for functional capacity.
CONCLUSIONS: Aerobic exercise is safe and may improve functional capacity but not motor function in pediatric NMDs. Evidence is limited and needs for cautious interpretation and high-quality trials to inform clinical practice.

title: Can Psychological Readiness Predict Successful Return to Sports After Patellar Stabilization Surgery in Adolescent Patients? A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: While many metrics are used to subjectively assess a patient's knee function with patellofemoral instability (PFI), psychological readiness to return to sport (RTS) after patellar stabilization surgery is not well established in this population. The Anterior Cruciate Ligament Return to Sport After Injury (ACL-RSI) scale assesses psychological readiness to RTS after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and may be similarly beneficial in understanding this domain in those with PFI.
HYPOTHESIS: Higher ACL-RSI scores in patients with PFI are associated with an increased likelihood of RTS after patellar stabilization surgery.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3.
METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of adolescent patients (10-19 years old) treated surgically for PFI (medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction [MPFLR] with or without tibial tubercle osteotomy) at a single institution from January 2020 to October 2024. Patients actively participating in sports at their first orthopaedic visit who completed the ACL-RSI during postoperative rehabilitation were included. Patient demographics, injury characteristics, surgical procedure, ACL-RSI scores, and RTS status were recorded. Descriptive statistics and bivariate analysis were performed. Based on the euclidean distance, the optimal ACL-RSI cutoff score for predicting successful RTS was determined, and diagnostic accuracy was evaluated with a receiver operating curve. A multivariate logistic regression, adjusted for sex, was used to identify predictors of RTS.
RESULTS: Study criteria identified 97 patients with a median (IQR) age of 15.6 years (14.2-16.4). Seventy underwent isolated MPFLR and 27 underwent MPFLR with tibial tubercle osteotomy. Successful RTS was achieved in 78.3% (n = 76). RTS was associated with higher ACL-RSI scores (P = .012), isolated MPFLR (P = .011), and male sex (P = .03). An ACL-RSI score ≥59.2 was identified as being indicative of successful RTS (area under the curve, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.56-0.83). While procedure type and ACL-RSI scores were both associated with RTS in univariate analysis, the multivariable analysis adjusting for sex revealed that the ACL-RSI cutoff remained the only significant predictor of RTS (odds ratio, 3.56; 95% CI, 1.10-11.51; P = .033).
CONCLUSION: ACL-RSI scores ≥59.2 are associated with an increased likelihood of successful RTS after surgical treatment for PFI in adolescents. Patient demographics and the studied injury characteristics do not appear to influence the likelihood of successful RTS.

title: Oral contraceptive use and anterior cruciate ligament injury or reconstruction in women: A systematic review and meta-analysis of very low-certainty evidence.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To determine whether oral contraceptive use is associated with anterior cruciate ligament injury or reconstruction in women and to examine whether associations vary according to age, contraceptive formulation, duration of use and outcome definition.
METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, Embase and Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature (LILACS) were searched through 31 July 2026 (LILACS rerun with multilingual terms on 16 September 2026). Comparative observational studies were meta-analysed. The primary analysis pooled adjusted or matched odds ratios (ORs) for reconstruction or operatively treated injury using random-effects restricted maximum-likelihood models with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman confidence intervals (CIs). Risk of bias was assessed with risk of bias in nonrandomised studies of exposures and certainty with grading of recommendations assessment, development and evaluation.
RESULTS: Ten studies were included; seven were meta-analysed. The primary analysis (four studies) showed no clear association (OR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.77-1.02; I 2 = 84%; τ 2 = 0.01; 95% prediction interval, 0.66-1.19). Two crude athlete studies and the active-comparator cohort (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.89-1.01) also had CIs including 1. Adding one crude database estimate yielded OR 0.85 (95% CI, 0.74-0.98; I 2 = 90%; 95% prediction interval, 0.61-1.19). Leave-one-out results were unstable. The certainty of evidence was very low.
CONCLUSIONS: The primary adjusted or matched analysis did not establish a clear association between oral contraceptive use and anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction or operatively treated injury; substantial heterogeneity, residual confounding and very low certainty of evidence preclude causal interpretation. Current evidence does not support initiating or selecting oral contraceptives for anterior cruciate ligament injury prevention. Well-designed prospective studies with standardised exposure and outcome definitions are needed.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of observational studies.

title: Persistent alterations in muscle activation patterns during landing tasks after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in return-to-sport cohorts: A systematic review and meta-analysis of electromyography studies.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To categorize landing tasks in electromyography (EMG) studies and compare muscle activity during landing between patients with anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) reported as having returned to sport and healthy controls.
METHODS: We systematically searched seven databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Scopus, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus) from inception to 10 December 2025. Studies using EMG to assess muscle activity during landing tasks were included when they compared the reconstructed limb of ACLR patients reported as having returned to sport with limbs from healthy controls. Random-effects meta-analyses evaluated between-group differences using standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with findings categorized using an internal evidence classification.
RESULTS: Thirty-two studies were included, comprising 556 individuals with ACLR from return-to-sport cohorts and 501 healthy controls. Thirteen landing tasks were analysed, involving fifteen lower-limb muscles and four EMG outcome measures. Each pooled comparison included 2-5 studies. Three findings were classified as moderate evidence: greater activation of the medial hamstrings during the reactive phase of single-leg drop landing (based on five studies, SMD = 0.35, 95% CI [0.01, 0.69], I2 = 0%), greater gluteus maximus activation during the reactive phase of single-leg drop vertical jump (based on three studies, SMD = 0.63, 95% CI [0.22, 1.03], I2 = 0%) and earlier rectus femoris onset in single-leg hop for distance (based on three studies, SMD = -0.64, 95% CI [-1.13, -0.14], I2 = 19%). Most other findings showed no between-group differences or were classified as limited or very limited evidence.
CONCLUSION: ACLR patients reported as having returned to sport may exhibit task-specific alterations in muscle activation patterns compared with healthy controls, and these alterations may be more readily detected during certain single-leg landing tasks. Further prospective and interventional studies are needed to clarify their clinical relevance.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.

title: Effects of caffeine supplementation on post-exercise recovery: a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of perceptual, functional performance, physiological, and sleep outcomes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of caffeine supplementation on perceptual recovery, functional performance during recovery, physiological recovery, and sleep recovery after exercise and explore potential moderators.
METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception to June 30, 2026, with supplementary searches of Google Scholar, ResearchGate, and reference lists. Randomized controlled trials comparing caffeine with placebo or a caffeine-free condition were included. Hedges' g was synthesized using three-level random-effects models with REML estimation and CR2 cluster-robust inference. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using RoB 2 and GRADE, respectively.
RESULTS: Seventeen studies were included, of which 16 contributed 120 effect sizes to the quantitative synthesis. Caffeine had no clear effect on perceptual recovery (g = -0.161, CR2 95% CI -0.528 to 0.205, p = 0.319) or physiological recovery (g = -0.104, CR2 95% CI -0.346 to 0.138, p = 0.293), but produced a small beneficial effect on functional performance during recovery (g = -0.208, CR2 95% CI -0.393 to -0.023, p = 0.035). Caffeine was associated with poorer sleep recovery (g = 0.751, CR2 95% CI 0.244 to 1.258, p = 0.018), based on four independent studies. Effects differed across recovery domains (CR2 robust Wald F(3, 3.88) = 9.76, p = 0.028). Exploratory domain-adjusted moderator analyses were inconclusive for recovery time, caffeine dose, ingestion timing or strategy, and exercise model. Effect directions remained generally stable, but statistical significance for functional performance and sleep varied in sensitivity analyses. Model-based 95% prediction intervals crossed the null for both domains (functional: -0.444 to 0.028; sleep: -0.002 to 1.503). GRADE certainty was very low for perceptual recovery, moderate for functional and physiological recovery, and low for sleep recovery.
CONCLUSION: Caffeine appears to have domain-specific effects on post-exercise recovery. It may modestly improve functional performance during recovery, does not clearly improve perceptual or physiological recovery, and may impair sleep. Functional and sleep findings should be interpreted cautiously because statistical significance varied in sensitivity analyses and prediction intervals included the null.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?ID=CRD420261467699, identifier CRD420261467699.

title: Acupuncture-Related interventions for exercise-induced delayed-onset muscle soreness in active adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis for sport rehabilitation.
abstract: BackgroundDelayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is a common post-exercise condition that can impair athletic performance, training quality, and rehabilitation.ObjectiveTo evaluate the efficacy and safety of acupuncture-related interventions for exercise-induced DOMS in active adults.MethodsPubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and CNKI were searched from inception to December 2025, with a manual reference-list update in January 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing acupuncture-related interventions with sham/placebo or no treatment in healthy adults with exercise-induced DOMS were eligible. Nine RCTs met the eligibility criteria, and seven contributed compatible pain data to meta-analysis. Two reviewers independently extracted data, assessed risk of bias using RoB 2, and rated evidence certainty with GRADE. Pain intensity on a 0-10 visual analogue scale was pooled using random-effects models.ResultsAcross seven RCTs, acupuncture-related interventions reduced DOMS pain at 24 h (MD -0.62, 95% CI -1.01 to -0.23), 48 h (MD -0.71, 95% CI -1.20 to -0.22), and 72 h (MD -0.84, 95% CI -1.35 to -0.32). Heterogeneity was low (I2 = 0%, 3%, and 23%, respectively). None of the pooled estimates reached commonly cited 1.0- or 1.3-point pain thresholds, and no DOMS-specific minimal clinically important difference has been established. Evidence certainty was moderate.ConclusionAcupuncture-related interventions may provide modest short-term reductions in DOMS pain, but their clinical importance remains uncertain. The evidence base is small and does not support dry-needling-specific conclusions. Larger, rigorously controlled, modality-specific RCTs are needed.

title: Application of antibiotic-loaded bone cement in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty: inhibiting IL-6 levels and reducing postoperative infection rate.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: We aim to clarify the inhibitory effect of antibiotic-loaded bone cement (ALBC) on inflammatory factors, and its preventive effect on postoperative infections in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA).
METHODS: This prospective randomized controlled trial enrolled 104 osteoarthritis patients undergoing UKA, randomly assigned to the non-ALBC group (n = 52, bone cement without antibiotics) and ALBC group (ALBC with 1.0 g vancomycin hydrochloride, n = 52). Primary outcomes were postoperative inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, TNF-α, IL-6); secondary outcomes included infection rate and HSS score. Independent-samples t-tests were used for continuous variables, χ2 test for categorical variables (infection rate, efficacy), and repeated measures analysis of variance for intra-group longitudinal comparisons.
RESULTS: The ALBC group demonstrated lower inflammatory markers at postoperative day 7 and at 3 months [CRP (3.52 ± 0.81 vs 6.92 ± 1.17, Cohen's d = 3.379), ESR (16.29 ± 2.31 vs 20.19 ± 4.05, Cohen's d = 1.183), TNF-α (29.71 ± 4.03 vs 36.25 ± 5.17, Cohen's d = 1.411), and IL-6 (17.05 ± 3.72 vs 22.05 ± 4.38, Cohen's d = 1.230)] (all p < 0.001), and also showed superior clinical outcomes, with lower postoperative infection rate (p = 0.016), higher HSS score (p < 0.001), and better overall clinical efficacy (p = 0.010) than the non-ALBC group.
CONCLUSION: The application of ALBC in UKA was associated with reduced postoperative inflammatory markers such as IL-6 and a lower incidence of postoperative infection. These findings suggest that ALBC may play a beneficial role in postoperative recovery and joint function rehabilitation.

title: Shear wave elastography for assessing lower extremity muscle stiffness after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) restores passive joint stability, yet athletes who meet strength benchmarks may still land stiffly, hesitate to push off, and re-injure. Muscle stiffness governs how rapidly force is transmitted to the joint, and shear wave elastography (SWE) quantifies it muscle by muscle, but SWE findings after ACLR have not been synthesized.
METHODS: Scopus, PubMed, SPORTDiscus, and CINAHL were searched through November 2025 following PRISMA 2020. Eligible studies compared SWE-derived lower-extremity muscle stiffness after ACLR with contralateral limbs or controls. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and appraised quality (Downs and Black). Findings were synthesized narratively with Hedges' g (95% confidence intervals) where data permitted.
FINDINGS: Six studies (173 ACLR participants, 79 controls; quality poor to good) were included. Reduced passive vastus medialis shear modulus was consistently observed in operative limbs (g - 1.10 to -1.21 versus controls) and was associated with quadriceps strength, knee function, and landing biomechanics. Semitendinosus stiffness was reduced after hamstring tendon harvest (g - 1.29 to -1.64) but not at mid-belly after return to sport. Longitudinal deficits persisted at three months; active-contraction findings conflicted. No study sampled the distal vastus medialis obliquus or the distal hamstring musculotendinous region.
INTERPRETATION: SWE detects muscle-specific mechanical deficits that relate to function beyond strength: a compliant vastus medialis offers a mechanical explanation for the strong patient who lands stiffly, and reduced semitendinosus stiffness marks donor-site morbidity. Standardized protocols that sample clinically relevant regions and follow patients to return to sport are needed before SWE can guide rehabilitation.

title: Effect of tangeretin supplements on simulated precompetition weight loss in female combat sports athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Weight reduction before competition has long been a major challenge for combat-sports athletes. Unscientific weight-loss practices not only increase the risk of hormonal imbalance, electrolyte disturbance, and impaired immune function but also compromise athletic capacities such as aerobic and anaerobic performance and explosive power. This study investigated the potential benefits of tangeretin, a natural citrus extract, on athletic performance. These benefits include the regulation of hormone secretion, the optimization of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, and the promotion of muscle synthesis and lipid utilization, which may help athletes reach their target weight.
OBJECTIVE: To examine the effects of tangeretin supplementation on body-composition and sports-performance indicators in female combat-sports athletes, and to evaluate its efficacy for simulated precompetition weight loss.
METHODS: Thirty female combat-sports athletes (4 wrestlers, 3 boxers, 9 sanda athletes, 3 judokas, and 11 taekwondo athletes) were recruited. A paired, randomized, double-blind design was used. All 30 participants were first paired according to sport and competitive level, then randomly allocated to either a tangeretin group or a placebo group (15 per group). The 30-day intervention comprised a double-blind nutritional supplement, a dietary questionnaire, blood sampling and analysis, body-composition assessment, isokinetic muscle-strength testing, and aerobic-capacity testing, to evaluate the effects of tangeretin (400 mg/day) on performance and health-related outcomes. These outcomes included body-composition indicators (e.g. body-fat percentage, fat mass, lean-body mass), fat-distribution indicators (e.g. limb and regional fat mass, gynoid fat mass), glucose and lipid-metabolism indicators (e.g. LDL-C, total cholesterol, free fatty acids), hormone indicators (e.g. cortisol, testosterone), muscle-strength indicators (e.g. peak torque of hip, knee, and ankle flexors and extensors), and maximal-oxygen-uptake-derived indicators (e.g. VO2max heart rate, time to exhaustion). Statistical significance was assessed using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA).
RESULTS: (1) Body weight: 80.0% of athletes in the tangeretin group lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% (5 athletes) reached their competition weight class. (2) Body fat: body-fat percentage in the tangeretin group decreased from 23.92 ± 0.87% to 22.92 ± 0.89%; trunk, upper-limb, lower-limb, and android-region fat mass decreased by 6.77%, 8.77%, 4.43%, and 8.09%, respectively. (3) Glucose and lipid metabolism: HDL-C increased by 8.86% (P = 0.002), whereas triglycerides decreased by 25.00% (P = 0.048). (4) Sports performance: peak torque during hip, knee, and ankle flexion and extension increased significantly in the tangeretin group. VO2max also improved from 42.80 ± 1.13 to 43.46 ± 1.32 ml/kg/min.
CONCLUSION: Tangeretin supplementation effectively reduced body weight and fat mass (both overall and regionally) in female combat-sports athletes. Among the participants, 80.0% lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% reached their competition weight class, indicating a strong effect on precompetition weight loss. Moreover, tangeretin improved aerobic capacity and lower-limb joint muscle strength, thereby enhancing competitive performance.

title: The effect of macular carotenoids and omega-3 supplementation on performance in precision sports: the sport nutrition intervention in performance exercise (SNIPE) study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Macular carotenoids improve visual performance in healthy individuals, but these benefits have yet to be tested on athletes. The SNIPE study examined how the macular carotenoids [lutein (L), zeaxanthin (Z), meso-zeaxanthin (MZ)] with omega-3 fatty acids (ω3) impact visual functions and sports performance in precision sports.
METHODS: In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 67 athletes and players randomly received either an active supplement containing L, Z, MZ + ω3 (the formulation), or a placebo containing sunflower oil over a 9 month period. Key measurements included blood serum L, Z and MZ concentrations, skin carotenoid score (SCS), visual acuity (VA) and contrast sensitivity (CS), subjective visual function, sleep health (SH), and sport specific performance tests during simulated competitions.
RESULTS: Results showed that the active group, compared to placebo, exhibited statistically significant improvements in L (88%), Z (107%), MZ (0 to 0.226 μmol/L) blood concentrations, SCS (25%), CS at 6 cpd during dim condition (p = 0.008, η2 = 0.141), and SH in archery (p = 0.023, η2 = 0.242) and Egame (p = 0.041, η2 = 0.237). Sports performance also improved for the active group, including total shooting score of 60 shots (p = 0.047, η2 = 0.081) for shooters and archers, and simple motor time (p = 0.018, η2 = 0.302) and a suggestive trend toward faster choice reaction time (p = 0.054, η2 = 0.213) for Egame players, when compared to the placebo group.
CONCLUSION: The study provides novel evidence that supplementing with carotenoids and omega-3 fatty acids enhances visual function and sports performance in precision sport athletes and players. Further research should attempt to identify the exact mechanisms by which these nutrients are enhancing visual function. These findings highlight the opportunity to add these complementary bioactive nutrients of the eye and brain to athletes' diets to help achieve peak performance in sports.

title: Are Asymmetry-Focused Training Interventions More Effective than General Programs in Reducing Interlimb Asymmetries and Improving Athletic Performance? A Systematic Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Interlimb asymmetries (ILA) have been associated with an increased risk of injury and decreased athletic performance. However, despite the growing number of training interventions targeting ILA, their comparative effectiveness relative to general strength and conditioning approaches has not yet been systematically reviewed.
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review aimed to compare the effectiveness of asymmetry-focused training interventions versus general training programs in reducing ILA and improving physical performance in athletic populations. Specifically, it sought to compare individualized training programs that first identify the weaker limb during pre-testing and subsequently prescribe a greater training stimulus to that limb with general training protocols that apply the same training stimulus to both limbs, as well as unilateral approaches with bilateral training strategies.
METHODS: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic search was conducted in Web of Science, PubMed, and SPORTDiscus up to April 2025. Eligible studies involved healthy athletes (aged 12-30 years) who completed ≥4-week lower-limb training interventions that either applied a greater stimulus to the weaker limb (e.g., starting sets with the weaker side or adding volume) or used unilateral training approaches that applied the same training stimulus to both limbs regardless of baseline ILA values. To be included, studies were required to assess both pre-to-post changes in ILA and at least one physical performance outcome. The risk of bias was assessed using a modified Cochrane tool.
RESULTS: Eleven studies comprising 297 athletes met the inclusion criteria. Reductions in ILA were more consistent in asymmetry-focused and unilateral training groups compared to general and bilateral training groups, respectively. Most interventions also led to improvements in physical performance, with asymmetry-focused and unilateral protocols typically producing greater gains in single-limb tasks, although bilateral training showed more favourable effects in bilateral tasks. However, variability in training protocols and outcome measures across studies limits the generalizability of these findings.
CONCLUSION: Asymmetry-focused strategies, such as starting unilateral exercises with the weaker limb or increasing its training volume, appear to be more effective for reducing ILA than non-individualized unilateral training. These approaches are practical, safe, and potentially beneficial in athletic settings. However, further high-quality research is needed to confirm their superiority over non asymmetry-focused unilateral or bilateral training and to establish clear guidelines for their implementation. title: Editorial Commentary: Measuring Surgical Success in Athletes Requires More Than Generic Scores: It Is Time to Prioritize Athlete-Specific Outcomes.
abstract: Shoulder instability disproportionately affects young contact and collision athletes, for whom successful treatment requires more than the restoration of basic shoulder function. Recent systematic review reveals that conventional patient-reported outcomes dominated outcome reporting, whereas fewer than half of studies reported return to sport and only 15% included objective sport-specific performance measures. Common scores such as American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons, Rowe, and Western Ontario Shoulder Instability inadequately capture return to preinjury level, athletic performance, and durability of return to sport. Outcomes in athletes should therefore combine sport-specific patient-reported outcomes, clearly defined return to sport, and objective performance measures. Artificial intelligence may further improve assessment by dynamically tailoring follow-up to an athlete's sport and position. Traditional shoulder scores may tell us how well the shoulder functions, but they are not enough to tell us how well the athlete performs.

title: Longitudinal Changes in Exercise Adherence and Associations with Rehabilitation Outcomes After Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Prospective HAPA-Informed Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exercise adherence is important after total knee arthroplasty (TKA), but its postoperative pattern and behavioral correlates remain unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To characterize exercise adherence and examine its associations with HAPA-related factors and rehabilitation outcomes.
METHODS: This prospective study included 128 patients undergoing unilateral TKA. HAPA-related variables were assessed preoperatively. EARS, VAS, HSS, and range of motion (ROM) were assessed at 1, 3, and 6 months. Linear mixed-effects models, correlations, and regression were used.
RESULTS: EARS scores changed over time (P<0.001), increasing from 17.78±3.27 at 1 month to 18.43±3.64 at 3 months and remaining stable at 6 months (18.36±3.68). Compared with 1 month, EARS was higher at 3 months (difference=0.651, 95% CI 0.340-0.962) and 6 months (difference=0.601, 95% CI 0.290-0.912; both adjusted P<0.001); 3- and 6-month scores did not differ. VAS decreased, whereas HSS and ROM increased (all P<0.001). At 6 months, action self-efficacy (B=0.248, 95% CI 0.065-0.431) and maintenance self-efficacy (B=0.209, 95% CI 0.032-0.387) were independently associated with higher EARS scores. EARS correlated with VAS (r=-0.360), HSS (r=0.326), and ROM (r=0.361; all P<0.001).
CONCLUSION: Exercise adherence improved mainly during the first 3 months and then stabilized. Self-efficacy was associated with adherence, while higher adherence was associated with less pain and better function. These findings do not establish causality.

title: Outcomes of a structured exercise and education program for hip and knee osteoarthritis across different clinical and geographic settings in Australia: A cohort study of 9,938 participants.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: In Australia, the Good Life with osteoArthritis from Denmark (GLA:D®) program is delivered across different settings. This study compared 3-month outcomes by clinic setting (public vs private), geographic location (rural/remote vs metropolitan), and education level among participants with hip and knee osteoarthritis.
DESIGN: This longitudinal registry-based cohort study used GLA:D® Australia registry data for participants enrolled between December 2017 and August 2025. Outcomes included pain, self-reported function, joint-and health-related quality of life, and physical function. Changes were estimated using mixed-effects linear regression.
RESULTS: Of 14,803 participants with baseline data, 9938 (67.1%) were included in complete-case analysis. About 74% attended metropolitan clinics, 84% attended private practices, and 44% had a university degree.At 3-months, participants with knee osteoarthritis attending private clinics had greater improvements compared to those attending public clinics, including pain (worst pain mean difference = -4.8 [95% confidence interval = -6.4 to -3.2]), Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS-12) total (1.7 [0.7 to 2.6]) and KOOS-12 pain subscale scores (2.0 [1.0 to 3.1]). Outcomes did not differ between public and private clinics for hip osteoarthritis, nor by geographical location or education level for hip or knee osteoarthritis.
CONCLUSIONS: Three-month improvements across all examined groups indicate that GLA:D® can deliver benefits in a wide range of settings, without statistically significant differences across geographic location or education level. Participants with knee osteoarthritis attending private clinics showed slightly better outcomes than those in public clinics, though the differences were small and likely not clinically meaningful.

title: Field-Based Assessment of Running Biomechanics Using Global Positioning System/Inertial Measurement Unit: Establishing Construct Validity in Elite Athletes.
abstract: Weber, JA, Peeling, P, Hart, NH, and Newton, RU. Field-based assessment of running biomechanics using global positioning system/inertial measurement unit: Establishing construct validity in elite athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-To examine the between-session reliability and construct validity of global positioning system (GPS)/inertial measurement unit (IMU)-derived biomechanical variables during field-based running in elite athletes. Fifty-four professional male Australian Football League players completed repeated 40-m runs across 1 competitive season (3,943 trials). Running speed for the 20-40 m segment was quantified via 10-Hz GPS and center-of-mass displacement metrics derived from a 100-Hz IMU. Between-session reliability (n = 25, mean (k) = 2.95) was assessed using a linear mixed-effects model with velocity as a fixed covariate, expressed as intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) (absolute agreement), SEM, and minimal detectable change95, with 95% confidence intervals from athlete-cluster bootstrap. Five candidate models were compared; Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines was selected based on lowest cross-validation root mean squared error (RMSE). Validity was assessed over 100 iterations of athlete-stratified cross-validation (80/20 split), with agreement quantified by ICC, RMSE, and athlete-level Bland-Altman analysis. Velocity-adjusted reliability ranged from moderate to good-to-excellent across 12 variables (ICC = 0.65-0.92), with 8 meeting good-to-excellent thresholds (ICC ≥0.75). Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines accounted for 93% of variance in running speed (R2 = 0.93; RMSE = 0.20 m·s-1; ICC = 0.96 ± 0.004). Athlete-level Bland-Altman analysis indicated negligible bias (-0.01 m·s-1; LoA: -0.243 to +0.223 m·s-1) with no proportional bias (p = 0.369); limits narrowed in athletes with adequate data volume (n = 47; -0.207 to +0.189 m·s-1). Mechanics-speed relationships persisted after accounting for within-athlete clustering (residual between-athlete ICC = 0.43), and the most influential predictors were consistent with established biomechanical determinants of speed. These findings support GPS/IMU-derived biomechanical variables as field-based indicators of running mechanics. Pending replication and criterion validation, this approach may offer practitioners an accessible framework for monitoring performance and rehabilitation.

title: Retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes (TRIUMPH-2): a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Retatrutide is an agonist of GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors, and is currently under investigation for the treatment of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other comorbidities, including knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnoea. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes.
METHODS: TRIUMPH-2 was a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial conducted at 92 medical and research centres and hospitals across eight countries. We enrolled adults (aged ≥18 years) with a BMI of 27 kg/m2 or higher and type 2 diabetes (glycated haemoglobin [HbA1c] 6·5-10·5%) on stable treatment for type 2 diabetes for at least 90 days before screening (diet or exercise alone, or up to three oral glucose-lowering medications), and a history of at least one self-reported unsuccessful dietary effort to reduce bodyweight. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1), using an interactive web-response system, to receive once-weekly subcutaneous injections (self-administered) of placebo or retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg. The primary endpoint was the percentage change from baseline to week 80 in bodyweight for the retatrutide 9 mg and 12 mg doses versus placebo, with 4 mg versus placebo a key secondary endpoint. Efficacy analyses included all randomly assigned participants, with missing data imputed with a primary multiple imputation strategy for the treatment regimen estimand. Safety analyses included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of study drug. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05929079 (completed).
FINDINGS: Between July 11, 2023, and Nov 1, 2024, 2047 participants were screened, and 1152 (mean age 55·1 years [SD 10·8], 554 [48%] females and 598 [52%] males, and 672 [58%] of White ethnicity) were randomly assigned to retatrutide 4 mg (n=292), 9 mg (n=284), or 12 mg (n=287), or placebo (n=289). At baseline, the mean BMI was 38·2 kg/m2 (SD 7·4), mean HbA1c was 7·71% (1·07), median duration of obesity was 21 years (IQR 11-31), and median duration of diabetes was 5·6 years (2·6-10·4). At baseline, 1055 (92%) of 1152 participants were on any oral glucose-lowering medication, including biguanides, SGLT2 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, and other oral glucose-lowering medications. Of 1152 participants, 965 (84%) completed the study drug. For the treatment regimen estimand, the mean percentage change from baseline in bodyweight at week 80 was -11·9% (SE 0·6) with retatrutide 4 mg, -16·8% (0·7) with retatrutide 9 mg, -18·8% (0·7) with retatrutide 12 mg, and -5·1% (0·7) with placebo. Estimated treatment differences compared with placebo for percentage change in bodyweight were -6·9% (95% CI -8·7 to -5·1) with retatrutide 4 mg, -11·8% (-13·7 to -9·8) with retatrutide 9 mg, and -13·8% (-15·8 to -11·8) with retatrutide 12 mg (p<0·0001 for all). The most frequently reported adverse events were gastrointestinal, which were more common in the retatrutide groups than in the placebo group (diarrhoea occurred in 80 [27%] of 292 participants in the 4 mg group, 95 [34%] of 284 in the 9 mg group, and 96 [34%] of 286 in the 12 mg group vs 38 [13%] of 287 in the placebo group, and nausea occurred in 40 [14%], 59 [21%], and 80 [28%] vs 23 [8%]). Hypotension and dysesthesia were more frequent with retatrutide than with placebo (four [1%] in the 4 mg group, 14 [5%] in the 9 mg group, and 18 (6%) in the 12 mg group vs one [<1%] in the placebo group with hypotension; 13 [4%], 16 [6%], and 21 [7%] vs two [1%] in the placebo group with dysesthesia). Permanent treatment discontinuation due to adverse events or death was more frequent in participants treated with retatrutide 9 mg (33 [12%]) and 12 mg (22 [8%]) compared with retatrutide 4 mg (11 [4%]) and placebo (14 [5%]). Two participants died in the retatrutide 4 mg group, three in the 9 mg group, one in the 12 mg group, and one in the placebo group; all deaths were deemed to be unrelated to the study intervention by the investigator.
INTERPRETATION: Treatment with retatrutide resulted in substantial improvements in bodyweight and was associated with improvements in glycaemic control in participants with obesity and type 2 diabetes, with a safety profile generally consistent with other molecules with GLP-1 receptor agonism. These results show that retatrutide might be effective for the treatment of obesity in people with type 2 diabetes.

title: Effects of acute Capsaicin analogue intake on athletic performance: a three-level meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Capsaicin analogues have been proposed as potential ergogenic aids, but their acute effects on athletic performance remain inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of acute capsaicin analogue intake on exercise performance using a three-level meta-analysis.
METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and the Cochrane Library were searched up to April 1, 2025. Randomized controlled trials examining acute oral capsaicin analogue intake in healthy adults were included. Outcomes were classified into strength, power, muscular endurance, and aerobic capacity. Hedges' g was calculated using a three-level random-effects model.
RESULTS: Twenty-one randomized crossover trials with 67 effect sizes were included. Acute capsaicin analogue intake significantly improved overall athletic performance compared with placebo (g = 0.20, 95% CI [0.07, 0.33], p < 0.01). Subgroup analyses showed significant effects on power (g = 0.39) and muscular endurance (g = 0.25), but not on strength or aerobic capacity. Phenylcapsaicin showed the largest effect, and benefits were more evident in trained participants. Dose-response analysis suggested a nonlinear pattern, with low-to-moderate doses showing more stable benefits.
CONCLUSIONS: Acute capsaicin analogue intake may produce small but significant improvements in athletic performance, particularly in power and muscular endurance. However, due to heterogeneity, publication bias, and very low certainty of evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

title: Effects of carbon dioxide hydrate cryotherapy on knee flexor muscle function recovery trajectory after muscle damage: a randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: This study investigated the effects of carbon dioxide hydrate (CDH) cryotherapy on the recovery trajectories of muscle function and physiological markers following exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) of the knee flexors.
METHODS: In a randomized parallel-group design, 24 young men were assigned to the CDH, conventional icing (ICE), or non-intervention control (CON) group (n = 8 per group). To induce muscle damage, participants performed 10 sets of eight maximal eccentric contractions of the knee flexors in a prone position (knee joint range: 75°-15° of flexion at 60°/s; 0° = the fully extended anatomical position). Maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) torque of the knee flexors was measured at 30° of knee flexion at baseline (PRE), immediately post-exercise (POST), and at 4.5, 24, 48, 72, and 168 h post-exercise. Secondary outcomes, including thigh circumference, hip joint range of motion (ROM), and hamstring muscle stiffness and pressure-induced soreness were assessed at all time points except POST. A 20-min intervention was administered after each assessment from POST to 72 h.
RESULTS: Linear mixed-effects models, adjusted for PRE values, revealed no significant group × time interactions for changes from PRE in any outcome across post-exercise time points (POST to 168 h for MVIC torque; 4.5 to 168 h for secondary outcomes; p = 0.177-0.914). A significant main effect of group was observed only for hip joint ROM (p = 0.039). Post-hoc comparisons revealed a significantly greater overall reduction from PRE in the CDH group than in the CON group (difference: 10.3°, 95% CI: 3.0° to 17.6°, p = 0.017), with no significant differences between the other group pairs (both p = 0.131). Given the multi-outcome testing, this isolated effect should be interpreted as exploratory.
CONCLUSION: Under the present experimental conditions, CDH cryotherapy did not accelerate the recovery of muscle function or attenuate secondary markers following EIMD relative to conventional icing or no intervention.

title: Neurophysiological and neuromuscular responses associated with the repeated bout effect following eccentric exercise in healthy adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Muscle damage severity decreases after repeated eccentric exercise bouts (the repeated bout effect [RBE]), but whether accompanying neural and neuromuscular changes contribute to protection or arise secondary to reduced damage remains unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis compared neurophysiological and neuromuscular responses between initial and repeated eccentric bouts in healthy adults. Eight databases were searched from November 1990 to January 2025, and Hedges' g was calculated where outcomes were comparable. Given the small number of contributing studies, all pooled analyses were considered exploratory. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria. Twitch/evoked force showed recovery-compatible point estimates at 24 h (g = 1.02, 95% CI -0.03-2.06) and 48 h (g = 0.50, 95% CI 0.08-0.92). Voluntary activation findings were mixed. TMS-derived voluntary activation produced positive single-study estimates at 24 h (g = 1.10, 95% CI 0.29-1.92) and 48 h (g = 1.06, 95% CI 0.26-1.87), whereas pooled ITT-derived estimates were imprecise at 24 h (g = 0.36, 95% CI -0.92-1.63) and recovery-compatible but based on only two studies at 48 h (g = 0.44, 95% CI 0.03-0.85). M-wave/Mmax showed no consistent between-bout pattern. Corticospinal, intracortical, spinal, reticulospinal, motor-unit and EMG findings were limited, inconsistent or directionally unclear. Neural and neuromuscular changes accompany the RBE, but whether they contribute to protection or reflect reduced damage remains unresolved. Peripheral contractile outcomes showed the most consistent recovery-compatible pattern, whereas evidence concerning central activation and motor-unit behaviour remained limited or inconsistent.

title: Short-term Rhodiola rosea supplementation improves premenstrual symptoms, reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Premenstrual symptoms may negatively influence psychological readiness, cognitive-motor performance, and perceived exertion in female athletes. Rhodiola rosea (RR) is an adaptogenic herb that has been investigated for its potential effects on fatigue, stress tolerance, mood, and exercise-related outcomes. However, its effects on premenstrual symptoms and performance-related responses in female athletes remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase on premenstrual symptoms, peripheral serum serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations, reaction time, perceived exertion, and aerobic performance-related indices in female taekwondo athletes with premenstrual syndrome (PMS).
METHODS: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 female taekwondo athletes with moderate-to-severe PMS symptoms were randomly assigned to receive either 500 mg/day of standardised RR extract (n = 12) or placebo (n = 12) for 10 days during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase. Premenstrual symptoms were assessed using the Premenstrual Symptoms Screening Tool (PSST). Visual reaction time, peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations, time to exhaustion (TTE), estimated VO₂max, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were evaluated before and after the intervention. Data were analysed using analysis of covariance with baseline values as covariates.
RESULTS: Compared with placebo, RR supplementation significantly reduced several PMS symptoms, including irritability, depression, anxiety, social withdrawal, decreased concentration, hypersomnia, food cravings, crying, skin problems, and abdominal pain (p < 0.05). The RR group demonstrated faster reaction time compared with placebo (adjusted mean difference: -60 ms; p < 0.001). Peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations were significantly higher in the RR group than in the placebo group (p < 0.001). In addition, RR supplementation reduced post-exercise RPE (adjusted mean difference: -1.40 Borg units; p = 0.006). However, no significant differences were observed between groups in TTE or estimated VO₂max (p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase may improve selected PMS symptoms, visual reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes with PMS. Larger trials with hormonal confirmation of menstrual cycle phase, longer intervention periods, direct physiological measurements, and sport-specific performance assessments are required to confirm these findings.

title: Photobiomodulation versus ischemic preconditioning for protection against exercise-induced muscle damage: protocol for a randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) occurs after unaccustomed eccentric exercise and may impair muscle recovery. Preconditioning with photobiomodulation (PBM) or ischemic preconditioning (IPC) may mitigate EIMD; however, no study has directly compared their effectiveness. This study aims to compare the effects of PBM and IPC applied prior to eccentric exercise on indirect markers of EIMD and associated perceptual responses. We hypothesized that MVIC trajectories would differ among the PBM, IPC, and sham groups, with PBM expected to provide greater preservation of MVIC than IPC. A prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial with concealed allocation, blinded outcome assessors and statistician, and intention-to-treat analysis will be conducted. Healthy men (18-35 years) will be randomly allocated to PBM, IPC, or sham groups (n = 15 per group). After the intervention, participants will perform an eccentric exercise protocol for the elbow flexors consisting of 30 repetitions using a dumbbell load numerically matched to maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) values, with 45-second rest intervals. The primary outcome will be MVIC. Secondary outcomes include rate of force development, delayed-onset muscle soreness, pressure pain threshold, ultrasound echo intensity, range of motion, perceived exertion, and affective responses. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, immediately after exercise (only MVIC), and at 24-, 48-, and 72-hours post-exercise. The primary analysis will assess the group × time interaction on MVIC using linear mixed-effects models, while secondary outcomes will be analyzed exploratorily. This study will provide, to our knowledge, the first direct comparison between PBM and IPC as preconditioning strategies to attenuate EIMD. The findings may help determine the most effective and clinically applicable intervention by considering both physiological and perceptual responses, thereby supporting decision-making in clinical and sports settings.Trial registrationBrazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (REBEC), RBR-6gr5kf; registered February 19, 2020; amended August 26, 2026.

title: Characterizing accuracy, retention, and dose-response of an 18-session real-time gait biofeedback program following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Individuals following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) commonly demonstrate aberrant walking biomechanics, characterized by a lesser first peak vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) during early stance. Gait biofeedback may address this deficit; however, the accuracy, retention, and dose-response characteristics of repeated training remain unclear.
METHODS: Thirteen individuals (8 females and 5 males; age 22.4 ± 3.4 years; 32.6 ± 18.7 months post-ACLR) completed 18 gait biofeedback sessions over 6 weeks. Participants completed rehabilitation and exhibited involved limb first peak vGRF ≤1.12 body weight (BW) during baseline assessment of treadmill walking. Bilateral, step-by-step visual biofeedback targeted a first peak vGRF of 1.15 BW. Feedback was continuous during sessions 1-10 and was partially tapered thereafter. Outcomes included first peak vGRF target accuracy, defined as the percentage of steps within ±1% of the 1.15 BW target, first peak vGRF during retention, and the estimated training dose required to achieve target loading.
FINDINGS: First peak vGRF target accuracy increased in both limbs from ∼13% during session 1 and plateaued by session 12 (20-25%). Retention testing of the involved limb showed significantly higher first peak vGRF than baseline beginning at session 3, with these improvements maintained through session 18. The median effective dose to achieve target loading was 5 sessions (95% confidence interval: 3-14 sessions).
INTERPRETATION: Bilateral first peak vGRF target accuracy improved across training, while involved-limb improvements were retained before completing the 18-session protocol. These findings support the feasibility of shorter gait biofeedback regimens and provide clinically relevant dosing parameters to inform future clinical trials.

title: Feasibility and Preliminary Effects of AI-Generated Personalized Sleep Feedback in High School Female Soccer Players: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adequate sleep supports mood regulation and injury prevention in high school female athletes; however, insufficient sleep is common in this population. Wearable devices enable continuous assessment of objective sleep metrics, but personalized feedback based on daily sleep data remains underexplored.
OBJECTIVE: This study evaluated the technical and operational feasibility of a multicomponent AI-supported mobile health (mHealth) intervention that delivered personalized sleep feedback to high school female soccer players. Sleep efficiency was the primary preliminary efficacy outcome; other sleep-related measures were secondary or exploratory outcomes, and mood state and sports injury severity were exploratory outcomes.
METHODS: We conducted a pilot randomized controlled trial among 25 high school female soccer players from a single team. The study briefing and system setup began on August 18, 2025, and the trial was retrospectively registered with the University Hospital Medical Information Network (UMIN) Clinical Trials Registry on April 7, 2026 (UMIN000061189). Weeks 1 to 4 constituted the baseline period. After the week 5 baseline questionnaires, participants were stratified by median baseline total sleep time (TST) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index score and randomly allocated 1:1 to the intervention (n=12) or control (n=13) group. During weeks 6 to 9, the intervention group received GPT-4o-generated personalized feedback via LINE on days with valid prior-night Fitbit data, whereas the control group received daily nonpersonalized sleep information. Technical and operational feasibility outcomes included message delivery success, valid Fitbit wear nights, questionnaire completion, technical problems, adverse events, and privacy breaches. Secondary outcomes included TST, wake after sleep onset (WASO), subjective sleep quality, sleep difficulty, and daytime sleepiness. Deep, light, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep durations, mood state, and sports injury severity were exploratory outcomes.
RESULTS: All 25 participants completed the trial. Message delivery success and questionnaire completion were 100% in both groups. Median valid Fitbit wear nights were 26 (IQR 24-28) in the intervention group and 22 (IQR 15-26) in the control group. No major technical problems, adverse events, or privacy breaches occurred. Change in sleep efficiency, the primary preliminary efficacy outcome, favored the intervention group (Hodges-Lehmann between-group difference 2%, 95% CI 0.50%-4%; P=.046; r=0.35). Nominal between-group differences were also observed for the Japanese version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI-J) total score and sleep difficulty score and, among exploratory outcomes, REM sleep duration and total mood disturbance. No between-group differences were observed in TST, WASO, deep or light sleep duration, daytime sleepiness, or sports injury severity.
CONCLUSIONS: The multicomponent AI-supported mHealth intervention demonstrated technical and operational feasibility in this single-team setting. Preliminary, hypothesis-generating between-group differences were observed in sleep efficiency and selected subjective sleep and mood outcomes. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence of established effectiveness and require confirmation in a sufficiently powered trial.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: UMIN Clinical Trials Registry UMIN000061189; https://tinyurl.com/tw3d7aku.

title: Effects of an 8-week core-strength program on smash accuracy in female badminton athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: To investigate the effects of an 8-week core-strength training program on smash accuracy in female badminton athletes.
METHODS: Forty female badminton players were randomly assigned to an experimental group (EG) and a control group (CG). Both groups continued regular badminton training, while the EG additionally completed an 8-week structured core-strength program. Smash accuracy was assessed under three conditions - stationary, jumping, and moving smashes - at baseline, mid-intervention (posttest 1), and post-intervention (posttest 2). Data were analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) to examine group effects, time effects, and group × time interactions, with age, training experience, height, and body mass included as covariates.
RESULTS: GEE analysis revealed significant group, time, and group × time interaction effects for in situ, jumping, and moving smash accuracy (p < 0.05). Post hoc analyses showed that the EG demonstrated significant improvements in smash accuracy from baseline to posttest 2 across all three smash conditions, whereas improvements in the CG were limited or non-significant. Effect size analysis further indicated that the magnitude of improvement in smash accuracy was substantially greater in the EG than in the CG. None of the covariates showed a significant influence on smash accuracy outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: An 8-week core-strength training program significantly enhances in situ, jumping, and moving smash accuracy in female badminton athletes. These findings highlight the importance of core stability and strength in optimizing technical performance and suggest that systematic core training should be incorporated into routine badminton training programs to improve smash accuracy and overall competitive performance.

title: Sciatic nerve involvement is associated with longer return to sport in collegiate American football players with acute hamstring injuries.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To assess if the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) grade and sciatic nerve involvement on MRI at time of hamstring strain injury (HSI) were associated with the time to return-to-sport (RTS) in National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I American football players.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Data were collected via a larger prospective cohort investigation of collegiate football players who sustained an HSI. MRIs at time of injury were assessed by a musculoskeletal radiologist using BAMIC. Sciatic nerve involvement was characterised by extent of adjacent oedema on MRI as no contact, partial (contacted by oedema) or complete (circumferentially surrounded by oedema). Spearman rank correlations, mixed-effects modelling and χ2 analyses were used to determine associations between imaging characteristics, HSI severity and days missed before RTS.
RESULTS: 96 unique HSI were included (100% male, mean age 20±1.58 years). Increasing BAMIC grade was associated with longer time to RTS (r=0.29, p=0.004). Sciatic nerve involvement was observed in 75/96 (78.1%) cases (35/96 (36.5%) partial, 40/96 (41.7%) complete), and no sciatic nerve involvement in 21/96 (21.9%) cases. There was a significant positive association between sciatic nerve involvement as BAMIC grade increased (p<0.001). While controlling for BAMIC grade, complete nerve involvement was associated with significantly longer time to RTS (33.7±20.0 days, p=0.01) compared with no involvement (21.5±14.8 days) and partial involvement (23.9±16.3 days, p=0.01). Partial sciatic nerve involvement (23.9±16.3 days, p=0.59) did not result in significantly longer RTS compared with no involvement.
CONCLUSIONS: Increasing radiologic severity, indicated by BAMIC grade and complete sciatic nerve involvement were associated with longer RTS following HSI. Sciatic nerve involvement on MRI should be considered in the assessment of acute HSI.

title: Association Between Early Postoperative Limb Symmetry Index Scores and 2-Year Patient-Reported Outcomes After Quadriceps Tendon Autograft ACL Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The limb symmetry index (LSI) is a measure comparing strength and functional movement between the surgical and nonsurgical limbs, used after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) to guide rehabilitation and assess return-to-sport readiness. With increasing use of the quadriceps tendon autograft (QT-ACLR), limited data exist on whether the LSI score correlates with patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).
HYPOTHESIS/PURPOSE: To evaluate the predictive value of postoperative strength and functional LSI tests at 3, 6, and 9 months for short-term PROMs, determine Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) thresholds, and assess differences based on PASS achievement. It was hypothesized that quadriceps strength LSI score would more strongly predict 2-year PROMs than hamstring strength LSI score, and that higher 9-month isokinetic quadriceps LSI scores would be associated with higher International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) and Lysholm scores.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
METHODS: Patients undergoing primary QT-ACLR from 2021 to 2024 with LSI testing during rehabilitation (isometric and isokinetic lower extremity strength, Y-Balance, hop testing) and no revision or additional knee surgery were included. The LSI score was assessed at 3, 6, and 9 months, and PROMs, including Lysholm and IKDC scores, were collected at a mean follow-up of 2.0 ± 0.7 years. Multivariable linear regression was used to evaluate associations between LSI measures and PROMs after adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index (BMI). Receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to determine PASS thresholds.
RESULTS: A total of 100 knees in 100 patients (mean age, 25.3 ± 11.2 years; BMI, 25.9 ± 6.5 kg/m2; 52% male) were included. Quadriceps and hamstring strength and functional performance progressively improved from 3 to 9 months, with the LSI score reaching 77% to 81% for quadriceps strength and 98% to 100% for hamstring strength by 9 months postoperatively. At a mean follow-up of 2.0 ± 0.7 years, the mean satisfaction score was 8.4 of 10, the Lysholm score was 90.7, and the IKDC score was 77.8. Linear regression, adjusted for age, sex, and BMI, demonstrated that 3-month isometric quadriceps LSI score had a strong effect on IKDC score, explaining substantial variance (β = 3.9; adjusted R2 [AdjR2] = 0.36; P < .03); 6-month isokinetic quadriceps and hamstrings showed moderate but significant effects (β = 2.9-3.7; AdjR2 = 0.13-0.17; P < .05) on IKDC score; and 9-month fast quadriceps had a strong effect explaining substantial variance in Lysholm and IKDC scores (β = 3.9-4.7; AdjR2 = 0.34-0.35; P ≤ .003). Lysholm and IKDC scores correlated with satisfaction and accurately discriminated PASS thresholds (area under the curve, 0.927-0.937; P < .001). Patients achieving the IKDC PASS demonstrated higher LSI scores across time points and all PROMs.
CONCLUSION: After QT-ACLR, strength-associated LSIs were independently associated with PROMs at a mean 2-year follow-up, after adjusting for age, sex, and BMI. Early isometric quadriceps strength at 3 months predicted higher 2-year IKDC scores, with PASS achievers generally attaining a 60% to 70% LSI score by 3 months. Isokinetic quadriceps strength at 9 months predicted both IKDC and Lysholm scores. These findings highlight the importance of early quadriceps strength recovery and the value of LSI measures in predicting PROMs and informing early rehabilitation.

title: The longitudinal relationship between physical capacity and self-perceived physical functioning after total hip and knee arthroplasty.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine longitudinal within-person effects between capacity and self-perceived performance during postoperative physiotherapy in patients with total hip and knee arthroplasty (THA/TKA).
METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial on physiotherapy after THA and TKA using random intercept cross lagged panel models. Capacity was assessed with the 40-m fast-paced walk test (40 m FPWT) and the 30-s chair-stand test (30-s CST), and self-perceived performance with the Oxford Hip/Knee Score functioning subscale (OHS/OKS) and the Hip disability/Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score-Physical function Short form (HOOS-PS/KOOS-PS). Assessments were performed preoperatively and at 3 and 12 months postoperatively.
RESULTS: 312 THA (mean age 66, SD: 9; 53% female) and 312 TKA (mean age 67, SD: 8; 55% female) were included. From pre-surgery to 3 months, no effects were found between capacity and self-perceived performance in either THA or TKA.From 3 to 12 months, in THA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect (β 0.34, 95% CI 0.05-0.63) on HOOS-PS scores at 12 months. In TKA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect on both OKS functioning (β 0.24 95% CI 0.05-0.43) and KOOS-PS (β 0.29 95% CI 0.11-0.47) scores at 12 months. No other effects were observed.
CONCLUSION: From pre-surgery to 3 months, capacity and self-perceived performance showed no effects within individuals. However, during the early postoperative phase, gait speed may be a relevant treatment target to improve long-term self-perceived performance.

title: Efficacy of a Meta-Analysis-Recommended Immersion Protocol vs. Field-Practical Cold-Water Immersion Protocol for Performance Recovery: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
abstract: Kaji, R, Takeuchi, K, Okubo, S, and Yoshida, N. Efficacy of a meta-analysis-recommended immersion protocol vs. field-practical cold-water immersion protocol for performance recovery: A randomized crossover trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-We examined the effects of 2 cold-water immersion (CWI) protocols-15° C for 11 minutes and 10° C for 2.5 minutes-on performance recovery following exercise-induced fatigue. Fifteen male collegiate athletes completed 3 randomized crossover conditions with a 2-week washout: 15° C-11 minutes (evidence-based method), 10° C-2.5 minutes (field-practical method), and a seated-rest control. Outcomes included 20-m sprint time (T20), countermovement jump (CMJ), and Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 2 (YYIR2). The 20-m sprint time and CMJ were assessed before exercise (PreEx), immediately after exercise, immediately after the intervention, and at 1, 24, 48, and 72 hours postintervention, whereas YYIR2 was assessed at PreEx and at 72 hours postintervention. Physiological measures (tympanic temperature, skin temperatures, and heart rate) and perceptual measures (subjective fatigue and muscle soreness) were recorded. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. The 10° C-2.5-minute protocol maintained T20 performance during the acute phase, whereas the 15° C-11-minute protocol facilitated later recovery. Countermovement jump performance transiently declined under both CWI conditions; however, a significant improvement at 72 hours occurred only with the 10° C-2.5-minute protocol. Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 2 performance did not differ between conditions. Thermal and cardiovascular responses varied by protocol and reflected recovery patterns. Subjective fatigue improved in both CWI conditions, whereas muscle soreness showed minimal differences. In conclusion, both evidence-based and field-practical CWI protocols enhanced recovery; however, they demonstrated distinct temporal profiles. The 10° C-2.5-minute protocol supported immediate restoration, whereas the 15° C-11-minute protocol promoted delayed recovery. For practical applications, protocol selection should align with sport-specific demands, recovery time, and performance objectives.

title: The Potential Impact of Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors on Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness: A Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are widely prescribed for mood disorders. Their association with musculoskeletal side effects raises the question of potential SSRI impact on exercise-induced muscle damage and recovery.
OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this prospective cohort study was to determine if SSRI use influences muscle function following a bout of eccentric exercise designed to induce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS).
METHODS: Subjects between 18 and 30 years of age were recruited in a university setting. This included 1 group taking SSRIs prescribed by their health care provider, and a control group not using SSRIs. Subjects performed a DOMS induction protocol consisting of 300 eccentric knee extensions on an isokinetic dynamometer. Muscle soreness, thigh circumference, quadriceps flexibility, and isometric quadriceps strength were measured at baseline and at 24-, 48-, 72-, and 96-hour post-DOMS protocol. Comparisons were made between SSRI users and control subjects.
RESULTS: Thirty-six subjects included 18 SSRI users and 18 controls. The DOMS protocol induced muscle soreness in both groups (P < .001 when compared with baseline). At 72 hours a between-group difference was observed for thigh muscle flexibility (MD = 11.2, SE = 5.0, 95% CI [0.9, 21.4], P = .033, ηp2 = .126) but no additional significant between-group differences in soreness, strength, thigh circumference, or flexibility were noted at any timepoint.
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this population, SSRI use had no effect on muscle soreness, circumference, or strength of the quadriceps following eccentric DOMS-inducing exercise. A difference in flexibility between SSRI and control groups at a single time point likely reflects a Type 1 error and is not likely of clinical consequence. These findings suggest SSRIs do not impair short-term recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage in healthy young adults, but potential SSRI impacts on longer-term training adaptations and recovery in athletic populations remain unknown.
