title: Sport-related Concussion Characteristics and Time-loss Among Male and Female Community Rugby Union Players Across 6 Seasons.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sport-related concussion (SRC) is a common injury in Rugby Union. There is currently a paucity of prospective research in SRC specific data in both male and female community Rugby Union players, which may restrict SRC prevention, recognition, and management practices.
HYPOTHESIS: Adult community SRC injuries would be common in match-play, forward players, and in the tackle event, alongside increased time-loss following SRC in female players.
STUDY DESIGN: Prospective cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2.
METHODS: Data were collected across 6 seasons between 2017/18 and 2023/24, from 5740 male and female player-seasons registered with the Irish Rugby Injury Surveillance system. SRC injury data included player demographics, setting (match, training), mechanism of injury, timing occurrence, and time-loss.
RESULTS: Of the 456 reported SRCs, 93.9% occurred on match days and 6.1% during training. SRCs reported during matches were more likely to occur during the second half (males 63.5% [95% CI 58.5%, 68.4%]; females 72.1% [95% CI 58.7%, 85.5%]). For male players, most match-day SRCs occurred when tackling 55.9% (95% CI 50.9%, 60.8%), compared to more evenly distributed mechanisms observed in females (tackling 38.6%; being tackled 29.5%; ruck 18.2%). Severe SRC time-loss injuries (>28 days absence) were significantly more likely in female players compared with male players (46% vs 30%; P = 0.013). Annual SRC prevalence ranged from 4.0% to 9.7% for male players and 3.1% to 7.0% for female players across the 6 seasons.
CONCLUSION: In adult community Rugby Union most recorded SRCs occurred during the tackle event, match-play, and were more likely to occur in the second half. Female players may be more at risk for greater time-loss following SRC than male players.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Sports medicine staff, coaches, and players should be aware of match time and mechanism of injury (eg, tackling) when SRCs are more likely to occur, alongside the potential increased time-loss risk in female players, to support SRC recognition and recovery.

title: Training exposure, recovery, and injury incidence among course-based and competitive university Wushu Taolu practitioners: a 12-week prospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether the large training-exposure difference between course-based and competitive-team university Wushu Taolu practitioners in China translates into a correspondingly different musculoskeletal health burden has not been well characterized prospectively.
METHODS: In this observational, non-randomized cohort study, 255 practitioners (128 course-based, 127 university-team; mean age 20.7 ± 1.5) were followed over four waves (T0-T3) across 12 weeks, with training load, sleep, recovery, health problems, and injury recorded using recall windows matched to each variable's time-scale.
RESULTS: University-team practitioners had substantially higher training exposure than course-based practitioners. The 12-week cumulative incidence of new injury was substantially higher in university-team practitioners than in course-based practitioners (68.9% vs. 20.0%; p < 0.001), with higher adjusted odds of injury (OR = 6.31, 95% CI 1.49-26.69). However, when injury occurrence was expressed relative to estimated training exposure, the between-group difference was much smaller: 10.56 versus 8.98 positive new-injury person-wave observations per 1,000 estimated training hours, respectively (IRR = 1.18, 95% CI 0.79-1.75). Prior injury within the preceding 12 months was strongly associated with subsequent injury (OR = 4.06, 95% CI 2.03-8.13).
CONCLUSION: University-team practitioners experienced a substantially greater absolute injury burden than course-based practitioners, whereas the between-group difference was much smaller when injury occurrence was expressed relative to estimated training exposure. Prior injury history was a strong marker of subsequent injury. Because group membership and training exposure were highly correlated and the study was observational, these findings should not be interpreted causally.

title: Determinants of Psychological Readiness to Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Psychological and physical factors influence recovery after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction (ACLR). However, the relative contributions of psychological, subjective, and objective recovery measures to psychological readiness for return to sport remain unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To identify psychological, subjective, and objective recovery factors associated with psychological readiness to return to sport approximately 6 months after ACLR.
DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
SETTING: University laboratory.
PATIENTS OR OTHER PARTICIPANTS: A total of 58 participants (31 [53%] females; age = 18.95 ± 5.20 years), who completed standardized postoperative rehabilitation and follow-up testing at approximately 6 months after primary unilateral ACLR, were included.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: We measured psychological readiness using the ACL-Return to Sport after Injury (ACL-RSI) scale and conducted hierarchical regression analyses to examine predictors of psychological readiness across 4 conceptually ordered domains: (1) demographics (age, sex, and time since surgery), (2) generalized anxiety (Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Anxiety Scale) and kinesiophobia (Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia 11), (3) knee-specific patient-reported outcomes (Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcomes Scale [KOOS] subscales of Pain, Symptoms, Quality of Life [QoL], and Sport), and (4) objective functional measures (quadriceps strength and single-legged hop symmetry). We conducted hierarchical linear regression in conceptually ordered blocks.
RESULTS: Demographic factors explained minimal variance in psychological readiness (1%-4%). Generalized anxiety contributed an additional 18.1%, and kinesiophobia (Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia 11, 22.3%), QoL (KOOS-QoL, 9.8%), and subjective sport function (KOOS-Sport, 5.3%) emerged as the strongest incremental predictors. Pain, symptoms, and objective function contributed little additional variance. The full model explained 70.5% of the variance in ACL-RSI scores (adjusted R 2 = 0.64, P < .001), and cross-validation produced a comparable R 2 (0.61), indicating good model generalizability and minimal overfitting.
CONCLUSIONS: Fear-related beliefs and perceived function exerted stronger influences on psychological readiness after ACLR than objective functional symmetry. These findings highlight the importance of biopsychosocial assessment models and sport-specific psychological measures to enhance return-to-sport decision-making and long-term recovery outcomes.

title: Strategic Application of Post-exercise Cold-Water Immersion to Enhance Performance Recovery and Adaptation: An Umbrella Review of 15 Published Systematic Reviews with Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletes commonly implement post-exercise cold-water immersion (CWI), with several meta-analyses having assessed its effectiveness.
OBJECTIVES: To thoroughly review, appraise, and summarise existing systematic reviews with meta-analyses (SRMA) examining the effects of post-exercise CWI on the recovery of exercise performance and adaptation.
METHODS: An umbrella review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines. Methodological quality was assessed using AMSTAR 2, and certainty of evidence using GRADE. PROSPERO registration: (CRD420251103267). Eight databases were searched, including Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Embase, MEDLINE, and PubMed. Systematic reviews with meta-analyses of peer-reviewed randomised controlled trials examining post-exercise CWI vs passive rest or other recovery modalities on performance, training adaptation, or physiological, biochemical, and perceptual outcomes in healthy humans were included, with restriction to the English language.
RESULTS: Fifteen SRMAs published between 2011 and 2025, comprising 161 unique studies, were included. Overall methodological quality was low to critically low, and certainty of evidence was low to very low, mainly due to inconsistency and imprecision. Protocols of 10-15 min at 10-15 or 5-10 °C appear to be most effective for improving performance and recovery. Post-exercise CWI resulted in significant improvements in muscular power at 24 h post-high-intensity exercise and at 24-48 h post-eccentric exercise, and in jump performance at 24-48 h, despite impaired jump performance in the initial hours after post-exercise CWI. Endurance performance improved immediately after CWI, but CWI produced no later benefits or positive effects on adaptations. CWI did not improve muscular strength performance, and impaired strength and hypertrophic gains. CWI improved heart rate variability immediately after exercise, reduced muscle soreness up to 96 h, and lowered creatine kinase (CK) concentrations between 24 and 72 h, with no significant effects on C-reactive protein or interleukin-6 up to 72 h. No immediate impact on blood lactate or lactate dehydrogenase was found, although some reductions appear 24-72 h post-exercise.
CONCLUSIONS: Post-exercise CWI confers outcome-specific recovery benefits but may impair resistance training adaptations with chronic use. These findings support a periodised, context-driven approach to CWI implementation rather than routine application after all exercise sessions.

title: Effects of high-intensity resistance training within concurrent training programs on athletic performance in elite athletes: a systematic review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effects of high-intensity resistance training (HIRT), operationally defined as resistance protocols utilizing loads ≥ 75% of one-repetition maximum (1RM), on athletic performance outcomes-including muscular strength, power, jumping performance, speed, preplanned change-of-direction (COD) speed, and endurance-among elite athletes.
METHODS: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic search was conducted in Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus to identify studies that applied HIRT in elite athlete populations. Google Scholar was additionally utilized for forward and backward citation tracking. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria and were assessed using the PEDro scale. Data on intervention characteristics, testing protocols, and performance outcomes were extracted and synthesized narratively.
RESULTS: HIRT interventions (range: 5-18 weeks) demonstrated significant improvements in maximal strength (e.g., squat and bench press 1RM) and neuromuscular power-related outcomes across the majority of studies. Improvements in sprint speed, sport-specific velocity, and preplanned COD speed were also observed, although evidence for COD performance was limited to a single study. Endurance-related outcomes, including time to exhaustion, movement economy, and selected time-trial measures, generally favored HIRT, with no clear evidence of detrimental effects on aerobic-capacity-related outcomes. However, all included studies implemented HIRT within concurrent training programs rather than as an isolated intervention.
CONCLUSIONS: The available evidence suggests that HIRT may be an effective training component for improving strength, power, and selected performance outcomes in elite athletes when integrated into concurrent sport-specific training programs. The strongest support was observed for maximal strength and neuromuscular power, whereas evidence for preplanned COD speed remains preliminary and requires replication. Given the concurrent training designs, the absence of a formal GRADE assessment, and the generally small sample sizes, these findings should be interpreted as likely low-to-moderate certainty evidence rather than as proof of the isolated effects of HIRT. The review protocol was prospectively registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) on 6 January 2025 (Registration No.: CRD42025634254).

title: Rehabilitation of Athletes With Hamstring Strain Injury: SONAFE-Brazil Clinical Practice Guideline.
abstract: SYNOPSIS: The National Society of Sports Physical Therapy (SONAFE-Brazil), the official organization representing sports physical therapists in Brazil, developed this clinical practice guideline to support clinicians and athletes in managing hamstring strain injury. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach was used to address the clinical question "Which interventions provided by physical therapists improve rehabilitation outcomes in athletes with hamstring strain injury?" The guideline provides an updated and targeted synthesis of evidence from randomized clinical trials, offering practical guidance to inform clinical decision making by physical therapists across diverse health care and sports settings. title: Effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate on exercise-induced biomarkers of muscle damage and inflammation in federated road cyclists.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial examined the effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate (CPH) on biomarkers associated with exercise-induced muscle damage and inflammation in federated male road cyclists.
METHODS: Twenty-four participants completed a 14-day intervention receiving either 12 g/day of chickpea protein hydrolysate (EXP) or a placebo (PLA) following training sessions. The selected dose was based on previous studies demonstrating antioxidant and immunomodulatory bioactive properties of the hydrolysate. Nutritional intake and training were registered. Body composition and biochemical markers of muscle damage and inflammation were assessed before and after the study.
RESULTS: No significant differences were observed in body composition, training load, or dietary intake between groups, indicating controlled experimental conditions. However, between-group analyses of change scores revealed significant differences for lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; p = 0.04) and C-reactive protein (CRP; p = 0.02), favoring the experimental group. LDH decreased in the EXP group while increasing slightly in the placebo group, whereas CRP decreased in EXP and increased in PLA. Although creatine kinase (CK) showed a favorable pattern in the EXP group, the between-group comparison did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.062). Myoglobin followed a similar downward trend. The high baseline protein intake (>2 g/kg/day) and short intervention duration may have limited changes in body composition, nevertheless, the observed biomarker responses suggest that CPH supplementation may influence selected physiological processes associated with exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress.
CONCLUSIONS: In trained cyclists with high habitual protein intakes, 14 days of CPH supplementation did not alter body composition but was associated with favorable changes in selected biomarkers related to exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress compared with placebo. Given the short intervention period and the absence of direct assessments of recovery or performance, these findings should be interpreted as short-term biochemical responses. Further studies are required to determine their physiological relevance and whether these biomarker changes translate into meaningful improvements in recovery, training adaptation, or athletic performance.

title: Evaluation, Management, and Return-To-Sport Guidelines for Cervical Spine Injuries in Athletes: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Study DesignNarrative review.ObjectivesTo synthesize current evidence on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, classification, evaluation, and imaging of cervical spine injuries (CSI) in athletes and propose a practical framework for return-to-sport (RTS) decision-making.MethodsA review of the most recent and relevant published studies and consensus statements was performed, focusing on athletic cervical spine pathology. Key domains included on-field assessment, imaging modalities, clinical clearance criteria, and sport-specific risk considerations. All literature published in reputable journals, preferably available through well-regarded databases such as Scopus and PubMed, was eligible for inclusion, with preference given to the most recent publications related to any given topic.ResultsThe reviewed literature supports that RTS across CSI types requires resolution of symptoms, normal neurologic examination, restoration of painless cervical range of motion and strength, and radiographic evidence of healing or stability. MRI is consistently recommended for identifying high-risk features such as canal stenosis, cord signal change, or ligamentous disruption. Sport-specific risk stratification is supported by data showing higher reinjury rates in collision sports. Evidence remains heterogeneous, with substantial variation in specialist recommendations.ConclusionsSafe RTS after CSI requires comprehensive clinical and imaging assessment, recognition of sport-specific risks, and shared decision-making to prioritize athlete safety while avoiding unnecessary restrictions.

title: Impact of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) intra-articular injection on functioning and kinematic analysis in knee osteoarthritis patients: A prospective observational study.
abstract: PurposeOsteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint disease primarily affecting elderly, with the knee being the most involved joint. Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) therapy has shown promise in OA management. Our study aimed to descriptively characterize changes over time in performance, pain, stiffness, and function among patients with knee OA undergoing a combined PRP and physiotherapy protocol.MethodsThis study included patients over 50 years of age with a Kellgren-Lawrence II-III grade of OA. The intervention involved three PRP injections and rehabilitation cycles. Outcomes assessed functional capacity with six minutes walking test (6MWT) and the time-up-and-go (TUG), via an inertial motion unit. OA clinical severity was assessed through Western Ontario and McMaster University Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), and EuroQol Visual Analogue Scale (EQ-VAS).ResultsWe included 64 patients (males/females = 23/41), of whom 42 had complete data across T0-T4. WOMAC and NRS scores decreased during the early follow-up period, reaching their lowest values at T2, followed by progressive increases at T3 and T4. TUG showed a significant overall change over time, although no consecutive comparison remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. No significant changes over time were observed in 6MWT or gait-related outcomes.ConclusionsUnder the combined PRP and physiotherapy protocol, early changes in pain and function were observed, followed by a partial reversal at later follow-ups. No statistically significant changes over time were observed in 6MWT or gait-related outcomes. Given the uncontrolled single-arm design, these findings are descriptive and cannot establish the effectiveness or specific contribution of PRP. Further controlled studies are required.

title: Conservative management of carpal tunnel syndrome during pregnancy and lactation: A systematic review of mixed study designs.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pregnancy-related carpal tunnel syndrome (PRCTS) is the most common entrapment neuropathy during pregnancy, caused by gestational hormonal changes and fluid retention leading to increased intracarpal pressure and median nerve compression. Although symptoms often resolve postpartum, many patients experience significant functional impairment. Conservative treatment is preferred due to maternal-fetal safety concerns, but comparative evidence across modalities remains heterogeneous. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of conservative and minimally invasive interventions for PRCTS.
METHODS: The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261308958). A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library was conducted from database inception to 24 November 2025 (full search strategies in Supplementary Table S1). Studies evaluating conservative or minimally invasive treatments for CTS during pregnancy or lactation were included, irrespective of study design; case reports and case series without a comparator group were excluded a priori. Two independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and methodological quality assessment using the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Quality Assessment Tools selected according to study design, and outcome-level certainty of evidence was additionally rated using the GRADE approach. Because of clinical and methodological heterogeneity, meta-analysis was not feasible; findings were synthesized qualitatively and supplemented with descriptive pooled summaries of reported outcomes by intervention.
RESULTS: Twelve studies met inclusion criteria. Night wrist splinting consistently improved symptoms in mild-to-moderate cases, particularly when combined with nerve and tendon gliding exercises. Ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injections provided effective short-term symptom relief in severe or refractory cases and appeared acceptable based on limited available evidence; however, no formal safety analysis was possible. Evidence supporting adjunct therapies, including kinesio taping, cupping, and laser therapy, was limited and inconsistent. Certainty of evidence, rated using GRADE, was low to very low for all principal outcomes, reflecting small sample sizes, methodological heterogeneity, and imprecision (Table 1b).
CONCLUSION: Night splinting remains the first-line treatment for PRCTS, with corticosteroid injection as a potential option for refractory cases when benefits outweigh risks. Further high-quality studies are needed to establish standardized treatment protocols and long-term maternal-fetal safety.

title: Noninvasive assessment of the anaerobic threshold in endurance athletes: an evidence-based narrative review of methods, validity, and field feasibility.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION OR BACKGROUND: The anaerobic threshold (AnT) marks the transition between heavy and severe exercise intensity domains and guides training prescription and performance monitoring. Criterion methods (blood lactate and gas exchange) are accurate but invasive, costly, or impractical outside laboratories, prompting the search for noninvasive surrogates. This review evaluates the validity of these estimation procedures rather than the underlying physiology.
SOURCES OF DATA: MEDLINE (via PubMed) was searched from inception without language restrictions, supplemented by reference-list and citation searching. Eligible studies compared noninvasive AnT indices, including heart rate variability (HRV; including detrended fluctuation analysis [DFA] α1), cardiac repolarization instability, heart rate deflection/field slope-variation methods, critical power (CP)/ critical speed (CS), near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), the talk test, and machine-learning (ML) models, with criterion standards. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Eighty-eight reports were synthesized narratively; no meta-analysis was performed.
AREAS OF AGREEMENT: DFA α1, NIRS breakpoints, and CP/CS show strong associations with laboratory criteria and increasing field applicability through wearables. Accuracy and feasibility trade-offs require method selection according to the threshold, sport, and required precision.
AREAS OF CONTROVERSY: Correlation indicates group-level association rather than individual agreement; Bland-Altman and reliability analyses are more informative for substitution. Criterion standards are not interchangeable, and heart rate deflection is not consistently identifiable. Evidence in female athletes remains limited.
GROWING POINTS: Multimodal wearables integrating HRV, muscle oxygenation, and running power with ML may improve field-based threshold estimation.
AREAS FOR DEVELOPING RESEARCH: Priorities include standardized reporting, transparent bias assessment, female-athlete validation, and broader systematic and meta-analytic synthesis.

title: Comparing high-intensity resistance training incorporating periodic eccentric-only exercise with blood flow restriction training in older men: physiological responses and exercise feasibility.
abstract:
AIM: This study aimed to compare the feasibility, strength adaptations, and physiological effects of high-intensity resistance training incorporating periodic eccentric-only exercise (HIRT) with blood-flow restriction training (BFRT) in older men.
METHODS: This three-group randomized controlled trial included 63 older men assigned to lower limb HIRT, BFRT, or a non-exercising control group for 12 weeks. BFRT was at 40% one-repetition maximum (1RM) and HIRT altered between eccentric-only exercises at 120% 1RM and traditional resistance exercise at 80% 1RM in a 1:3 ratio. Outcome measures included ratings of perceived exertion (RPE), delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), lactate and creatine kinase (CK) levels, 1RM and adverse events.
RESULTS: BFRT was associated with higher RPE and more frequent training till failure, as well as greater lactate responses. Eccentric sessions in HIRT resulted in higher DOMS and CK levels. Both interventions significantly improved 1RM compared to controls, with HIRT demonstrating greater strength gains in leg extension and leg press. Adverse events included elevated blood pressure (n=1) and headache (n=2) in BFRT, and knee pain (n=2) in HIRT.
CONCLUSION: Both interventions were effective but imposed different physiological demands, with BFRT inducing greater metabolic and HIRT greater mechanical stress. HIRT led to slightly greater strength gains, while BFRT remains a viable alternative for those unable to perform high-load exercise. Incorporating eccentric exercise may further optimize adaptations and manage muscle damage.

title: Meniscal Repair Achieves Comparable Mid-Term Functional Performance to Partial Meniscectomy Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Highly Active Patients.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Concomitant meniscal injuries accompany 40%-60% of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures. Surgeons often face a clinical choice between meniscal repair, which prioritizes long-term joint preservation, and partial meniscectomy, which is traditionally perceived to facilitate earlier functional recovery. Despite the biological advantages of repair, persistent concerns remain that its restrictive postoperative protocols might impede mid-term functional performance compared to meniscectomy. This study aims to compare quadriceps/hamstring strength, dynamic balance, functional hop performance, and patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) at 2-5 years post-ACLR between patients undergoing concomitant meniscal repair versus partial meniscectomy.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study evaluated highly active patients who underwent ACLR between 2019 and 2023. Of 68 patients who underwent ACLR with a concomitant meniscal injury and a pre-injury Tegner score ≥ 6,16 were excluded: 5 due to revision ACLR or secondary meniscal procedures during the follow-up period, 8 due to concurrent multi-ligament injuries or full-thickness articular cartilage defects requiring surgery, and 3 due to knee joint deformities (varus or valgus malalignment > 5°)The remaining 52 patients were stratified into meniscal repair (n = 20) or partial meniscectomy (n = 32) groups. Outcomes included isokinetic strength (60°/s, 180°/s; Limb Symmetry Index, LSI), Y-balance test, single-leg hop (SLH), and PROMs (IKDC, Lysholm, and ACL-RSI).
RESULTS: At mid-term follow-up (mean 4.1 ± 1.2 years for repair, 4.2 ± 1.2 years for meniscectomy; p = 0.59), no significant differences existed in strength (quadriceps/hamstring LSI 60°/s and 180°/s), dynamic balance (Y-balance), hop tests (SLH, SLCH, and SLTH), or PROMs (all p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: At mid-term follow-up (2-5 years), concomitant meniscal repair yielded objective functional performance and patient-reported outcomes equivalent to partial meniscectomy in highly active patients undergoing ACLR, despite more restrictive early rehabilitation. These findings indicate that the initial postoperative restrictions associated with repair do not result in persistent functional deficits. Although meniscal preservation confers established long-term chondroprotective advantages, the present analysis addresses functional parity only; the surgical strategy should weigh both mid-term function and long-term joint health on an individual basis.

title: Uefa consensus guidelines on anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in women's football - Part Two: rehabilitation, return to play, and players' perceptions.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries remain a major challenge to player health and performance in women's football. They are associated with lengthy rehabilitation, a high risk of re-injury, and potential long-term knee issues that can impact both career longevity and quality of life. Building on Part One of the UEFA consensus, which addressed risk factors and prevention, Part Two addresses the continuum of care after ACL injury, from rehabilitation to return to play (RTP) and beyond. A multidisciplinary panel of 26 experts in sports medicine, physiotherapy, orthopaedics, and performance science developed evidence-informed statements using a modified RAND-UCLA Appropriateness Method. Through three Delphi rounds, 180 statements were assessed and refined, resulting in consensus on 170 (94%). The panel supported a player-centred, criterion-based approach where progression relies on clinical and functional milestones rather than fixed timelines. Key recommendations emphasise restoring quadriceps strength as a central milestone, integrating neuromuscular and psychological readiness assessments, and adopting phased RTP protocols that gradually re-expose players to the physical and cognitive demands of the game. Psychological and social factors (fear of re-injury, motivation, communication, and support networks) are recognised as vital influences on recovery. These guidelines offer practical, evidence-based advice for medical and performance staff working in women's football. By combining scientific research with expert consensus, they support a holistic, collaborative approach to ACL rehabilitation aimed at protecting player health, lowering re-injury risk, and enabling a confident, sustained return to performance.

title: Cardiovascular Effects Associated with the Female Athlete Triad: Emerging Evidence Statement from the Female and Male Athlete Triad Coalition.
abstract: This is an emerging evidence statement from the Female and Male Athlete Triad Coalition. This paper complements the 2025 updates to the Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statements addressing the State of the Science and Clinical Guidelines for Screening, Diagnosis, Treatment and Return to Play. This paper examines emerging evidence of cardiovascular alterations in Triad-affected female athletes with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea and functional hypothalamic oligomenorrhea, including vascular, hemodynamic, autonomic and lipid perturbations. The clinical significance of these surrogate markers of cardiovascular function and their long-term cardiovascular implications remain to be determined. Notwithstanding, the current work extends existing Triad frameworks by recognizing cardiovascular perturbations potentially associated with energy deficiency and hypoestrogenism as an important consideration in female athlete health. We outline an evidence-informed research framework, including longitudinal, dose-response, and multimodal assessments, to characterize the onset, magnitude, physiological significance, and reversibility of cardiovascular alterations in athletes with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea and functional hypothalamic oligomenorrhea. By integrating evidence from sports physiology, endocrinology, and cardiovascular medicine, this state-of-the-science synthesis provides a roadmap for future research, screening, and intervention strategies. It also underscores the importance of evaluating cardiovascular health as a potential component of the broader physiological consequences of energy deficiency, alongside menstrual dysfunction, and impaired bone health.

title: Functional recovery of athletes through rehabilitation training after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This article aims to introduce neuromuscular electrical stimulation into rehabilitation training after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and to assess its impact on the functional recovery of the knee joint.
METHODS: Twenty athletes undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction were allocated into a neuromuscular electrical stimulation group (neuromuscular electrical stimulation + rehabilitation training) and a conventional group (conventional rehabilitation training) for a 10-week training program. Indicators such as Lysholm scores and thigh circumference were assessed before and after training for comparison.
RESULTS: After training, the neuromuscular electrical stimulation group demonstrated a Lysholm score of 86.56 ± 11.67 points, a thigh circumference on the affected side of 47.15 ± 2.56 cm, and an active knee flexion angle of 105.12 ± 9.87°. Moreover, the score of the Y-balance test under left- and right-foot support was 93.67 ± 0.43 and 91.72 ± 0.48 points, respectively. It achieved a 10-meter walk speed of 1.01 ± 0.15 m/s. It achieved a performance of 264.39 ± 29.36 cm in three consecutive single-leg jumps on the healthy side and a performance of 178.16 ± 21.26 cm on the affected side. Its anterior cruciate ligament return-to-sport after injury scale score was 84.21 ± 5.32 points. These outcomes were significantly superior to those of the conventional group.
CONCLUSIONS: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation combined with rehabilitation training yields positive effects on functional recovery after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, surpassing the outcomes of conventional rehabilitation training. This approach holds promise for practical application.

title: The Current State of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: Graft Selection, Lateral Augmentation, Rehabilitation, and Return-to-Play.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) reliably restores anteroposterior stability; however, the rate of return to prior level of play and incidence of recurrent ACL injury have improved little over the past two decades. The purpose of this review is to describe the current state of ACLR with respect to graft selection, lateral extra-articular augmentation, rehabilitation and return to play, including the role of psychological readiness, and the specific rehabilitation protocol utilized by the senior author.
RECENT FINDINGS: Graft utilization has shifted substantially. Quadriceps tendon autograft accounted for less than 5% of primary reconstructions prior to 2014 and approximately 20% by 2023. Contemporary registry data demonstrate smaller differences in revision risk between autograft types than previously reported. Randomized and comparative data support lateral extra-articular tenodesis in selected high-risk knees, with the largest effect reported in the revision setting. Return-to-play practice has shifted from fixed timelines toward criteria-based clearance. However, a subset of athletes do not pass a full clearance battery, and some athletes who do pass and observe recommended timeframes still sustain reinjury. Limb symmetry index may overestimate functional recovery, while test batteries and thresholds vary considerably between institutions. Psychological readiness is independently associated with both return to sport and second ACL injury. Graft selection should be matched to the patient profile, and lateral augmentation should be reserved for high-risk knees. Return to play should be determined by a combination of time from surgery, functional criteria, and psychological readiness. Future study should focus on validating return-to-play criteria against reinjury endpoints and on standardizing how these criteria are defined and reported.

title: The Use of Cupping (Hijama) Therapy Among Athletes and Its Relationship With Sleep Quality: A Cross-Sectional Study in Palestine.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Wet cupping, or Hijama, is commonly used by athletes for recovery, yet evidence regarding its relationship with sleep quality remains limited. This study examined cupping use, perceived benefits, adverse effects, and factors associated with self-reported sleep quality among Palestinian athletes.
METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Palestinian athletes. Of 754 athletes screened at nine sports clubs and training centers across the West Bank, 470 (62.3%) reported previous wet-cupping use; 468 had sufficient primary-outcome data and were analyzed. Data were collected using a structured paper-based questionnaire incorporating the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Analyses included descriptive statistics, exact and chi-square tests, Spearman correlations, multiple linear regression, and path analysis.
RESULTS: Improved mobility (30.8%), reduced muscle cramps (25.6%), enhanced immunity (16.2%), and increased endurance (9.0%) were the most frequently reported intended benefits. Cupping was commonly reported for chronic or recurrent conditions (99.6%), muscle strain (41.5%), and headaches (41.2%). Higher BMI and greater cupping-session frequency were associated with greater perceived cupping benefit (p = 0.010 and p < 0.001, respectively). Reported inflammation was associated with BMI category, gender, and competition level, while mild pain was associated with BMI category and competition level. Lower PSQI scores were associated with higher BMI, greater cupping-session frequency, and greater perceived cupping benefit. In the multivariable model, higher BMI, vitamin use, greater cupping-session frequency, greater perceived benefit, and manual rather than automated suction were independently associated with lower PSQI scores. The model explained 35.2% of the variance in sleep quality.
CONCLUSION: Cupping-related practices and participant characteristics were associated with sleep quality. More frequent sessions, vitamin use, manual suction, higher BMI, and greater perceived benefit were associated with better sleep quality. These findings do not establish causality. Prospective studies are needed before cupping can be recommended to improve sleep or recovery.

title: Screening-based low energy availability risk, disordered eating risk, and their co-occurrence among female volleyball players: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: Low energy availability (LEA) and disordered eating (DE) are important health concerns in female athletes, yet their occurrence and co-occurrence in team-sport contexts, particularly volleyball, remain underexplored. This cross-sectional online survey study examined the proportions of athletes classified as being at risk of LEA and DE overall and across competition levels, and assessed the co-occurrence between the two risk classifications in female volleyball players in Türkiye, using the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q) and Eating Attitudes Test-26 (EAT-26). It also examined correlations between EAT-26 total score and LEAF-Q total and domain scores. A total of 213 athletes, recruited via non-probability convenience sampling, completed the LEAF-Q and EAT-26 to assess LEA risk and DE risk, respectively. In this sample, 33.3% of athletes were classified as being at risk of LEA, with no difference across competition levels (p = 0.825). A total of 17.4% were classified as being at risk of DE, with variation across competition levels and the highest proportion among Turkish Women's Volleyball Second League athletes (p = 0.034). LEA risk and DE risk co-occurred in 10.3% of the sample, and DE risk was associated with higher odds of LEA risk (unadjusted OR = 3.80, 95% CI: 1.82-7.92). EAT-26 total score was positively correlated with LEAF-Q total and gastrointestinal function scores (p < 0.001) and injury history score (p = 0.004), but not menstrual function score (p = 0.133). These results suggest that LEA risk was commonly identified in this sample, DE risk was comparatively less common, and their co-occurrence was only partial, highlighting the value of screening for both risks rather than assuming one from the other.

title: Work-related musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, and dietary habits in athletic trainers and physical therapists providing sports team support.
abstract: BackgroundAthletic professionals (athletic trainers and physical therapists) perform injury prevention, health management, evaluation, emergency care, post-injury protection, rehabilitation, and administrative duties. Their focus on athletes' health may lead them to overlook high physical and psychosocial demands that may increase musculoskeletal pain (MSP), fatigue, and unhealthy dietary habits.ObjectiveTo examine MSP, fatigue, and dietary habits among athletic professionals who provide on-site team support and explore how fatigue and dietary habits relate to MSP.MethodsParticipants were required to be athletic professionals providing on-site team support. This cross-sectional online survey assessed 3-month work-related MSP in body regions, fatigue using a modified Fatigue Assessment Scale, and dietary habits using a structured food-frequency questionnaire. Logistic regression and mediation analyses examined associations and indirect associations, adjusting for relevant confounders.ResultsA total of 132 valid responses were included. MSP was highly prevalent, particularly in the lower back (83%), wrists/fingers (80%), and neck (67%). Fatigue (OR = 3.1, 95% CI = 1.34-7.45) and several suboptimal dietary habits (e.g., irregular meal timing, inadequate intake, fast eating, unbalanced diet, replacing meals with snacks, emotional eating) were significantly associated with MSP. Exploratory mediation analyses indicated statistically significant indirect associations via inadequate intake, replacing meals with snacks, and emotional eating, suggesting these behaviours may partially account for the fatigue-MSP association.ConclusionsAthletic professionals experience a high burden of MSP, fatigue, and suboptimal dietary habits that may be interrelated in ways that exacerbate work-related health. Workplace strategies should address workload, fatigue management, and access to healthy eating options to support sustainable practice and well-being.

title: Pain Intensity and Knee Extensor Strength Across Different Ranges of Motion During Knee Extension Exercise in Individuals With Patellofemoral Pain.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Knee extensor weakness has been identified as one of the strongest risk factors for the development of patellofemoral pain (PFP), and strengthening exercises for the quadriceps are widely recommended to improve pain and function. However, conflicting biomechanical findings and small studies-often conducted in pain-free individuals-limit guidance on the optimal range of motion (ROM) for knee extension exercises in PFP. This uncertainty hinders clinical decision-making, despite knee extension being one of the most commonly prescribed exercises for this population.
OBJECTIVE: To compare pain intensity and knee extensor strength at different ROMs in individuals with PFP.
DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
SETTING: Data were collected at the Human Movement Analysis Laboratory of the Federal University of Ceará between July and November 2024.
PATIENTS OR OTHER PARTICIPANTS: One hundred individuals with a clinical diagnosis of PFP were included.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Pain intensity assessed using the numeric pain rating scale (0-10) and knee extensor strength using an isokinetic dynamometer at ROMs of 90°-45°, 70°-25°, and 45°-0°.
RESULTS: Ninety-four percent of participants with PFP reported knee pain in at least 1 ROM. The 70°-25° ROM demonstrated greater pain intensity than the 45°-90° ROM (mean difference [MD] = 1, 95% CI = 0.4, 1.6). No significant differences in pain intensity were observed between 45°-0° and 90°-45°. Participants had lower knee extensor strength in the 45°-0° ROM than the 70°-25° (MD = -27.5, 95% CI = -32.6, -22.5) and 90°-45° (MD = -29.9, 95% CI = -32.6, -22.5) ROMs.
CONCLUSIONS: Knee pain during resisted knee extension is highly prevalent in individuals with PFP. Although the 70°-25° ROM elicited greater pain, the 45°-0° ROM produced lower torque. Clinicians may tailor the ROM during knee extension exercises based on symptom response and the balance between pain exacerbation and torque generation.

title: Sleep-timing irregularity moderates the within-participant association between training load and next-morning heart rate variability in university sport participants: a 28-day study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Heart rate variability (HRV) describes beat-to-beat variation in cardiac intervals; the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) is a time-domain index of short-term cardiac vagal modulation. We examined whether nightly deviation from habitual sleep midpoint moderated the association between prior-day internal training load and next-morning natural-log-transformed RMSSD (lnRMSSD), and whether analogous interactions were present for resting heart rate, wellness strain, and countermovement-jump (CMJ) height.
METHODS: University students engaged in regular sport training completed 28 days of habitual monitoring. Internal load was session duration multiplied by session rating of perceived exertion. Wrist actigraphy and sleep diaries estimated sleep midpoint, and 5-min morning RR recordings yielded lnRMSSD. Mixed models separated within- and between-participant components and tested within-participant load (per 100 arbitrary units [AU]) × absolute midpoint deviation (per 30 min).
RESULTS: The analysis included 1,232 mornings from 54 participants (57.4% female; age 21.0 ± 1.7 years). At each participant's mean midpoint deviation, greater-than-usual load was associated with lower next-morning lnRMSSD (β = -0.0089, 95% CI -0.0127 to -0.0051; p < 0.001). At mean load, greater-than-usual midpoint deviation was also associated with lower lnRMSSD (β = -0.0156, 95% CI -0.0268 to -0.0045; p = 0.006). The interaction was negative (β = -0.0101, 95% CI -0.0153 to -0.0048; p < 0.001). Thus, the inverse within-participant association between load and lnRMSSD strengthened as sleep-timing irregularity increased. No load-by-midpoint interaction was detected for resting heart rate, wellness strain, or CMJ height after false discovery rate adjustment. The primary interaction persisted after adjustment for prior-morning lnRMSSD (β = -0.0096, 95% CI -0.0147 to -0.0046; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The within-participant association between training load and next-morning cardiac vagal modulation was moderated by sleep-timing irregularity. These field-based associations do not establish a sleep mechanism, causal recovery effect, or decision threshold.

title: Effects of 30- and 90-Minute Afternoon Nap Opportunities on Field-Test Performance in Female Collegiate Basketball Players.
abstract: Afternoon napping is used as a recovery strategy in sport, but a scheduled nap opportunity is not equivalent to objectively verified sleep. This study compared no-nap seated wakefulness (N0), a 30-minute scheduled nap opportunity (N30), and a 90-minute scheduled nap opportunity (N90) in 18 female collegiate basketball players using a randomized, fully counterbalanced, three-period within-participant crossover design. Conditions were separated by at least 72 h and ended at 14:30, followed by a common 60 min wakefulness buffer, a standardized 15 min warm-up, and a fixed basketball field-test battery. Linear mixed-effects models included condition, period, and sequence as fixed effects, with participant as a random intercept; the nine omnibus condition tests were controlled for using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. Four of nine outcomes remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction: the modified-505 first 10 m split, combined modified-505 completion time, three-quarter-court sprint time, and 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test final velocity. N90 differed from both N0 and N30 for these outcomes, whereas N30 did not differ from N0. The other five outcomes did not meet the false-discovery-rate threshold. Sensitivity analyses, including reanalysis of the pre-correction modified-505 data, preserved the same four-outcome pattern. Because sleep onset and duration were not objectively measured, the findings estimate the effects of assigned recovery-opportunity conditions rather than a physiological sleep-duration dose-response.

title: Excellent 2-Year Outcomes of MUIB All-Inside ACL Reconstruction: A Registry-Based Analysis of 63 Patients With Zero Graft Failure.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) remains a cornerstone of orthopedic sports medicine, yet graft failure rates are high despite advances in surgical techniques. The Modified UKM Internal Bracing (MUIB) technique combines all-inside ACLR with internal suture augmentation, potentially offering enhanced graft protection and improved outcomes.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study evaluated 63 patients who underwent isolated primary all-inside ACLR using the MUIB technique (19 allograft, 44 autograft) between 2020 and 2024. Outcome measures included International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores, Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain scores, graft failure rates, Single Leg Hop Test (SLHT) performance, and complication profiles at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months postoperatively.
RESULTS: Both allograft and autograft groups demonstrated significant improvement from preoperative to 2-year follow-up (p < 0.001). There were no statistically significant differences observed between allograft and autograft groups across all outcome measures, suggesting that the MUIB technique may yield comparable outcomes regardless of graft type. Complete pain resolution (VAS 0) was achieved by 6 months in both groups. Notably, no graft re-tears were documented throughout the 2-year follow-up period, with 95.2% of patients achieving SLHT > 90% at 12 months. No infections, arthrofibrosis, or hardware-related complications requiring reoperation were recorded.
CONCLUSION: The MUIB all-inside ACLR technique yielded excellent 2-year outcomes in this cohort, characterized by a zero graft failure rate, complete pain resolution, and exceptional functional recovery. However, given the retrospective, uncontrolled design, these findings should be interpreted as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Prospective comparative studies are necessary to establish the efficacy and potential superiority of the MUIB technique relative to conventional ACLR approaches.

title: Urinary metabolomic signatures of muscle injury and recovery in elite football players.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Muscle injuries are a leading cause of time-loss in elite football, highlighting the need for objective biomarkers capable of reflecting the athlete's physiological state. Monitoring strategies rely predominantly on external load metrics and may not fully capture internal physiological responses to training and competition. Urinary metabolomics offers a non-invasive approach to characterize injury related physiological processes.
OBJECTIVES: To identify urinary metabolomic signatures associated with muscle injury in elite football players and to explore their potential utility for monitoring injury-related physiological stress and recovery.
METHODS: This observational longitudinal study included 287 urine samples collected from 121 elite male football players across two consecutive seasons. Samples were clinically classified as muscle injury (n = 30) or control (n = 257). Targeted UPLC-MS quantified amino acids and tryptophan-related metabolites. Univariate analysis, pathway over-representation analysis, and PLS-DA were applied to identify injury-associated metabolic patterns RESULTS: Muscle injury was associated with alterations in amino acid turnover, purine metabolism, energetic stress, and tryptophan catabolism. Exploratory pathway analysis suggested enrichment of amino acid-related pathways, although interpretation was limited by the targeted nature of the analytical panel. PLS-DA identified an injury-associated metabolic signature with a cross-validated AUROC of 0.88 (sensitivity 73%, specificity 88%; p < 0.003). Key discriminant metabolites included β-aminoisobutyric acid, hypoxanthine, xanthurenic acid, β-alanine, and alanine. Exploratory visual assessment of individual longitudinal trajectories suggested a return toward baseline during rehabilitation.
CONCLUSIONS: Urinary metabolomics identifies coordinated metabolic alterations associated with muscle injury in elite football players, supporting its potential as a future complementary tool to external load monitoring. Further validation in larger cohorts is required before these systemic signatures can be applied to clinical monitoring or recovery assessment.

title: A Longitudinal Study Analyzing Sprint Performance in Relation to Biological Maturity in Youth Soccer Players.
abstract: Bezzina, D, Price, P, Cimadoro, G, and Cleather, D. A longitudinal study analyzing sprint performance in relation to biological maturity in youth soccer players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Understanding the influence of biological maturation on athletic performance is crucial for improving youth training programs. This study examined the longitudinal development of sprint performance in youth soccer players across different stages of biological maturation. Forty male soccer players (ages 10-16) were categorized into pre-peak height velocity (PHV) and circa-PHV groups based on maturity offset values estimated using the Mirwald equation. Sprinting speed was assessed using a 30-m sprint test. A linear mixed model analysis revealed significant improvements in sprint performance over time (p < 0.002, d = 0.78), with the circa-PHV group consistently outperforming the pre-PHV group (p < 0.001, d = 0.43). There was no significant time × maturity interaction (p = 0.722), indicating that the rate of change in sprint performance over the 12-month interval did not differ between pre- and circa-PHV players. These findings support the critical role of biological maturity in sprint progression, as more mature athletes demonstrated faster 30-m sprint performance. However, this study does not support the notion that sprinting develops at a significantly higher rate during circa-PHV than during pre-PHV.

title: Quadriceps Strength Recovery Trajectories Associate with Pre-Operative Predictors but not Clinical Outcomes Following ACL Reconstruction.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Quadriceps weakness following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is common, however distinct longitudinal strength trajectories not have been examined. This study aimed to i) identify strength trajectories measured pre-operatively to 12 months post-ACLR, and determine associations with ii) pre-operative demographics, patient-reported outcomes (PROs: Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score [KOOS], Tegner, Marx) and ACLR concomitant surgeries, and iii) clinical outcomes post-ACLR including cartilage compositional changes (via magnetic resonance imaging [MRI] T1ρ relaxation times) and 12-month KOOS.
METHODS: Isometric quadriceps strength was measured bilaterally pre-operatively and at 4, 6, and 12 months. Group trajectory modeling characterized longitudinal strength recovery in ACLR and uninvolved limbs, which were combined to define dual-limb recovery patterns. Tibiofemoral and patellofemoral cartilage composition was measured pre-operatively and at 12 months post-ACLR. Dirichlet regressions examined associations between trajectories and demographics, surgeries, PROs, and cartilage changes.
RESULTS: 59 participants were included (58% female; age, 21.9 ± 4.7y; BMI, 24.55 ± 3.7kg/m 2). Three combined trajectories were identified: bilaterally weak (51%), which demonstrated uninvolved limb strength declines and failure to recover ACLR limb pre-operative strength; bilaterally strong (38%), which demonstrated minimal uninvolved limb declines and ACLR limb pre-operative strength recovery; and weak uninvolved, strong ACLR limb (12%). Lower pre-injury Tegner scores associated with bilaterally weak membership (p = 0.01), where probability increased from 0.27 (score of 10) to 0.61 (score of 0). Medial meniscectomy associated most with bilaterally weak membership (p<.001, 0.86 probability). No associations were found between trajectories and clinical outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: While individuals who failed to restore ACLR limb strength demonstrated bilateral quadriceps weakness pre-operatively, persons who demonstrated greater pre-operative bilateral strength recovered ACLR limb strength. Medial meniscectomy associated with an inability to restore quadriceps strength.

title: Unsupervised Machine Learning Identifies Shared Biomechanical and Clinical Variation in Individuals with Knee Osteoarthritis and High BMI: A Secondary Analysis of the IDEA Trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: High body mass index (BMI≥27 kg/m2) and aberrant gait biomechanics are primary risk factors for knee osteoarthritis (KOA), yet the specific loading patterns linked to clinical disease features remain unclear. Unsupervised machine learning (ML) was used to identify vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) waveform modes of variation and characterize the shared and individual variation between vGRF profiles and clinical features in individuals with KOA and high BMI.
METHODS: Baseline gait and clinical data from the Intensive Diet and Exercise for Arthritis (IDEA) trial (n=431; 29% male; 65±6 years; 34±4 kg/m2) were analyzed. vGRF waveforms (n=2,394) were represented using three functional data analysis methods: time- and bodyweight-normalization; elastic shape analysis; and optimal transport (OT). Principal component analysis extracted the dominant vGRF modes of variation, and Data Integration Via Analysis of Subspaces (DIVAS) quantified shared and individual variation among vGRF profiles and 40 clinical features.
RESULTS: A sustained loading phenotype emerged across all vGRF representations (lesser early and late stance vGRF; greater midstance vGRF). DIVAS identified shared variation between sustained loading and higher BMI, elevated inflammatory biomarkers, greater pain, worse KL grade, and slower walking speed. OT identified a temporal loading phenotype that shared variation with female sex.
CONCLUSIONS: Unsupervised ML identified a sustained loading biomechanical phenotype that shared variation with greater BMI, increased inflammation, worse radiographic severity, and slower walking speed. These data highlight the complex interplay among gait biomechanics and clinical KOA features in individuals with high BMI and may help to guide future work evaluating targeted gait retraining interventions.

title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
abstract: Kolb, DE, Cipriano, NL, Moody, RA, Stephens, JA, Caldwell, LK, Lindley, MR, Ware, ME, and Deemer, SE. Bone mineral density in physique-focused and non-physique-focused female collegiate athletes: Associations with relative energy deficiency in sport risk factors. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Bone mineral density (BMD) is a critical indicator of skeletal health and long-term injury risk in athletic populations. Female athletes are susceptible to changes in BMD because of sport-specific training demands, hormonal dysregulation, and energy availability. The present study aimed to compare BMD between physique-focused (PF; endurance, aesthetic, and weight-dependent sports) and non-physique-focused (NPF; ball, power, and skill-based sports) female collegiate athletes and assess risk factors associated with relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) across both groups. Thirty-three female athletes were evaluated for BMD by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), REDs risk using the Clinical Assessment Tool 2 (CAT2), anthropometric measurements, blood biomarkers, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), and the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q). Group differences were assessed using independent t-tests with significance set at p < 0.05. Physique-focused athletes demonstrated significantly lower DXA-derived z-scores at anteroposterior spine, right and left femur, and total body sites than NPF athletes (p < 0.001). There were no differences in leptin (p = 0.35), cortisol (p = 0.16), vitamin D (p = 0.29), LEAF-Q total score (p = 0.72), or global EDE-Q score (p = 0.10). No group differences in CAT2 REDs risk were observed; thus, subjects were combined: 19 athletes were classified as "green;" 12 were "yellow;" and 2 were "orange." Lower BMD in PF athletes supports the importance of early screening and targeted interventions to support bone health. These findings suggest sport type may influence skeletal outcomes independent of traditional REDs indicators, emphasizing the need for sport-specific assessment strategies.

title: Consumer Grade Wearable Sensor Metrics Are Associated with Internal Forces at Common Running Injury Locations.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Inexpensive consumer-grade wearable sensors have expanded possibilities to assess, monitor, or modify a runner's gait. However, it is unclear which sensor-measured gait metrics are strongly associated with internal loading at common injury locations.
PURPOSE: To measure the association between gait metrics measured by consumer-grade wearable sensors and internal forces at the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint.
METHODS: 55 healthy runners wearing consumer-grade chest straps foot-pods completed a 38-minute run on an instrumented treadmill at 12 speeds from 70%-125% of self-reported typical running pace. A scaled musculoskeletal model derived from motion capture data and driven by static optimization was used to calculate Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint forces during stance for each speed. Functional regression models were used to estimate the associations of each of nine sensor-measured gait metrics with internal forces across stance, after adjusting for body mass and running speed.
RESULTS: At both the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint, cadence, vertical oscillation, and vertical ratio (vertical oscillation divided by step length) showed the strongest associations with internal forces (maximum of 0.4-0.6 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric). Other wearable sensor-measured gait metrics, including stance time, leg stiffness, and stance time percent showed weaker associations (<0.4 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric).
CONCLUSIONS: Runners with higher-than-average cadence, vertical oscillation, or vertical ratio values experience marked differences in internal forces at the Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint. Of these gait metrics, cadence is the most practical for out-of-lab use because of its ease of accurate measurement with consumer-grade devices.

title: Reflections on 20 Years of Research on Tai Chi for Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain: An Updated Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Chronic musculoskeletal pain (CMP), including osteoarthritis (OA), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), fibromyalgia, and chronic low back pain (cLBP), contributes substantially to disability and reduced quality of life. Contemporary pain science supports biopsychosocial, multimodal management addressing nociceptive, neuropathic, and nociplastic mechanisms. Tai Chi is a multicomponent mind-body exercise integrating gentle movement, breathing, relaxation, balance, and attentional focus. This narrative review summarizes approximately 20 years of research on Tai Chi for CMP and considers its evolving evidence in contemporary rheumatology and pain management.
RECENT FINDINGS: Findings are strongest for knee and hip OA, with randomized trials and systematic reviews demonstrating improvements in pain, mobility, physical function, and stiffness compared with non-exercise controls. For cLBP, studies suggest potential improvements in pain and physical function, although heterogeneity and limitations in the certainty of evidence warrant cautious interpretation. In fibromyalgia, Tai Chi may improve pain and selected symptoms, but findings remain variable and the certainty of evidence is limited. In RA, research is sparse and inconsistent, with insufficient data to establish clinically meaningful effects on disease activity, pain, or physical function. Across conditions, Tai Chi has a generally favorable safety profile, although variations in interventions and outcome measures limit direct comparisons. Over two decades, research on Tai Chi for chronic musculoskeletal pain has expanded from relatively small efficacy trials to larger randomized studies, as well as mechanistic and pragmatic investigations. Findings are most supportive for knee and hip OA, whereas evidence for cLBP and fibromyalgia remains promising but heterogeneous, with limitations in the certainty of evidence. Evidence for RA remains insufficient to draw firm conclusions. Overall, Tai Chi appears to be a feasible and generally safe nonpharmacological intervention that may complement multimodal management of musculoskeletal pain. Further high-quality studies are needed to establish the magnitude and clinical relevance of its benefits, determine comparative effectiveness and optimal dose and delivery, and evaluate longer-term outcomes.

title: Implementing exercise therapy for hip and knee osteoarthritis in the clinic: a best practice narrative review.
abstract: Major guidelines recommend exercise for hip and knee osteoarthritis (OA), yet few provide guidance on how to prescribe it. This narrative review synthesizes high-quality and clinically relevant evidence on exercise therapy for hip or knee OA, prioritizing systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials. Findings were summarized across nine topics, with a focus on translating the evidence into specific guidance for clinicians. Clinicians should consider measuring pain, physical function, quality of life, and global assessment for most patients with hip or knee OA. When educating about OA, clinicians should focus on what patients can do and avoid impairment-based language. Exercise therapy is safe and provides small to moderate improvements in pain and function, although effects appear smaller for hip OA than for knee OA. No exercise type has proven superior, nor has a dose-response relationship been established. Patients with higher baseline pain and poorer function may benefit somewhat more, but effects differ little across other patient characteristics, including comorbidity burden and radiographic severity. Whether increasing adherence leads to greater improvements in pain and function remains unclear, but helping patients start and sustain exercise remains a priority, given its wide-ranging health benefits. In-person, telehealth, and self-directed delivery can all improve pain and function, and they appear to offer benefits of similar magnitude. Overall, exercise is safe, with the most common adverse event being temporary muscle or joint soreness. Clinicians do not need to search for an optimal program but can instead build one around the patient's priorities, preferences, and needs.

title: Patient and healthcare professional perceptions of weight reduction in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis: A systematic literature review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Weight reduction confers significant clinical benefits in knee osteoarthritis (OA) management. This systematic review examined patients' and healthcare professionals' (HCPs) perceptions of weight reduction for surgical, pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions, with emphasis on barriers to implementation.
METHOD: The review was conducted across Embase, MEDLINE, Cochrane, and PsycInfo for eligible studies using the Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome, Timeframe, and Study type framework.
RESULTS: The search identified 2134 publications; of these, 203 had full-text screening, with 46 studies included: 23 qualitative studies, 15 cross-sectional studies, 6 randomized-controlled trials, one quasi-experimental and one observational cohort study. Four main themes of barriers to weight reduction were identified, including limited knowledge, lack of access to interventions, OA-specific barriers to exercise, and non-OA-specific barriers to dieting and exercise. The patient-reported barriers included intrapersonal barriers (i.e., difficulty achieving weight reduction, lack of motivation), physical barriers (i.e., age, challenges with general movement), and social barriers (i.e., lack of social support). The HCP-reported barriers included knowledge barriers, communication barriers, and systemic barriers (i.e., time constraints and resource limitations). Both patients and HCPs had varying expectations and satisfaction levels regarding the impact and delivery of weight reduction interventions.
CONCLUSIONS: Despite broad recognition of weight reduction's benefits in knee OA, substantial barriers hinder adherence and implementation. Targeted strategies addressing patient-HCP communication, alongside enhanced education and training for both groups, are critical to improving weight reduction outcomes in this population. There is currently a gap in evidence around barriers to gastric surgery and pharmacological treatment specific to patients with knee OA.

title: Creatine supplementation in soccer players: a systematic review.
abstract:
AIM: Soccer places repeated demands on short-duration, high-intensity performance, including sprints, accelerations, jumps, and technical actions performed over the course of a match. Because these efforts depend heavily on rapid adenosine triphosphate (ATP) resynthesis, creatine is a plausible ergogenic aid for soccer players. However, findings in soccer-specific studies have been inconsistent, and previous reviews have addressed narrower questions using smaller evidence sets. This systematic review therefore examined the effects of creatine supplementation on performance, body composition, and recovery/fatigue-related outcomes in soccer players.
METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 15 May 2025 in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. We included controlled clinical trials of creatine supplementation in male or female soccer players of any age or competitive level when an eligible placebo, control, or comparison condition was available. Outcomes were grouped into performance, body composition, and recovery/fatigue domains. Domains from the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2) and the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool were used to produce study-level methodological summaries rather than formal result-specific risk-of-bias assessments. Because the studies differed substantially in design, supplementation protocols, populations, and outcomes, findings were synthesised qualitatively rather than pooled in a meta-analysis.
RESULTS: Source-level verification left 45 eligible reports representing 41 unique studies: 28 randomised parallel-group studies, 2 randomised crossover/repeated-condition studies, and 11 non-randomised or allocation-unverifiable controlled studies. Some trials reported favourable findings for repeated-sprint performance, anaerobic power, and muscular strength, but the comparative evidence was inconsistent and the certainty of evidence was very low. Findings for vertical jump performance and technical skills were mixed, while change-of-direction and endurance outcomes showed no consistent benefit. Recovery- and fatigue-related findings were also largely null or inconsistent. Body mass often increased, particularly after loading protocols, whereas evidence for gains in lean mass was limited and inconsistent.
CONCLUSION: The soccer-specific evidence for creatine supplementation remains suggestive rather than conclusive. Favourable findings have been reported for some repeated-sprint, anaerobic-power, and strength outcomes, but the comparative evidence is heterogeneous, often limited by unclear or nonsignificant between-group effects, and of very low certainty. Firm conclusions about efficacy are therefore not possible. Body mass commonly increased, especially after loading protocols, while effects on lean mass, endurance, change-of-direction ability, and recovery/fatigue-related outcomes remain uncertain.

title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points.
METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles.
RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions.
CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

title: Early sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing characteristics and six-month knee extensor strength after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a prospective longitudinal study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether quadriceps motor unit firing rates measured pre-operatively and during the first three months after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction are associated with isometric knee extensor strength at six months, and to explore the relationship between motor unit action potential (MUAP) amplitude and firing rate.
METHODS: Twenty-seven participants (15 female) underwent surface electromyography of vastus medialis and vastus lateralis during sub-maximal isometric knee extension from pre-operation to three months post-reconstruction. Six-month knee extensor MVC force was modelled using Bayesian regression and interpreted using a region of practical equivalence (ROPE; ±15 N). A secondary hierarchical analysis examined MUAP amplitude and firing rate.
RESULTS: Motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with six-month knee extensor strength across time points and limbs. In the ACL reconstructed limb at two weeks, a 1-SD greater mean firing rate was associated with 45.8 N greater six-month strength (95% credible interval [CrI] - 18.5 to 114.6 N). Six-month strength was greater in the contralateral limb (β = 198.4 N, 95% CrI 171.6 to 225.1 N), in males (β = 184.3 N, 95% CrI 32.0 to 325.1 N), and with greater body mass (β = 119.9 N per 1-SD, 95% CrI 33.4 to 207.2 N). Greater relative MUAP amplitude was associated with lower firing rate (-3.7 Hz per 1-SD, 95% CrI -3.8 to -3.6 Hz).
CONCLUSIONS: Sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with later knee extensor strength, although a stronger positive association was suggested in the reconstructed limb at two weeks. Firing rate was strongly related to relative MUAP amplitude, and its predictive value for later strength appears limited.

title: Artificial intelligence across the continuum of care for the aging musculoskeletal patient: From longitudinal phenotyping to personalized surgery and recovery monitoring.
abstract: Musculoskeletal care is being reshaped by population aging, multimorbidity, frailty, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, polypharmacy and increasing vulnerability to postoperative loss of independence. Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered orthopaedic research, but its clinical translation remains constrained. Many models address isolated diagnostic, imaging or short-term prediction tasks rather than the longitudinal care trajectories that determine outcomes in older musculoskeletal patients. The central limitation is therefore not simply whether older adults are represented in datasets, but whether AI systems are valid across the continuum of geriatric orthopaedic care. This review argues for a transition from task-specific orthopaedic AI toward continuum-of-care AI for the aging musculoskeletal patient. Upstream, radiomics, longitudinal osteoarthritis phenotyping, opportunistic computed tomography (CT)-based skeletal assessment and AI-augmented dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) modelling may improve prediction of disease progression, fracture risk, treatment failure and surgical timing. At the point of intervention, AI-assisted arthroplasty planning may help move total knee arthroplasty from generic alignment targets toward phenotype-specific reconstruction strategies that account for constitutional alignment, bone morphology, ligament envelope, neuromuscular control, frailty and functional reserve. Perioperatively, automated frailty and sarcopenia phenotyping, wearable gait analysis and multimodal temporal models integrating imaging, electronic health records, laboratory data, medications, patient-reported outcomes and wearable signals may support dynamic risk prediction. After discharge, continuous monitoring of mobility, sleep, pain trajectories, wound-related symptoms and rehabilitation adherence may help close the high-risk surveillance gap during the 90-day postoperative episode. However, clinical adoption requires more than high discrimination. Explainable AI should be understood as one component of a broader trust framework that also includes calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision-curve analysis, external and prospective validation, workflow integration, post-deployment monitoring and accountability. The future of orthopaedic AI is not simply better diagnosis or more precise surgery, but longitudinal, multimodal support across the full care continuum: predicting progression, selecting treatment, personalizing surgery, optimizing perioperative care, monitoring recovery and preserving mobility and independence. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.
