title: Rotator cuff tendon augmentation and inter-user reproducibility assessment of a novel patch fixation technique compared to a conventional technique for rotator cuff repair: a biomechanical validation study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Rotator cuff (RC) tears present a major socioeconomic burden with high rates of retear after repair surgery. The interlocked patch augmentation represents a novel approach using direct fiber interlocking of a nonwoven polyethylene terephthalate patch into tendon tissue. This study evaluated the biomechanical strength and properties of human cadaveric RC augmentation with direct patch interlocking and its reproducibility.
METHODS: Two complementary studies were conducted: (1) a biomechanical human cadaver study on paired infraspinatus tendons comparing 2 horizontal mattress stitches with and without interlocked patch augmentation (n = 5 per group) measuring cyclic loading and load-to-failure testing; (2) a user performance reproducibility evaluation with 6 orthopedic surgeons (first-time users group) and 3 interlocked patch augmentation experts (control group), each performing 4 arthroscopic procedures using ovine infraspinatus tendons.
RESULTS: In the human cadaver study, direct patch interlocking demonstrated significantly higher ultimate tensile strength and linear stiffness compared with the nonaugmented group (519.4 ± 150.8 N vs. 294.6 ± 84.1 N; P = .0195 and 44.7 ± 13.2 N/mm vs. 21.2 ± 6.4 N/mm; P = .0016). Cyclic stiffness and elongation did not show significant differences. In the user performance study, no significant difference in ultimate tensile strength was found between first-time users (392.1 ± 62.1 N) and experts (322.6 ± 86.3 N, P = .0991). Inter-user comparison among surgeons showed no significant differences (P = .4830).
CONCLUSION: The interlocked patch augmentation significantly improves biomechanical suture retention properties in a human cadaveric RC model and enables reproducible outcomes when used by orthopedic surgeons without prior device training. These preliminary biomechanical findings support further evaluation of direct patch interlocking for RC repair augmentation in further biomechanical and clinical studies.

title: Calf Injuries: An Anatomy-Based Approach to Diagnosis, Management and Return to Sport.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Calf muscle injuries are common in athletes but represent a heterogeneous group of lesions involving different muscles and myoconnective structures. This review provides a practical overview of gastrocnemius-soleus injuries, with particular emphasis on how anatomical characterization can contribute to diagnosis, management and return-to-sport decision-making. It also examines the limitations of current evidence and the extent to which increasingly detailed imaging findings translate into clinically meaningful information.
RECENT FINDINGS: Advances in ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging have improved the identification of specific injury patterns involving the gastrocnemius and soleus. Recent studies support moving beyond a muscle-based diagnosis towards more precise characterisation of the myoconnective structures involved. However, evidence linking individual anatomical patterns to prognosis and return-to-sport outcomes remains limited and largely observational. Current rehabilitation approaches favour progressive, criteria-based loading rather than fixed timelines, while return-to-sport decisions increasingly integrate clinical recovery, functional capacity, sport-specific demands and acceptable risk. No validated calf-specific rehabilitation or return-to-sport criteria are currently available. Anatomical characterization provides a useful framework for understanding the heterogeneity of calf muscle injuries but should inform rather than determine clinical management. Rehabilitation should remain function-led and progressively restore the mechanical capacities required for sport, while return to sport should be considered a multifactorial decision rather than the result of isolated imaging findings, tests or predefined timelines. Future prospective studies should determine which anatomical features provide clinically relevant prognostic information and develop validated calf-specific functional and return-to-sport outcomes.

title: Perineural Release with or Without Balloon Decompression for the Treatment of Lumbosacral Discogenic Syndromes in Professional Athletes.
abstract: Background: Lumbosacral discogenic syndrome (LSDS) is a common cause of low back pain (LBP) and lower limb pain (LLP) in athletes, often resulting in impaired sporting performance and delayed return to sport (RTS). Evidence regarding minimally invasive interventions, such as epidural perineural release (PNR), remains limited in athletic populations. Aim: This study aimed to compare outcomes following PNR with versus without balloon decompression neuroplasty in athletes with LSDS. Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of PNR performed between 2019 and 2024 for the treatment of LSDS among professional athletes. Demographic, clinical, and outcome data were collected from medical records and follow-up assessments. Pain intensity was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), while patient-reported outcomes were evaluated using the EuroQoL-5D (EQ-5D). Additional outcomes included pain-free walking, standing, and sitting durations, and self-reported health scores. Results: A total of 33 patients who had one intervention were included. Significant improvements were observed in all pain, functional, and quality-of-life outcomes following treatment (all p < 0.001). Maximum, minimum, and average pain intensity decreased from 7.5 ± 1.7 to 2.8 ± 2.2, 3.8 ± 2.3 to 0.3 ± 0.7, and 5.6 ± 1.7 to 1.5 ± 1.2, respectively. All EQ-5D domains and quality of sleep also improved significantly (all p < 0.001). Pain-free walking, standing, and sitting durations increased significantly, from 24.8 ± 23.2 to 49.7 ± 26.7 min, 18.4 ± 20.0 to 44.1 ± 23.1 min, and 25.5 ± 23.7 to 44.6 ± 24.9 min, respectively (all p < 0.001). Self-reported health scores improved from 51.9 ± 22.6 to 83.0 ± 14.3 (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Epidural perineural release, with or without balloon decompression neuroplasty, was associated by significant improvements in pain, functional capacity, and quality of life among athletes with LSDS refractory to conservative management. These findings suggest that PNR may be a promising minimally invasive treatment option; however, controlled prospective studies are required to establish its effectiveness and determine the additional benefit of balloon decompression.

title: A Narrative Review on Intra-Articular Injection Therapies for Knee Osteoarthritis: Current Evidence and Future Perspectives.
abstract: This narrative review summarises current evidence on intra-articular injection therapies for knee osteoarthritis. Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a major global cause of disability, particularly among older adults, prompting growing interest in non-operative strategies that alleviate symptoms, preserve joint function, and delay surgical intervention. Established options including corticosteroids and hyaluronic acid, remain widely utilized for short and intermediate-term symptom relief. Regenerative approaches such as platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have gained prominence due to their potential anti-inflammatory and reparative effects. Novel biologic agents, including exosomes, atelocollagen, and isolated growth factors, show promise in supporting tissue repair and modulating joint homeostasis. Given the wide variability in mechanisms, efficacy, and safety profiles, selection of treatment regimen should be individualized based on disease severity, patient goals, and regulatory considerations. Overall, intra-articular injection therapies represent a diverse and rapidly evolving component of knee OA management. Continued high-quality randomized trials and standardized treatment protocols are essential to support evidence-based clinical decision-making and optimize patient outcomes.

title: Mapping evidence on kinesiophobia after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a scoping review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This review identified, synthesized, and mapped the scientific evidence on kinesiophobia, as assessed by the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK), in individuals following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), to provide clinicians with a comprehensive evidence map.
INTRODUCTION: Kinesiophobia can negatively impact rehabilitation and return-to-sport outcomes after ACLR. Despite its clinical relevance, the available evidence is fragmented, making it challenging for clinicians to find clear answers to their clinical questions and apply findings consistently in practice.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We considered studies that assessed kinesiophobia using the TSK in individuals of any age or sex following ACLR, regardless of sport participation or geographical setting. Included sources comprised peer-reviewed primary and secondary research.
METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted in the PubMed, Scopus, Academic Search Ultimate (EBSCOhost), SPORTDiscus (EBSCOhost), CINAHL Plus (EBSCOhost), and MEDLINE (EBSCOhost) databases up to September 2025. Research alerts were then maintained throughout the review process to identify newly published studies. A framework synthesis approach was adopted, whereby studies were systematically charted across 10 thematic domains, reflecting how kinesiophobia has been investigated in ACLR.
RESULTS: A total of 145 studies were included in this review. Most were cross-sectional and conducted in high-income countries, while longitudinal studies were limited. Adolescents and females were underrepresented, and the sample sizes and participant characteristics varied widely. Kinesiophobia was examined in relation to personal, clinical, functional, and neurophysiological variables. Intervention studies were scarce but explored cognitive-behavioral, educational, physical, and multimodal strategies for managing kinesiophobia. Only 2 studies adapted the TSK specifically for ACLR.
CONCLUSIONS: Clinicians now have access to a structured map of the evidence on kinesiophobia post-ACLR, which may inform clinical reflection. Future research should address methodological limitations and expand investigations in underrepresented populations and contexts.

title: Integrated physical, cognitive and psychological rehabilitation following multiple ACL reconstructions in a professional handball player: a case report.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries with repeated surgical interventions and postoperative complications pose a major challenge in sports rehabilitation. Beyond neuromuscular deficits, psychological and cognitive readiness often remain impaired, increasing reinjury risk and threatening athletic careers. This case highlights an integrated rehabilitation strategy addressing physical, psychological, and cognitive domains in a professional athlete with a complex surgical history.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 31-year-old white Serbian male professional handball player with a history of two ACL reconstructions, meniscal repairs, a postoperative knee infection, and multiple arthroscopic interventions presented with persistent knee instability, pain, and psychological distress. Following repeated failed return-to-play attempts, he underwent a ten-week intervention combining therapeutic exercises, sports psychology sessions, and neurocognitive dual-task training. Pre- and post-intervention assessments included gait analysis, postural control, strength testing, ACL-specific functional tests, and psychological evaluations. Post-intervention assessments showed improvements in gait mechanics, postural stability, neuromuscular strength, and reduced functional asymmetries, alongside lower cognitive anxiety and greater motivation.
CONCLUSIONS: This case suggests that an interdisciplinary, multimodal rehabilitation approach, integrating physical, psychological, and cognitive strategies, may help address both physical deficits and psychological barriers in athletes with multiple ACL surgeries and complex postoperative courses. Such integration may support function, confidence, and readiness in high-performance athletes facing career-threatening injuries.

title: Ultrasound-guided injection treatments for tendinopathy: an update.
abstract: The choice of treatment for chronic tendinopathy and related peritendinous conditions has become challenging as multiple options are available. When conservative treatments fail, injections of platelet-rich plasma (PRP), corticosteroids, and hyaluronic acid have become important in the management of these conditions. Other interventions, such as dry-needling, percutaneous tenotomy, percutaneous release, and hydrodissection, may also be used. Ultrasound guidance allows real-time visualization of the needle relative to its target and adjacent neurovascular structures. This is particularly advantageous for deep or small-caliber tendons, for procedures requiring precise intratendinous or peritendinous needle placement (e.g., PRP injection, hydrodissection), and for percutaneous release, where a blind approach carries a materially higher risk of neurovascular or tendon injury. This review summarizes the mechanism of action, technique, evidence, and indications for the injection treatments currently used for tendinopathy, and outlines the general principles of ultrasound-guided injection technique.

title: Persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain in young athletes: an overlooked biopsychosocial determinant of return to sport trajectories - a focused narrative review.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain is common in young athletes, yet its role in recovery and return to sport (RTS) decision-making remains insufficiently acknowledged. In youth sport, pain is often normalized or viewed primarily through an injury-centered lens, despite its potential to shape function, participation patterns, and athletic trajectories over time.
AREAS COVERED: This focused narrative review aimed to (1) synthesize current evidence on persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain in young athletes and (2) propose a developmentally informed biopsychosocial framework for understanding its implications for RTS. Electronic searches were conducted in PubMed, PsycINFO, and SPORTDiscus for studies published from 1 January 2006, through 28 February 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking and targeted hand-searching of reference lists. It integrates evidence on definitions, prevalence, clinical presentation, psychosocial and contextual factors, functional interference, and RTS decision-making, conceptualizing ongoing pain as an overlooked determinant of RTS trajectories.
EXPERT OPINION/COMMENTARY: In young athletes, pain should not be treated as a peripheral symptom or addressed only when recovery is delayed. More informed RTS decisions require attention not only to physical recovery markers, but also to how pain is experienced, interpreted, and managed throughout recovery. A developmentally informed biopsychosocial perspective may support earlier recognition, safer return decisions, more stable participation, and better long-term health outcomes.

title: Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness.
abstract: Optimizing astronaut mission readiness is a multidisciplinary endeavor that should integrate concepts from aerospace medicine, human performance, sports science, nutrition, and engineering. Situating astronauts within a theoretical framework similar to that of operational athletes, while addressing top human systems capability needs outlined for future missions, may be optimal for promoting sustained health and performance before, during, and after missions to low-Earth orbit, the lunar surface, and Mars. Mission readiness can be optimized by enhancing physiological and behavioral/psychological performance through data-driven and individualized exercise countermeasures, health and performance monitoring, precision nutrition, and rehabilitation strategies. Appropriate and stable space food systems that facilitate adequate provision of nutrients and fluids to prime astronauts for mission-critical tasks and operational demands are needed, though research is needed into potential nutritional considerations that might be useful for future missions. Behavioral readiness programs should emphasize stress inoculation, adaptive decision-making, communication, Earth-independent operation functionality, conflict resolution, leadership, and team-based problem-solving before flight to promote healthy team dynamics in-flight, along with proper society reintegration and uptake of family and occupational roles post-flight. Exercise remains an essential countermeasure during spaceflight, with an emphasis on maximizing fitness before launch to mitigate in-flight declines and on maintaining fitness levels and functionality during flight through high-intensity multimodal exercise. Following return to Earth, rehabilitative programs serve to restore cardiovascular, sensorimotor, and skeletal function, followed by enhancing skill-based performance components through a phase-based training program. Continuous monitoring systems that provide insight into health, performance, sleep, cognitive, nutritional, and recovery status should enable data-driven decision-making on physical readiness across all mission phases. By integrating insight from multiple disciplines, this unifying approach delivers a theoretical framework for sustaining astronaut health and performance during extended-duration missions.

title: Resistance-trained young men exhibit enhanced carotid vasoreactivity during the cold pressor test.
abstract: The function of the common carotid artery (CCA) is integral to the regulation of cerebral perfusion. Although endurance training is associated with consistent vascular benefits, the effects of resistance training on CCA function are unclear. The cold pressor test (CPT) assesses CCA vasoreactivity via sympathetic stimulation, with peak CCA vasoreactivity (CAR%peak) reflecting integrated endothelial-autonomic vascular function. In this study, we compared CAR%peak during the CPT in resistance-trained and untrained young men and examined associations with CCA stiffness and haemodynamics. CCA ultrasound was performed in 10 resistance-trained [24 years (95% confidence interval: 22,26)] and 10 untrained [24 years (22,25)] men at baseline, during a 3-min CPT and after recovery, with simultaneous haemodynamic assessment via finger plethysmography. CAR%peak was defined as the maximal percentage increase in mean diameter from baseline. Secondary outcomes included CCA stiffness indices and haemodynamics. Both groups exhibited CCA vasodilatation during CPT; however, CAR%peak was greater in resistance-trained men (P = 0.046). The resistance-trained group also displayed greater increases in systolic diameter at end-CPT (P = 0.033), alongside attenuated pulse pressure (P = 0.050; η2 p = 0.201) and β1-stiffness (P = 0.041) responses during CPT. CAR%peak was negatively correlated with baseline β2-stiffness in resistance-trained men (r = -0.655; P = 0.040), whereas in untrained control subjects it was positively correlated with peak pulse pressure (r = 0.677; P = 0.031). In conclusion, resistance-trained young men exhibit enhanced CCA vasoreactivity and attenuated pulse pressure and stiffness responses to sympathetic stimulation, reflecting favourable adaptations in endothelial-autonomic vascular regulation. These findings highlight the potential of resistance training to improve central vascular function in early adulthood.

title: Ergometer Testing for a New Olympic Discipline: Criterion Validity in Beach Sprint Rowing.
abstract: Beach Sprint rowing debuts at the 2028 Olympics without an established ergometer test for athlete selection. We examined the criterion validity of two ergometer protocols against Beach Sprint performance, each evaluated within its own season. In 2024, 21 athletes (14 men and 7 women) completed a 3-minute maximal effort (T3'), performed 3 months after the national championship. In 2025, 31 athletes (12 men and 19 women) completed two 2'30″ efforts separated by 6 minutes of recovery (T2×2'30″), performed approximately 2 months before the championship. The criterion was each athlete's mean time across all rounds. T3' correlated with mean competition times at r=-0.94 (95% confidence interval: -0.97 to -0.85), and T2×2'30″ at r=-0.73 (95% confidence interval: -0.86 to -0.50); adjusting for sex attenuated these correlations to r=-0.79 and r=-0.50, respectively. Models including sex explained 90% and 53% of the variance (standard error of the estimate: 5.3 s and 14.4 s), with leave-one-out cross-validation yielding Q 2 values of 0.87 and 0.43. Sex was an independent predictor under T3' (p=0.034) but not T2×2'30″. The between-effort decrement in T2×2'30″ was unrelated to competition performance. Ergometer performance was associated with Beach Sprint competition times under each protocol, evaluated separately within its own season.

title: Timing Matters: Assessing Fatigue During and After Resistance Training.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Monitoring neuromuscular fatigue during resistance training informs load prescription and recovery management. Two common approaches, namely within-training assessment (immediately after each set) and post-training assessment (after session completion), differ in their methodological demands, yet their acute responses and within-session reliability remain insufficiently characterized.
HYPOTHESIS: Fatigue levels would be influenced by training protocol, value type (maximum vs average), and set number or timepoint, with corresponding differences in within-session reliability.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized, counterbalanced crossover study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2.
METHODS: A total of 13 well-trained male athletes completed 3 protocols in randomized order: 5 sets of fixed-repetition squats (Fixed), 5 sets of velocity-loss-threshold-controlled squats (VLT), and a control condition. Countermovement jump (CMJ) height was assessed at baseline, after each set, and at 8 post-training timepoints (5-60 minutes). Fatigue was quantified as the percentage of CMJ height relative to baseline, using both maximum and average values of 2 trials. Within-session reliability was evaluated via coefficient of variation (CV) and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).
RESULTS: For within-training assessment, significant main effects emerged for protocol (P = 0.006), value type (P = 0.031), and set number (P < 0.001), with lower values (greater fatigue) observed when using average values and in the final 2 sets. All protocols demonstrated acceptable within-session reliability (CV ≤ 5.29%, ICC ≥ 0.745). For post-training assessment, time point significantly affected fatigue (P < 0.001), with the lowest values at 30 to 40 minutes. ICC was low during 0 to 15 minutes post-training; acceptable reliability was achieved only with maximum values from 10 minutes onward (CV ≤ 7.29%, ICC ≥ 0.750).
CONCLUSION: Both within-training and post-training fatigue assessments are feasible for monitoring resistance training fatigue, but methodological choices substantially influence measured values and reliability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For within-training fatigue monitoring, average values provide greater sensitivity in detecting fatigue; for post-training assessment, maximum values should be used after ≥10 minutes of rest to ensure acceptable reliability.

title: Assessment of Countermovement Jump Performance in Collegiate Baseball Athletes: A Longitudinal Multilevel Modeling Approach.
abstract: Burke, AA, Saine, ND, King, EL, Fields, JB, Jagim, AR, Miller, AD, Green, BC, and Jones, MT. Assessment of countermovement jump performance in collegiate baseball athletes: A longitudinal multilevel modeling approach. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Given the length and demands of the collegiate baseball season, monitoring body composition and neuromuscular performance can help optimize load management and athlete readiness. Relationships between body composition and countermovement jump (CMJ) performance were examined during a competitive baseball season. Pitchers and position athletes (n = 32) completed pre- and post-season dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scans and weekly CMJ testing. Countermovement jump variables included jump height (JH), reactive strength index modified, peak braking force (PBF), and peak propulsive force (PPF), all normalized to body mass (BM). Repeated-measures multivariate analyses of variance assessed time and group (pitcher vs. position player) effects. Pearson correlations evaluated associations between CMJ and body composition metrics, and hierarchical linear models (HLMs) quantified individual performance trajectories. Preseason-to-postseason reductions were observed in BM, fat free mass (FFM), JH, and PPF (p < 0.05). Peak braking force declined in pitchers, while PPF declined across both groups. Body composition showed negligible correlations with CMJ metrics, except for a moderately negative correlation between JH and body fat percentage (r = -0.52, p < 0.001). Hierarchical linear models revealed curvilinear CMJ performance trajectories (p < 0.001), with position players exhibiting lower PBF throughout the season (β = -1.47, p = 0.03) and preseason FFM positively predicting PBF (β = 0.118, p = 0.010). Findings suggest that reductions in lean mass and force output occur across the competitive season and vary by position. It is recommended that practitioners implement routine longitudinal monitoring when using CMJ and body composition assessments, as they may assist in detecting neuromuscular fatigue and guide individualized training interventions.

title: Trajectories of physical activity following digital education and exercise therapy-a longitudinal registry study among 15,197 persons with knee or hip osteoarthritis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study examined trajectories of physical activity (PA) and associated factors among individuals with knee or hip osteoarthritis (OA) participating in a digital education and exercise therapy program. We additionally compared patterns of patient-reported outcomes (PROs) across the identified trajectories.
METHODS: A longitudinal registry-based study. Individuals aged 40 + years with a diagnosis of knee or hip OA-confirmed through referral documentation or based on the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines and Swedish national criteria- participating in the digital program with responses to validated self-reported PA questions at enrolment and at least one follow-up (3-month intervals up to 1 year after enrolment) were included (n = 15,197). The recommended PA level was defined as ≥ 150 min/week of moderate to vigorous physical activity (yes/no). We used group-based trajectory modelling (GBTM) to identify distinct PA trajectories and multinomial logistic regression to explore associated factors. Changes in PROs from enrolment up to 1-year follow-up across PA trajectories were analysed using random intercept models.
RESULTS: The proportion of participants reaching the recommended PA levels rose from 51.4% (95% CI: 50.6, 52.2) at enrolment to 58.5% (57.1, 59.9) at one year. GBTM identified four distinct PA trajectories: persistently high (41.2%), persistently low (30.4%), increasing (16.5%), and declining (11.9%). Body mass index (BMI) followed by physical function were the most important factors associated with PA trajectory. All PA trajectories experienced clinically comparable improvements in PROs.
CONCLUSIONS: About 60% of participants reached or maintained recommended PA levels. The results suggest possible PA promotion by targeted strategies for individuals with higher BMI and poorer function. Comparable improvements in PROs across PA trajectories may support the provision of education and exercise therapy to all individuals with OA regardless of their PA level.

title: Role of the posterior tibial tendon in plantar pressure distribution across progressive stages of ligamentous insufficiency in a cadaveric flatfoot model.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Progressive collapsing foot deformity involves failure of both static and dynamic medial arch stabilizers. The relative timing and interaction between posterior tibial tendon dysfunction and ligamentous attenuation remain unclear. This study investigates whether the posterior tibial tendon can compensate for progressive ligament failure in distributing pressure under the foot in a cadaveric progressive collapsing foot deformity model at balanced stance.
METHODS: Eight cadaveric lower limbs underwent sequential ligament transections replicating progressive collapsing foot deformity. Plantar pressure was recorded during balanced stance using TekScan sensors under both loaded and unloaded posterior tibial tendon conditions. Axial and tendon loads mimicked physiologic forces. Medial-lateral and hindfoot-forefoot pressure ratios were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
FINDINGS: Unloading the posterior tibial tendon significantly increased hindfoot-to-forefoot loading ratios and shifted the center of pressure posteriorly across all ligamentous transection stages (P < 0.05). Medial-to-lateral loading for the entire foot shifted laterally only after the deltoid ligament transection (P = 0.016). In intact feet and short and long plantar ligament conditions, posterior tibial tendon unloading caused a medial shift in hindfoot force (P = 0.039 and P = 0.016, respectively).
INTERPRETATION: This study demonstrates the posterior tibial tendon plays a critical role in distributing plantar load and minimizing hindfoot overload through various stages of ligamentous failure. While posterior tibial tendon unloading consistently increased hindfoot loading, its influence on medial-lateral balance was variable. These findings support early interventions that preserve or augment posterior tibial tendon function to maintain biomechanical stability of the hindfoot.

title: Sleep-related metrics that predict training intensity: an exploratory study in women's college athletics.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In recent years, the development of wearable monitoring technologies has expanded objective assessments of workload and fatigue, predominantly via heart rate (HR)-based markers (e.g., heart rate variability, resting heart rate). There are also perception-based markers of exertion commonly used in high-performance training settings, such as rating of perceived exertion (RPE) scales. Previous research has shown that these markers do not measure identical but rather complementary aspects of exertion, but limited data exist on the relationships between objective and subjective markers at the daily level; data which may be especially important for understanding how to best monitor for effort or overtraining. This study will characterize both HR- and perception-based markers of exertion at the daily level in women's college athletes. Additionally, given the powerful influence of sleep on both athletic performance and perceptions of physical exertion, we further explored how sleep behaviors at the within- and between-person level relate to daily assessments of subjective and objective exertion.
METHODS: Thirteen women's college athletes continuously wore a WHOOP activity monitor for this two-week observational study. RPE was self-reported within 30 min of completing a training session or competition and prior to viewing WHOOP data.
RESULTS: A series of descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation were conducted to describe the relationship between RPE and activity strain on a daily level among the population studied. A series of linear mixed-effects models demonstrated worse sleep on average (i.e., more debt, poorer sleep performance) was associated with higher HR-based markers of exertion; however, within-person elevations in sleep consistency, but more sleep need on average was associated with higher HR-based measures of exertion and lower perceptions of exertion.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings support the need for additional research to better understand the drivers of daily markers of exertion to enhance the health and performance of athletes.

title: Technical evaluation of transport-derived movement trajectories during knee osteoarthritis rehabilitation.
abstract: Wearable inertial sensors enable repeated movement recording during knee osteoarthritis rehabilitation, but methods for summarizing multivariable changes across routine sessions remain exploratory. This retrospective technical evaluation examined a normalized transport-derived deviation (NTD) constructed from paired shank-mounted inertial measurement units. Seven participants contributed 46 paired-sensor sessions over 45 d. An approximately 30 s active movement segment from each session was divided into 13 windows and represented using 58 time-domain, frequency-domain and cross-sensor features. Session distributions were compared with each participant's first usable sensor session using an archived entropically regularized transport implementation. The output was normalized by the baseline-to-final-session value. Mean NTD values at the scheduled assessment days were 0.00, 0.02, 0.23, 0.63 and 1.00. 14 of the 46 displayed values were structurally constrained baseline or final values; no monotonic constraint was applied to the 32 interior observations, which formed non-decreasing trajectories. At interior scheduled days 5, 15 and 30, absolute differences between mean NTD and participant-adjusted normalized elapsed time were 0.057, 0.076 and 0.019. 21 of the 46 archived calculations reached the 500-iteration limit without meeting the 1 × 10-6residual criterion. A log-domain stabilized recomputation of all 46 primary comparisons satisfied a 1 × 10-8criterion, with a mean absolute archived-to-stabilized NTD difference of 0.004 (maximum 0.018) across the 32 interior observations. Across support-point counts of 100-1000, interior archived NTD values changed by 0.009-0.026 on average. Routine paired-shank recordings were organized into ordered longitudinal trajectories and the resulting trajectory structure was numerically reproducible under the evaluated implementation. NTD should presently be interpreted as an implementation-specific retrospective coordinate rather than a validated rehabilitation outcome. By defining the requirements for standardized movement tasks, prospective normalization and reproducible sensor placement, these findings provide a practical foundation for prospective validation of transport-based rehabilitation assessment.

title: An Intensified Training Period Reduces REM Sleep but this Decline Can Be Mitigated by Ketone Ester Supplementation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We previously showed that a strenuous training day disrupts sleep efficiency and REM sleep, and that these disturbances can be counteracted by ketone monoester (R)-3-hydroxybutyl-(R)-3-hydroxybutyrate (KE) supplementation. However, the impact of prolonged intensified training on sleep quality, as well as the potential modulating effect of KE are unknown.
METHODS: We performed a double-blind study in which twenty-four trained male athletes completed a 7-week training program with a gradual increase in training load while receiving either 25g of a control drink (CON, n=12) or 25g of KE (n=12) after each training session and 30 minutes before sleep. At the start (PRE), week 3 (MID), and the end (POST) of the training program, we evaluated sleep using polysomnography, and perceived stress/recovery balance using the REST-Q questionnaire. Timing, duration, and relative intensity of exercise on each testing day were identical.
RESULTS: The progressive increase in training load induced a decrease in the perceived stress-recovery state in both groups (PRE: 73±21 vs. POST: 40±37, p<0.001, Hedges' g = 1.097). From PRE to MID, sleep efficiency improved by 3% in both groups (p=0.003, Hedges' g = 0.663) while wakefulness after sleep onset reduced by 2% (p=0.031, Hedges' g = 0.716). However, from PRE to POST, total REM sleep decreased by 2% in CON but increased by 3% in KE (p=0.002, for KE vs. CON, Hedges' g = 0.939). Perceived sleep quality did not differ between groups throughout the intervention.
CONCLUSIONS: Our data indicate that KE supplementation did not enhance the beneficial effect of an initial increase in training load on sleep but prevented the decline in REM sleep upon a further training load increment.

title: Central and peripheral vascular recovery following resistance exercise with and without blood flow restriction across age groups: a parallel group crossover randomized trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: High-intensity resistance training (HIRT) benefits musculoskeletal and vascular health but may be poorly tolerated by older adults. Low-intensity resistance training (LIRT) is an alternative, yet evidence on arterial stiffness is mixed, and it often fails to improve vascular health due to insufficient stimulus. Blood flow restriction (BFR) enhances hemodynamic stimulus, but its acute cardiovascular effects in older adults remain unclear.
PURPOSE: To compare central and peripheral vascular responses following acute LIRT with BFR versus HIRT across age groups.
METHODS: In a randomized crossover design, 19 young (22±3 years) and 19 older (70±9 years) adults completed three sessions: HIRT (3 × 10 reps at 75%1RM), LIRT+BFR (4 × 20 reps at 30%1RM with continuous cuff occlusion), and no exercise. Central and peripheral vascular function were assessed via oscillometric pulse wave analysis at rest, 5-min (RECOV1), and 30-min (RECOV2) post-exercise.
RESULTS: In older adults, neither HIRT nor LIRT+BFR altered total peripheral resistance (TPR), aortic reservoir function, or subendocardial viability ratio (SEVR) throughout post-exercise, with no differences observed between conditions. Conversely, young adults exhibited reductions at RECOV1 following HIRT in TPR (Δ = - 0.176 PRU), reservoir function (Δ = - 11.9%), and SEVR (Δ = - 47.1%), persisting at RECOV2 (all p < 0.05). LIRT+BFR elicited minor changes. Most variables normalized within 30 min for both groups.
CONCLUSION: In older adults, LIRT+BFR elicits post acute central vascular responses comparable to HIRT, with stable coronary perfusion and rapid recovery supporting the short-term tolerability of both modalities. LIRT+BFR thus represents a viable alternative to HIRT for older population.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT06596304).

title: Error Related Negativity and Error Positivity: Neural Indices of Double-Faults in Elite Athletes.
abstract: ObjectiveError-related negativity (ERN) and error positivity (Pe) are key neural responses of human error monitoring. However, their relationship to behavioral adjustments after the mistakes in speeded laboratory experiments has shown mixed results. The present study examined whether ERN and Pe amplitudes would be better predictors of performance recovery following an error in a sport context than in a speeded laboratory task.MethodsFifteen male professional basketball players (18-26 years) performed a letter-based Eriksen Flanker task while their brain activity was recorded using 32-channel electroencephalography (EEG). Then, they completed a standardized 100-shot free-throw protocol on their home court. Recovery in the laboratory was measured as the ratio of back-to-back errors to total errors in the Flanker task, while recovery on the court was measured as the ratio of consecutive missed free throws to total misses. Pearson correlations and linear regression analysis were used to examine how ERP magnitudes relate to each recovery measure.ResultsAlthough ERN and Pe amplitudes were not associated with the laboratory consecutive-error ratio (all p values >.05), they were significant predictors of the field consecutive-miss ratio. Athletes with larger Pe and ERN amplitudes had significantly fewer consecutive misses (p < .001 and p = .017).ConclusionsERN and Pe may be less relevant for predicting specific post-error adjustments to immediate task demands and more relevant for predicting overall regulatory capacity in ecologically valid settings. Our findings highlight the need to use real-world performance measures when linking error monitoring with the realm of athletic performance.

title: Cross-sectional associations of maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors with athlete engagement among provincial- and municipal-level athletes in Sichuan, China.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors are potentially modifiable daily practices, yet their relationship with the psychological state that sustains sport involvement remains unclear. This study examined cross-sectional associations among maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors (MSHB), multidimensional fatigue, difficulties in emotion regulation, and athlete engagement, including three model-based indirect associations.
METHODS: A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was completed by 317 adult athletes recruited from provincial- and municipal-level teams in Sichuan Province, China. Participants represented table tennis, badminton, tennis, basketball, volleyball, and football. The Sleep Hygiene Index, the Chinese Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory, the DERS-16, and the Athlete Engagement Questionnaire were administered. A reflective partial least squares structural equation model was estimated with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Measurement quality, construct differentiation, common-method diagnostics, out-of-sample prediction, demographic adjustment, alternative cross-sectional specifications, and subgroup robustness were evaluated.
RESULTS: More frequent MSHB were associated with greater fatigue [β = 0.491, 95% CI (0.408, 0.573)], greater difficulties in emotion regulation [β = 0.178, 95% CI (0.079, 0.274)], and lower athlete engagement [β = -0.264, 95% CI (-0.370, -0.161)]. Fatigue was associated with greater difficulties in emotion regulation [β = 0.588, 95% CI (0.500, 0.673)] and lower engagement [β = -0.325, 95% CI (-0.446, -0.205)]; difficulties in emotion regulation were also associated with lower engagement [β = -0.232, 95% CI (-0.351, -0.108)]. The total indirect association was [β = -0.268, 95% CI (-0.338, -0.204)], and the model explained 47.2% of engagement variance. Demographic adjustment yielded comparable estimates. Reverse-order and parallel specifications fitted the cross-sectional covariance structure equally well.
CONCLUSION: Within the sampled setting, more frequent MSHB co-occurred with greater fatigue, more difficulties in emotion regulation, and lower athlete engagement. Fatigue accounted for the largest specific indirect association. The single-occasion self-report design leaves actual sleep disturbance, temporal sequence, and causal effects unresolved.

title: Cardiac autonomic and hemodynamic responses to two-stage cycling and post-exercise recovery with partial blood flow restriction in young males.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study compared acute cardiovascular and cardiac autonomic responses during graded (two-stage) aerobic cycling and subsequent recovery performed with and without partial blood flow restriction (BFR).
METHODS: Fifteen young males completed two sessions in a crossover design (control vs. bilateral thigh BFR). Each session included rest, 5 min of cycling at 40% maximal power output (Pmax), 5 min at 60% Pmax, and 10 min of recovery; BFR was released immediately at exercise cessation. ECG and arterial blood pressure were recorded. RR interval, mean arterial blood pressure (MBP), HRV (lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, LF, LF/HF), and composite indices of cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic activity (SNS, PNS) were derived from 3-min segments at rest, exercise, and recovery. Heart rate recovery at 30, 60, and 120 s after exercise cessation (HRR30, HRR60, HRR120) was calculated. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested condition, time, and interaction.
RESULTS: Time × condition interactions were observed for RR interval (p=0.015) and MBP (p=0.003), indicating altered hemodynamic kinetics under BFR, primarily during recovery. HRV indices showed no time × condition interactions; however, BFR produced lower lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, and PNS and higher SNS than control (all p<0.05), whereas LF and LF/HF were unchanged. HRR30 (p=0.040), HRR60 (p<0.001), and HRR120 (p=0.010) were attenuated under BFR.
CONCLUSIONS: BFR modifies cardiovascular regulation during two-stage cycling and recovery and induces sustained autonomic shifts toward reduced parasympathetic and increased sympathetic modulation, largely independent of exercise intensity. Altered recovery kinetics following cuff release highlight the importance of careful monitoring during the recovery phase when applying BFR.

title: The Sonographic Muscle Injury Classification in Soccer: proposal for an ultrasound-based muscle injury classification.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To propose a novel ultrasound-based classification system for muscle injuries in soccer players, termed the Sonographic Muscle Injury Classification in Soccer (SOMICS), and to evaluate its association, ordinal consistency, and agreement with the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a cross-sectional observational study including 51 adolescent male soccer players (11-19 years of age) with suspected acute myotendinous injuries. All athletes underwent ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 24 h after injury. Four experienced radiologists, working independently, reviewed the images.
RESULTS: Interobserver agreement was substantial for ultrasound (κ = 0.65) and MRI (κ = 0.70). A strong ordinal correlation was observed between SOMICS and BAMIC categories (ρ = 0.80; p < 0.001), with a statistically significant association (χ2 = 52.53; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The SOMICS demonstrated significant association, ordinal consistency, and substantial agreement with the BAMIC for severity stratification of muscle injuries. Although not intended to replace MRI-based classifications for prognostic decision-making, the SOMICS provides a structured, reproducible ultrasound-based approach that may be useful in clinical settings where MRI is not readily available or as a first-line imaging tool.
authors: Claudio Henrique Ivo de Araújo Ribeiro

title: Sleep Quality and Adherence to the Mediterranean Diet in Male Young Adults: An Exploratory Study Among Amateur Soccer Players, Physically Active Individuals, and Individuals with High Sitting Time.
abstract: Amateur soccer players represent a relatively understudied population and often combine training with study or work, facing daily challenges that can impact sleep, diet, and circadian-related behaviors. Since these factors are important for health, recovery, and well-being, this study aimed to examine sleep quality, adherence to the Mediterranean diet, and chronotype in amateur soccer players compared with physically active individuals and individuals with high sitting time. The sample comprised 55 male young adults (23.36 ± 3.11 years): amateur soccer players (n = 20), physically active individuals (n = 18), and individuals with high sitting time (n = 17). All participants completed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the PREvención con DIeta MEDiterránea (PREDIMED), and the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ). Group comparisons were performed using appropriate parametric or non-parametric tests, and exploratory correlation analyses were used to examine associations among sleep quality, Mediterranean diet adherence, and chronotype. Lower PSQI scores (p < 0.001) were observed in soccer players (3.80 ± 1.32) and physically active individuals (4.17 ± 1.92) than in individuals with high sitting time (6.24 ± 2.05). No significant between-group differences were found in PREDIMED (soccer players = 6.80 ± 2.22; physically active individuals = 7.50 ± 1.89; individuals with high sitting time = 7.29 ± 2.42) and MEQ (soccer players = 51.60 ± 5.90; physically active individuals = 50.89 ± 7.70; individuals with high sitting time = 51.82 ± 11.43). Exploratory correlation analyses, without correction for multiple testing, identified a negative association between MEQ and PSQI in individuals with high sitting time (r = -0.514, p = 0.035). These findings describe group differences in self-reported sleep quality, whereas Mediterranean diet adherence and chronotype appeared similar across groups.

title: Biomechanical comparison of an ultrasound-guided minimally invasive modified Kessler construct and an open Krackow construct for Achilles tendon repair: a cadaver study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Open Achilles tendon repair can cause wound-related complications. Ultrasound-guided minimally invasive repair may reduce soft-tissue disruption, but its biomechanical performance requires further evaluation. This study compared the initial biomechanical performance of an ultrasound-guided minimally invasive modified Kessler construct with an open Krackow construct in a cadaveric model.
METHODS: Twelve fresh-frozen cadaveric Achilles tendons were transected 4 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion and allocated to an open Krackow group (n = 6) or an ultrasound-guided minimally invasive modified Kessler group (n = 6). Testing included 10 loading cycles (50 N at 2.1 mm/s) followed by pull-to-failure testing (25 mm/s). Maximum load to failure and failure modes were recorded.
FINDINGS: No statistically significant difference in maximum load to failure was observed between the Krackow (149.2 ± 39.0 N) and ultrasound-guided minimally invasive modified Kessler (148.5 ± 22.8 N) constructs (Mann-Whitney U test, U = 18, p > 0.05). All specimens completed the initial cyclic loading phase. In the minimally invasive group, three specimens failed after 5-mm gapping and three by suture knot breakage; in the Krackow group, five failed after 5-mm gapping and one by suture rupture.
INTERPRETATION: The ultrasound-guided minimally invasive modified Kessler construct demonstrated load-to-failure performance comparable to the open Krackow construct. When both repairs use four core strands crossing the repair site, the overall construct may reduce the mechanical difference expected from suture configuration alone. However, this small cadaveric cohort does not establish formal biomechanical equivalence or isolate the independent contribution of ultrasound guidance.

title: Female Versus Male Differences in Burnout With Sport: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Burnout is a widely recognized problem in sports. Female athletes have been found to experience more emotional exhaustion and less depersonalization, key components of burnout, than their male counterparts. Researchers have found varied results when comparing rates of burnout between male and female athletes.
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to review the current literature with the goal of determining what differences exist between male and female athletes regarding sport burnout.
DATA SOURCES: PubMed (Medline), Cochrane library, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL, Embase, and Web of Science.
STUDY SELECTION: Articles that were originally written in English, included athletes participating in organized sport, evaluated athletic burnout, and compared rates of burnout among different sexes were included in this review. Articles that were cadaveric, animal, review, or expert opinions were excluded.
STUDY DESIGN: Systematic review.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4.
DATA EXTRACTION: The age, sex, sport, and level of athletic competition of individual athletes were extracted from each article in addition to burnout rates and outcome scores of male and female athletes.
RESULTS: Of the 18 studies included in this review, 10 (56%) found no significant differences in sport burnout among male and female athletes, 7 (39%) found that female athletes experienced greater burnout than male athletes and 1 (5.6%) found that male athletes experienced greater burnout than female athletes. Reduced sense of accomplishment and physical/emotional exhaustion were implicated in creating more burnout among female athletes than their male counterparts in 4 studies.
CONCLUSION: It remains unclear how the constructs of sex and gender affect athlete burnout. The heterogeneity of studies included in this review prevented the analysis of how participation in team sports, participation in individual sports, level of competition, and the coach-athlete relationship influence sport burnout. More standardized studies are needed to better evaluate the effect sex and gender have on athlete burnout as well as how athletes involved in various sports are affected by burnout.

title: Hitting Volume Demands during Men's Australian Open and Roland Garros: Effects of Tournament, Competition Phase, and Player Level.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hitting volume is a key component of external load in tennis, as it reflects the cumulative demands associated with the repetitive execution of complex stroke actions during match play. Despite its relevance for workload monitoring and injury prevention, limited information is available regarding how hitting volume demands vary according to playing surface, tournament progression, and player level in elite professional tennis.
HYPOTHESIS: Hitting volume demands vary according to tournament, competition phase, and player ranking level.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional observational study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Match data were collected from 474 player-match observations (236 at the Australian Open and 238 at Roland Garros). Complete stroke count data were available for 384 player-match observations, comprising 214,874 analyzed strokes. Match duration, stroke counts, and rally length distributions were compared across tournaments, competition phases, and ranking groups.
RESULTS: Roland Garros matches were characterized by greater overall hitting volumes than Australian Open matches (P = 0.04), despite a similar number of points played. These differences were reflected in higher groundstroke volumes and a greater proportion of medium and long rallies at Roland Garro (P < 0.05). Competition phase was associated with differences in selected stroke-count variables and rally structure, with later-round matches showing a greater proportion of prolonged rallies (P < 0.05), although overall match duration and total stroke volume remained comparable. Differences according to player level were also identified. Top 10 players accumulated lower overall hitting volumes (P < 0.05) and exhibited a lower proportion of short rallies together with a greater proportion of prolonged exchanges than lower-ranked players (P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Hitting volume demands were associated with tournament, competition phase, and player ranking level. These contextual factors should be considered when interpreting competition loads and planning training and recovery strategies during Grand Slam competition.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The reported competition reference values may assist coaches and sports medicine practitioners in optimizing surface-specific training prescription, workload monitoring, fatigue management, and return-to-play strategies in professional tennis.

title: Ergogenic effects of beetroot juice supplementation on neuromuscular function and simulated combat demands in elite female taekwondo athletes.
abstract: Beetroot juice supplementation has been widely examined across various sport disciplines due to its potential ergogenic effects. However, evidence regarding its impact on combat sports particularly in female athletes remains limited. The aim of this study was to evaluate the acute effects of beetroot juice supplementation on simulated taekwondo combat performance and neuromuscular function in elite female taekwondo athletes. Seven elite female Olympic taekwondo athletes (age: 20.3 ± 3.7 years), participated in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study consisting of two experimental trials). Each trial involved the consumption of either 140 mL of beetroot juice (which contains 12.8 mmol NO₃⁻) or 140 mL of a placebo (with 0.08 mmol NO₃⁻) followed by a simulated taekwondo combat session and assessments of neuro-muscular function (i.e., vertical jump and visual cognitive performance). In addition, metabolic (i.e., blood lactate), and perceptual responses (i.e., rate of perceived exertion) were measured before, after, and 3 minutes post-combat. No significant differences during the simulated taekwondo combat (e.g., attack time; p = 0.531-0.989; ηp² = 0.01-0.05), neuromuscular function battery (p = 0.302-0.700; ηp² = 0.02-0.04), blood lactate concentrations (p = 0.705; ηp² = 0.13), or rate of perceived exertion values (RPE) (p = 0.717; ηp² = 0.12) were obtained between beetroot juice and placebo conditions. Acute ingestion of beetroot juice (140 mL) did not enhance simulated combat performance or neuromuscular function in female Olympic taekwondo athletes.

title: Physical examination of the cervical spine should be conducted in female athletes with a history of concussion.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Female athletes may be at increased risk of injury following sports-related concussion (SRC), even after symptom resolution. Residual cervical spine impairments have been proposed as a potential contributor; however, these have not been well characterised in female athletes. This study aimed to examine whether a history of SRC was associated with clinical assessments of the cervical spine in female athletes.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, 156 elite and pre-elite female athletes from water polo, soccer, diving, rugby-7s and cycling/BMX were recruited. History of SRC within the previous 12 months was self-reported. Assessments included questionnaires and physical examination of the cervical spine, comprising range of motion, manual examination, joint position error (JPE) and maximal isometric neck strength. Between-group differences were examined using univariable statistical analyses.
RESULTS: Athletes with a history of SRC demonstrated a higher prevalence of reduced cervical range of motion, positive findings on manual examination, increased JPE and a history of headaches or migraines compared with athletes without concussion history. No deficits in maximal isometric neck strength were observed in athletes with a history of SRC.
CONCLUSION: Cervical spine impairments were more commonly observed in female athletes with a history of SRC within the previous 12 months, including in athletes who did not report current neck pain. These findings suggest consideration of targeted cervical spine assessment beyond symptom-based screening in athletes with a concussion history. Whether identification and management of cervical spine impairments influence subsequent injury risk requires investigation in prospective and interventional studies.

title: Endocrine dynamics of special operations forces across mission cycles: implications for human stress physiology.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study investigates the endocrine responses and muscle damage markers in elite male Special Operations Force operators across operational phases to understand hormonal adaptations to extreme operational stress and recovery.
METHODS: Fifty-six operators (28-42 years) participated in a longitudinal study conducted at a Special Operations Forces unit. Blood samples were collected at three visits: Visit 1 (baseline recovery), Visit 2 (intensive pre-deployment training), and Visit 3 (post-deployment recovery). Serum concentrations of testosterone (T), cortisol (CORT), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S), growth hormone (GH), insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I), progesterone (P4), creatine kinase (CK), and myoglobin (Mb) were analyzed.
RESULTS: Post-deployment (Visit 3), T levels increased (+ 20%, p < 0.05), and CORT decreased (- 23%, p < 0.05), resulting in a significantly higher testosterone-to-cortisol ratio compared with Visit 1 and Visit 2 (p ≤ 0.05). DHEA-S correlated with CORT (r = 0.37, p < 0.05), suggesting a compensatory adrenal response under stress. GH concentrations were markedly reduced post-deployment (- 84%, p ≤ 0.05), while IGF-I remained stable, indicating differential regulation within the GH-IGF-I axis during recovery. P4 concentrations remained elevated across all phases, reflecting a consistent endocrine feature across operational phases rather than a defined mechanistic adaptation. No significant changes were observed in CK or Mb, underscoring effective physical stress management at the time of post-deployment sampling.
CONCLUSION: These findings emphasize the importance of tailored training and recovery strategies for sustaining endocrine balance, resilience, and operational readiness in elite military personnel.

title: Programmable 4D printing of sustainable multifunctional photoresins with tissue-matched mechanics for interfacial tissue regeneration.
abstract: The integrative regeneration of articular cartilage and subchondral bone remains a major clinical challenge due to the difficulties of mimicking the spatial and compositional complexity of native osteochondral tissues in artificial implants. To overcome these limitations, 3D printing has enabled personalized solutions, going beyond traditional plug-shaped scaffolds that are limited to repairing small, cylindrical focal defects. In this study, we report solvent-free 4D printing of olive oil-derived fatty amide-based acrylate photoresin for osteochondral tissue engineering applications. The physicochemical properties of the printed polymers were fine-tuned using acrylic acid as a comonomer. With optimized printing conditions, the resin can be printed into high-resolution objects with each layer of ∼50-100 μm. Depending on the resin composition, the mechanical properties of the printed polymers vary between ∼200-1400 kPa with ∼210-420% strain under tensile setting, and ∼26-98 MPa at ∼80% strain under compressive setting. The mechanical properties of the printed polymers are comparable to those of various interfacial soft tissues, including ligaments, articular cartilage, and soft collagenous bone, indicating their potential for interfacial tissue engineering applications. Furthermore, the printed polymers showed near-body temperature-responsive shape memory (4D) properties with a recovery ratio of ∼99% for optimized resin composition. In addition, the printed polymers exhibited excellent bactericidal antimicrobial activity against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, highlighting their multifunctional nature. More importantly, the printed polymers exhibited good cytocompatibility (cell viability ∼≥90% across all samples compared to control) toward adipose-derived human mesenchymal stem cells, facilitating growth factor-free osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiation, which confirms their potential for osteochondral tissue regeneration. Overall, the newly developed biobased resin offers a low-cost, sustainable alternative for 4D printing of personalized implants for osteochondral tissue regeneration.

title: UEFA consensus guidelines on anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in Women's football - part one: risk factors and prevention.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are among the most burdensome injuries in women's football, carrying significant consequences for players and the football community. To develop practical, evidence-based guidelines for ACL injury prevention, UEFA convened a multidisciplinary expert panel of 31 doctors, sports scientists, physiotherapists, and a player. Using the RAND-UCLA Appropriateness Method, 101 evidence statements were synthesised from existing literature and subjected to a modified Delphi process with three rounds of confidential voting. Consensus was reached on 88 statements. Through online and in-person discussions, this evidence was integrated with expert and clinical and practical judgement to produce actionable recommendations tailored to women's football. The guidelines conclude that ACL injuries in women's football typically occur in non-contact situations during high-intensity movements such as cutting, pressing, or landing, and may be influenced by a combination of modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors. Proposed modifiable factors include deficits in neuromuscular control, strength, and movement quality, which can be addressed through multicomponent prevention strategies. These programmes were identified as the most effective, incorporating plyometric, strength, and proximal control exercises performed two to three times per week for 15 to 20 minutes, with evidence showing they can reduce non-contact ACL injuries when adherence is high. Successful implementation requires context-specific tailoring, embedding programmes into routine training, and addressing barriers such as limited resources, time constraints, and lack of coach education. The guidelines recommend enhancing buy-in through co-creation with coaches and players, integrating prevention into existing practice, and strengthening organisational and policy support to sustain long-term adoption.

title: Biceps rerouting and derotational radial osteotomy: A technique for correcting forearm supination in NBPBP.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Forearm supination deformity is a recognized late sequela of neonatal brachial plexus birth palsy (NBPBP) that can impair functional positioning of the hand and limit activities requiring forearm pronation. Surgical options include forearm osteotomy, tendon rerouting, tendon transfer, and combined procedures. We describe a modified technique combining derotational radial osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation.
METHODS: This was a single-patient technical case report. An 18-year-old male with longstanding fixed forearm supination deformity secondary to NBPBP underwent radial derotational osteotomy and biceps tendon rerouting. The biceps tendon was detached with the forearm in maximal supination, rerouted through the interosseous space, and secured with a cortical button with the forearm in maximal pronation. A radial osteotomy was subsequently performed toward pronation with approximately 30° to 45° of rotational correction. Postoperative rehabilitation included protected immobilization followed by progressive range of motion and strengthening.
RESULTS: Preoperatively, the forearm rested in approximately 15° of supination, with active pronation limited to neutral and active supination to approximately 50°. Following surgery, the forearm rested in approximately 15° to 20° of pronation. Passive forearm rotation improved from 45° of supination to 40° of pronation preoperatively to 60° of supination to 75° of pronation postoperatively. At 12 months, active pronation improved from neutral to 55° of pronation. No postoperative complications were reported during follow-up. The patient participated in occupational therapy 1 to 2 times weekly during recovery.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of combining radial derotational osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation for longstanding supination deformity following NBPBP. The technique provides an additional fixation option for tendon rerouting while addressing the underlying osseous rotational deformity. Given the single-patient design and absence of comparative or biomechanical data, further study is required to determine whether cortical button fixation offers advantages over established tendon fixation methods and to evaluate the reproducibility and clinical efficacy of this approach.

title: ATG5-overexpressing MSCs improve ligament healing with an associated shift toward M2 macrophage polarization in aged rats.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Autophagy is crucial for maintaining mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) function, yet its role in age-related ligament healing deficits remains unclear. This study examined the relationship between MSC autophagic activity and age-related ligament healing and evaluated ATG5 overexpression effects on autophagy and regeneration.
METHODS: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury models were established in young and aged rats. Healing was assessed using ultrasound, histology, immunohistochemistry, apoptosis assays, and biomechanical testing. Aged MSCs were engineered to overexpress ATG5 and transplanted into injured ligaments. Repair outcomes and macrophage polarization changes were evaluated.
RESULTS: Aged rats exhibited impaired ligament healing, and aged MSCs displayed reduced autophagic activity. ATG5 overexpression enhanced autophagy in aged MSCs, and transplantation of ATG5-overexpressing MSCs was associated with improved ligament repair in aged rats, including increased proliferation, angiogenesis, collagen organization, and biomechanical strength, alongside reduced apoptosis. ATG5-overexpressing MSC transplantation was also associated with lower M1 and higher M2 macrophage markers and a more anti-inflammatory cytokine profile. Reduced MSC autophagy was associated with age-related ligament healing deficits.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings support a potential relationship among ATG5-associated autophagy, macrophage phenotype, and improved ligament repair, while the causal dependence of therapeutic effects on autophagy and macrophage polarization remains to be established.

title: More than fuel: Why athletes need better language around food.
abstract: "Food is fuel" is a widely used phrase in sport settings intended to emphasize the importance of nutrition for performance. While nutrition is essential for health and success, this framing may unintentionally reinforce a narrow, performance-oriented understanding of eating that has implications for athletes' relationships with food and their bodies. Athletes are at heightened risk for eating concerns, low energy availability, and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs), and aspects of sport culture may contribute to rigid, rule-based approaches to eating. This commentary argues that "food is fuel" language reflects and reinforced broader sports norms centered around optimization, control, and performance. Potential consequences include reduced attunement to internal cues and the moralization of food choices, particularly in sport environments where appearance and performance are closely intertwined. Language is proposed as a modifiable factor for prevention and more flexible, athlete-centered approaches to discussing food and eating are identified. Rather than dismissing the importance of nutrition in athletics, this commentary advocates for broader conceptualizations of eating that acknowledge its physical, psychological, social, and cultural functions and support athletes in developing sustainable relationships with food throughout and beyond their athletic careers.

title: Early-stage calcification promotes tendon damage under cyclic loading through alterations in interfascicular matrix viscoelastic properties.
abstract: Calcification is a prevalent condition that alters mechanical and structural properties of soft tissues. While significant efforts have been devoted to the characterization of tendon mechanics, little work has been done so far on understanding the impact of calcification on tissues such as tendons. In this work, we investigate the influence of cycling loading and forced fluid flow on the mechanical and structural properties of tendon fascicle bundles of varying interfascicular matrix (IFM) content at an early stage of calcification. The calcification process was modeled using sample incubation in concentrated simulated body fluid. To evaluate the biomechanical responses of the tendon over the course of calcification, we compared four sets of samples incubated for 7 days in simulated body fluid, forced fluid flow and under cyclic uniaxial loading against a non-incubated control. Mechanical and structural properties were investigated using uniaxial tests, scanning electron microscopy and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy. The study revealed that the initial phase of calcification causes an increase in the elasticity, as well as a drop in the normalized value of hysteresis for both IFM-rich and IFM-poor regions of the tendon. However, the relaxation behavior of the tissue remained unchanged during calcification proving that calcium phosphate deposits do not affect the IFM viscoplastic behavior but tissue viscoelasticity instead, which is manifested by a change in hysteresis. The greatest changes in stiffness are observed for statically incubated samples, while cyclically loaded samples were the most susceptible to fibril damage although they did not demonstrate the greatest increases in elastic modulus. The results presented in this work show that the calcification process modifies the collagen-matrix interactions, which leads to a change in their mechanical properties depending on the loading conditions. These findings contribute to our understanding of the pathogenesis of tendinopathy and have the potential to assist in the identification of effective treatment strategies for calcification-induced disorders.

title: Macrophages in rotator cuff injuries and tendon-to-bone healing: Heterogeneity, pathophysiology, and therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Rotator cuff tears (RCTs) are a leading cause of shoulder disability, with high postoperative failure rates primarily attributed to poor tendon-to-bone healing. Macrophages act as central regulators of the inflammatory and regenerative microenvironment in the injured enthesis, tendon stump, subacromial bursa, and rotator cuff musculature. This review highlights the spatiotemporal heterogeneity and phenotypic plasticity of macrophages revealed by single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. Rather than following a simple M1-to-M2 transition, macrophages adopt context-dependent inflammatory, resolving, remodeling, and profibrotic programs across different stages and tissue compartments of rotator cuff injury. Persistent inflammatory programs are associated with chronic inflammation, matrix degradation, fatty infiltration, and muscle atrophy, whereas resolving and reparative programs may support inflammation resolution and fibrocartilaginous regeneration; sustained remodeling or profibrotic states may also contribute to pathological fibrosis. The review further explores macrophage-stem cell crosstalk under mechanical loading and the contribution of dysregulated macrophage function to the progression of cuff tear arthropathy. Advanced strategies including stem cell-derived exosomes, immuno-engineered scaffolds, and targeted immunomodulation, have shown therapeutic potential in preclinical studies, but their clinical efficacy and translational applicability remain to be established.

title: Adipose-Derived Orthobiologics and Extracellular Vesicles in Foot and Ankle Surgery: Current Evidence and Clinical Limitations.
abstract: Interest in adipose-derived orthobiologics and extracellular vesicles (EVs) has expanded as clinicians seek minimally invasive treatments for musculoskeletal disorders. However, culture-expanded adipose-derived stromal cells, stromal vascular fraction, microfragmented adipose tissue (MFAT), and isolated EVs are biologically and regulatorily distinct products. This narrative review summarizes their biological rationale, processing, clinical evidence, regulatory considerations, and potential application in foot and ankle surgery. Randomized studies in knee osteoarthritis suggest that MFAT may provide symptomatic improvement, but it has not consistently demonstrated superiority over other orthobiologic injections, and the certainty of evidence remains low. Preclinical EV studies provide biological plausibility for effects on tendon healing, tendon-to-bone integration, and cartilage repair. However, substantial heterogeneity in cellular source, preparation, dose, and experimental model limits translation. Human orthopaedic EV evidence remains confined to early studies in knee osteoarthritis using placental or umbilical cord derived products, with limited and conflicting evidence of efficacy and no completed studies specific to the foot and ankle. No adipose-derived regenerative medicine or EV product is Food and Drug Administration-approved for an orthopaedic indication. Current evidence therefore does not support routine clinical use or claims of tissue regeneration. Standardized product characterization and well-designed comparative trials are required to establish safety, efficacy, and appropriate clinical applications.

title: Stem cell senescence as a regenerative bottleneck in age-related skeletal degeneration: Mechanistic crosstalk and translational strategies.
abstract: Skeletal degeneration is a major cause of pain, disability, fragility fracture, and loss of independence in aging populations. Although osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration are usually managed as anatomically separate disorders, they share a common regenerative failure: endogenous stem and progenitor cells lose renewal capacity, acquire inflammatory secretory programs, and become less able to rebuild damaged matrix. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on senescence in bone marrow mesenchymal stem/stromal cells, skeletal stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells, cartilage progenitor cells, synovial mesenchymal stromal cells, and disc-derived progenitor populations. Priority is given to primary mechanistic, omics, translational, and early clinical studies that connect senescence markers with functional impairment or intervention response. We discuss telomere-associated DNA damage, mitochondrial and oxidative stress, nutrient- and mechanosensing pathways, epigenetic remodeling, dysregulated autophagy and mitophagy, and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype as interlocking mechanisms that reshape skeletal niches. Disease-specific sections then examine how senescent progenitor compartments drive osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration through impaired osteogenesis or chondrogenesis, matrix catabolism, inflammatory vesicle signaling, and maladaptive mechanical feedback. Finally, we compare senolytics, senomorphics, metabolic and mitochondrial regulators, cell rejuvenation, extracellular vesicle engineering, biomaterials, and gene-based delivery platforms from a regenerative medicine perspective. Stem/progenitor cell senescence should be treated not simply as a biomarker of aging, but as a compartment-specific therapeutic bottleneck. Translation will require rigorous cell identity, multi-parameter senescence assays, disease-stage stratification, and therapies that restore regenerative competence without suppressing physiological repair.
