title: Editorial Commentary: Want to Try Anterior Cruciate Ligament Repair? Maximize Your Chances of Success by Choosing the Right Anterior Cruciate Ligaments to Repair Rather Than Reconstruct.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) repair represents an attractive choice for certain patients because of a higher rate of return to sport as well as a potentially faster recovery time. Recent evidence has shown that younger age and synovial sheath integrity <50% are associated with increased risk of failure after arthroscopic ACL repair. This makes sense because the synovial sheath is responsible for providing blood supply and proprioceptive nerve endings to the ACL, as well as protection of the ligament from the degradative environment of synovial fluid. As with any procedure, indications are refined over time based on new evidence. Although I believe that ACL reconstruction will remain the gold standard for the treatment of ACL tears, I also believe that our rates of success with ACL repair will improve as indications are further refined over time.

title: Running-based rehabilitation does not improve muscle function after volumetric muscle loss despite improving hindlimb weight-bearing asymmetry in mice.
abstract: Volumetric muscle loss (VML) is a traumatic skeletal muscle injury characterized by chronic functional impairments in the affected muscle and adjacent uninjured bone. Rehabilitative strategies aimed at restoring limb function following VML, including voluntary running, have shown limited efficacy and in some cases have been detrimental. One potential explanation is disproportional loading of the uninjured contralateral limb during running, but evaluation of unilateral weight-bearing following VML has not been explored. This study was designed to evaluate if the limited response to rehabilitation following VML could be explained by limb loading asymmetry. Twelve-week-old C57Bl/6J mice (n = 24; equal males/females) were randomized to three groups: Naïve-Run, VML, and VML-Run. Two weeks post-VML, mice in running groups were provided free access to wheels for 6 weeks. Weight-bearing asymmetry was assessed before injury and biweekly thereafter. Terminally at ∼20 weeks of age, in vivo muscle function was evaluated, and muscles and bones were saved for analyses. Prior to injury, no difference in weight-bearing asymmetry was observed across groups. VML-injured mice exhibited similar weight-bearing asymmetries prior to running. Following 6 weeks of running, VML-Run mice regained weight-bearing symmetry comparable to Naïve-Run. Despite this, remaining muscle function remained persistently impaired following VML injury. Collectively this works suggests that voluntary running promotes favourable weight-bearing adaptations following VML, but does not improve muscle function or the mechanical properties of the adjacent bone.

title: Effects of anti-aging diets and exercise on age-related musculoskeletal diseases via gut microbiota modulation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: This review summarizes evidence on how anti-aging diets and exercise influence age-related musculoskeletal diseases through modulation of the gut microbiota. With population aging, these diseases are public health concerns. The gut microbiota regulates bone, joint, and muscle health via the gut‑joint, gut‑bone, and gut‑muscle axis. Few reviews integrate diet-exercise synergy with mechanistic pathways linking microbial changes to tissue outcomes.
DISCUSSION: Anti‑aging dietary strategies, classified into caloric restriction (ketogenic diet, fasting‑mimicking diet, intermittent fasting, time‑restricted feeding) and isocaloric nutrient restriction (e.g. protein or amino acid restriction), reshape gut microbiota composition and function. Caloric restriction and intermittent fasting reduce inflammation and benefit joint and muscle health, whereas long‑term ketogenic or protein/amino acid restriction may adversely affect bone density and muscle anabolism. Moderate exercise increases microbial diversity, enriches beneficial taxa (Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium), and boosts short‑chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, especially butyrate. Exercise also strengthens intestinal barrier integrity, reduces lipopolysaccharide (LPS)‑induced systemic inflammation, and alleviates osteoarthritis (OA), bone loss, and sarcopenia in preclinical models. Combined diet and exercise may provide greater benefits than either alone. However, most evidence derives from animal or small human studies, and causality remains unclear. Future research should clarify causal mechanisms via multi‑omics and germ‑free models.
CONCLUSION: This review suggests that both anti-aging diets and moderate exercise may improve age-related musculoskeletal diseases partly through gut microbiota modulation. Given substantial inter‑individual variability, future research should prioritize personalized nutrition and exercise prescriptions tailored to microbiota, genetic background, and lifestyle. These findings inform precision strategies to promote healthy aging.

title: Culturally Embedded Participation Restrictions in Indian Adults With Knee Osteoarthritis: An ICF-Based Qualitative Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To identify culturally relevant functioning issues experienced by Indian adults with knee osteoarthritis (KOA) using the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework.
METHODS: A qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured focus group interviews was conducted with 38 ambulatory adults (35-85 years) diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Participants were recruited from physiotherapy outpatient departments and community settings using maximum variation sampling. Interviews were conducted in Gujarati, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Meaningful concepts were systematically linked to ICF categories using established linking rules. Dual independent coding and consensus discussions ensured the analytic rigour.
RESULTS: This study included 38 participants with KOA. Fifty-five meaningful second-level categories were identified. The most represented components were activities and participation (41.2%) and body functions (29.4%). Frequently mapped first-level categories included mobility (n = 22), neuromusculoskeletal and movement-related functions (n = 9), d6 domestic life (n = 10), community, social and civic life (n = 7) and products and technology (n = 9). Sixteen additional categories not represented in the existing ICF Core Set for OA emerged, particularly relating to culturally embedded activities such as floor sitting, squatting for toileting and religious participation. Environmental barriers, including inaccessible infrastructure and limited rehabilitation services, influenced disability experience.
CONCLUSION: Functioning among Indian adults with KOA is influenced by culturally embedded participation demands and contextual barriers that are insufficiently captured in the existing ICF Core Set for osteoarthritis (OA). These findings provide preliminary empirical support for contextual validation of the ICF Core Set for OA and inform potential culturally responsive adaptation for KOA.

title: Anatomic feasibility of using Shark Screw tendon for humeral ligament re-construction in medial and posterolateral elbow instability.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medial and posterolateral rotational instability of the elbow, often resulting from collateral ligament insufficiency, can lead to pain and functional impairment. Surgical re-construction is indicated when conservative treatment fails, yet complications such as graft failure and donor-site morbidity persist. This study investigates the anatomic and biomechanical feasibility of the Shark Screw tendon as a representative human allogeneic bone screw for humeral ligament fixation in cases of elbow instability.
METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen cadaveric specimens were used to evaluate the feasibility of the use of a Shark Screw tendon for humeral fixation on both medial and lateral sides. Cyclic loading and failure testing were performed to assess time-zero fixation characteristics and failure load.
RESULTS: A total of sixteen testing scenarios were conducted on the specimens. Implantation was technically feasible without anatomic limitations related to implant size or positioning. Six graft failures occurred (38%), all attributable to poor tissue quality. Tendon slippage was observed in 9 of 16 cases (56%) under progressively increasing axial load, while the Shark Screw tendon remained seated. The mean failure load was 101 N (±50) for medial insertions, 118 N (±77) for lateral insertions, and 110 N (±64) overall. After 100 cycles, tendon displacement averaged 1.1 mm (±0.4) during extension-flexion on the medial side, 1.0 mm (±1.0) on the lateral side, and 1.0 mm (±0.7) overall. During supination-pronation, displacement was 0.8 mm (±0.7) medially, 1.0 mm (±0.8) laterally, and 0.9 mm (±0.7) overall. No anchor pullout was observed, although one anchor tip fractured during insertion.
CONCLUSION: The Shark Screw tendon appears to be a feasible biologically integrative alternative for humeral fixation in medial and posterolateral elbow ligament re-construction, demonstrating preliminary time-zero fixation characteristics in a cadaveric model. Further biomechanical and clinical studies are needed to confirm long-term outcomes.

title: From donor programming to therapeutic performance: An evidence-calibrated narrative review of dental mesenchymal stromal/stem cell-derived extracellular vesicle preparations in oral and maxillofacial regeneration.
abstract: Dental mesenchymal stromal/stem cell-derived extracellular vesicle preparations are being investigated as cell-free interventions for oral and maxillofacial regeneration, but the evidence is heterogeneous in donor state, product identity, delivery context and endpoint level. This critical narrative review separates mechanistic confidence from translational readiness. Representative studies are mapped across dental pulp, periodontal ligament, deciduous-tooth, dental follicle, apical-papilla and gingival sources, while conditioned medium, secretome, small extracellular vesicle preparations, author-labelled exosome preparations, combined carrier-drug interventions and apoptotic vesicle preparations are kept distinct. The synthesis indicates that donor programming can yield directionally different outcomes across study-specific contexts; carrier-associated structural outcomes cannot automatically be assigned to a particle preparation; and molecular, histological and imaging outcomes do not establish durable organ function. Translation requires defined identity and purity, justified dose normalization, potency, batch comparability, stability, exposure, safety, manufacturing controls and indication-matched functional testing.

title: Emerging therapies for knee osteoarthritis.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is the most prevalent form of OA and a leading cause of chronic pain and disability worldwide. Its growing burden, driven mainly by ageing and obesity, is associated with major societal costs and increased cardiovascular mortality. Knee OA is now recognized as a heterogeneous whole-joint disease involving biomechanical, metabolic, inflammatory, osteochondral and neurovascular mechanisms. This complexity helps to explain why existing analgesics have modest efficacy and why disease-modifying OA drug development has repeatedly faltered. The therapeutic landscape is nevertheless evolving rapidly. Emerging symptomatic strategies include incretin-based therapies (semaglutide is the first to show substantial benefits for pain and function), neurotrophin modulation, extended-release intra-articular glucocorticoids, lubricating injectables and image-guided neurovascular interventions. In parallel, candidate disease-modifying OA drugs target cartilage anabolism, Wnt signalling, matrix-degrading enzymes, subchondral bone remodelling, immunometabolic pathways and local gene therapy. Several treatments, including locally administered GLP1 receptor agonists, the anabolic agent TPX-100 and intra-articular IL-1 receptor antagonist gene therapy, have shown encouraging signals, whereas mesenchymal stromal cell therapies have thus far demonstrated inconsistent efficacy across phase III clinical trials, highlighting the need for further standardization of mesenchymal stromal cell products and optimization of patient selection. Recent advances signal a shift towards a more diverse therapeutic landscape for knee OA, with emerging opportunities to target both symptoms and the underlying mechanisms of disease.

title: Small extracellular vesicles in osteoarthritis: A double‑edged sword regulating inflammation and cartilage homeostasis (Review).
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a progressive degenerative joint disease and a leading cause of pain, disability and loss of joint function in older adults worldwide. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) are small vesicles secreted by cells and found in various body fluids. They carry a range of bioactive molecules, including nucleic acids, proteins and lipids, and participate in numerous cellular physiological activities, such as cell death, inflammation, immunity, proliferation, migration and differentiation. Depending on their cellular origin, sEVs can exert opposing effects on OA: They may either aggravate inflammation and cartilage damage or suppress inflammation and promote cartilage repair. Therefore, this review focuses on the preclinical research evidence regarding the dual mechanism of 'promoting or treating' by sEVs in the disease of OA, aiming to construct a theoretical framework to provide a theoretical basis for the development and translational application of OA treatment strategies based on sEVs.

title: Imaging of Pediatric Hip Disorders in the Young Athlete.
abstract: Pediatric hip pain in young athletes encompasses a wide range of disorders related to skeletal immaturity and increasing athletic demands. Timely and accurate diagnosis is important, as delayed recognition may result in growth disturbances, instability, and long-term morbidity. Imaging plays a central role in differentiating clinically significant abnormalities from normal developmental variation and less consequential conditions. This review presents a pattern-based framework for evaluating pediatric hip pathology, organized into key categories based on dominant imaging patterns. Emphasis is placed on imaging findings that influence management and return-to-play decisions, including high-risk features and common pitfalls related to skeletal maturation. This approach provides a practical framework for diagnosis, risk stratification, and effective multidisciplinary communication.

title: Cannabigerol Enhances Muscle Strength and Performance in Dexamethasone-Treated Mice.
abstract: Sarcopenia is a major clinical condition associated with aging and is characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass and function. Resistance training is an effective intervention to counteract muscle atrophy; however, strategies that selectively enhance functional performance remain limited. Cannabigerol, a phytocannabinoid that is not a CB1 receptor agonist and therefore lacks psychotomimetic activity, has emerged as a potential modulator of neuromuscular function, although its role in skeletal muscle adaptation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of resistance exercise and cannabigerol, alone and in combination, in a dexamethasone-induced model of muscle atrophy in mice. Animals received dexamethasone (20 mg/kg, i.p.) for 12 days and were subsequently subjected to a 4-week ladder-based resistance exercise protocol. Cannabigerol (10 mg/kg, i.p.) was administered on training days. Resistance exercise restored muscle morphology and improved fatigue resistance. In contrast, cannabigerol acted mainly on neuromuscular performance, increasing muscle power while producing only a small increase in fiber cross-sectional area. Cannabigerol potentiated training-induced power output, increasing performance by ∼55% in the first week and up to ∼87% after 4 weeks compared to exercise alone. In addition, cannabigerol increased peak grip strength (∼10%) and lowered post-exercise blood lactate in sedentary animals (∼48%). These findings show that resistance exercise and cannabigerol exert complementary effects on skeletal muscleexercise promoting structural recovery and cannabigerol enhancing neuromuscular performance and lowering post-exercise lactateand support further investigation of cannabigerol as an adjunct to exercise in glucocorticoid-induced muscle atrophy.

title: The Effect of Training Exercise on Cartilage Zonal Composition and Structure at Two Differently Loaded Sites in the Juvenile Equine Metacarpophalangeal Joint.
abstract: BackgroundThe aim of this study was to investigate the depth related spatial distribution of biochemical and structural components in articular cartilage at different topographical sites experiencing different loading within the juvenile equine metacarpophalangeal joint in two groups of foals subjected to different exercise conditions.MethodsSixteen Warmblood foals were included in the study and were randomly assigned into 1 of 2 exercise groups (box rest and box rest plus training) during the first 5 months of life and subsequently euthanized. Osteochondral plugs were harvested from two sites which have previously been shown to experience different load levels and sectioned into 100 μm thick slices. Cartilage slices were analysed for glycosaminoglycan, DNA, and total collagen content, as well as content of hydroxylysine residues (HYL) in collagen and the collagen cross-link Hydroxylysylpyridinoline (HP). Collagen fibril architecture (Orientation Angle and Parallelism Index) was determined using quantitative polarized light microscopy.ResultsThe constantly loaded site 2 exhibited higher glycosaminoglycan (GAG) and HP content with HYL higher in the superficial and middle layers of the trained group, while the intermittently peak loaded site 1 showed greater collagen accumulation in deeper layers but lower cross-link density. Structural analyses (Oa and PI) confirmed that collagen fibril orientation and alignment adapt regionally, with training enhancing fibril organization in superficial zones.ConclusionThis study illustrates that mechanical loading is a key driver of functional adaptation, resulting in distinct zonal and topographical differences in the biochemical and structural composition of equine cartilage at 5 months.

title: A wearable vibroarthrography system with PID-controlled negative-pressure suction and synchronized posture estimation.
abstract: BackgroundVibroarthrography (VAG) is a non-invasive technique for evaluating joint health through acoustic signals generated during movement. However, reliable signal acquisition during dynamic activities remains challenging due to sensor displacement, motion artifacts, and inconsistent skin contact.ObjectiveThis study proposes an advanced wearable VAG system integrating PID-controlled negative-pressure suction and real-time posture estimation to improve signal stability and enhance the assessment of knee joint mechanics during movement.MethodsThe proposed system combines a wearable acoustic sensing module with a vacuum-assisted suction cup and a PID controller that consistently maintains sensor adhesion. Real-time posture estimation is achieved using MediaPipe Pose, which computes knee flexion angles. VAG signals and kinematic data are synchronously acquired during OKC and CKC exercises for integrated analysis.ResultsIn this single-subject pilot test, the system achieved stable sensor attachment and repeatable vibroacoustic recordings throughout dynamic movements. Distinguishable frequency-domain characteristics were observed at relevant knee flexion angles, including approximately 30°, 63°, and 129°.ConclusionsThis pilot feasibility study demonstrates that the proposed wearable VAG platform can achieve stable acquisition of synchronized vibroacoustic and kinematic signals during dynamic knee movement in a single subject. These preliminary findings suggest potential future applications in osteoarthritis screening, rehabilitation assessment, and ambulatory monitoring, pending validation in larger, statistically powered cohorts.

title: Heart-to-kidney signal by extracellular vesicles promotes kidney injury in cardiorenal syndrome.
abstract:
AIMS: Cardiorenal syndrome type-1 (CRS1), defined as acute kidney injury occurring in the setting of acute cardiac illness, is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Our objective was to determine whether extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from the injured heart localize to the kidneys and contribute to renal injury in CRS1, and to elucidate mechanisms by which cardiac-derived EVs mediate kidney damage.
METHODS AND RESULTS: Using cardiomyocyte-specific EV reporter mice, we characterized the release of cardiac-derived EVs and their biodistribution to the kidneys. Acute myocardial infarction increased circulating levels of these EVs and enhanced their uptake by proximal tubular epithelial cells. To directly assess their impact on the kidney, EVs derived from cardiomyocytes cultured under normoxic (N-EV) or hypoxic (H-EV) conditions were injected into the renal arteries of wild-type mice. H-EV, but not N-EV, induced proximal tubular epithelial cell injury and worsening of kidney function. To identify EV biomarkers, we performed proteomic profiling of cargo from N-EV and H-EV, and validated the muscle-specific protein TRIM72 as a biomarker of EVs originating from injured cardiomyocytes. In a porcine CRS1 model, plasma levels of TRIM72 positive-EVs were increased, and we demonstrate their delivery to the kidney. Similarly, in CRS1 patients, higher plasma levels of TRIM72-positive EVs correlated with the development of acute kidney injury. Mechanistically, uptake of H-EVs by proximal tubular epithelial cells induced transcription of lipogenic genes and caused lipid accumulation, whereas lipogenesis blockade protected these cells from H-EV-induced injury. We subsequently found that reduced expression of the transcription factor FOXO3 drove H-EV-induced transcriptomic reprogramming. H-EV cargo was enriched with specific Foxo3-targeting miRNAs, whose delivery promoted proximal tubular epithelial cell cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, and suppressed FOXO3 levels.
CONCLUSIONS: Overall, this work demonstrates that a Foxo3-targeting miRNA heart-to-kidney signal mediated by injured cardiac-derived EVs contributes to kidney injury in CRS1.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of Osteoarthritis: A Review and Opportunities for Novel Therapeutics.
abstract: ➢ Osteoarthritis (OA) represents a biologically dynamic disease characterized by progressive failure of cartilage homeostasis through interconnected molecular mechanisms. Chondrocytes shift from an anabolic to a catabolic phenotype, marked by increased matrix metalloproteinase activity, while the synthetic capacity of articular cartilage diminishes.➢ Key signaling cascades including NF-κB (nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells) and MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase) become dysregulated, driving matrix degradation. Declining autophagy impairs cellular quality control while senescent cells accumulate, releasing inflammatory mediators that amplify tissue damage. The immune response extends beyond macrophage polarization to involve adaptive immune cells, including T cell subsets that sustain chronic synovial inflammation.➢ Emerging disease-modifying strategies-including Wnt pathway inhibitors, FGF (fibroblast growth factor) 18 analogs, senolytic agents, gene therapy approaches, and allogeneic MSC (mesenchymal stem cell) implantation-offer the first genuine prospects for altering the natural history of this disease. However, translational challenges remain, as highlighted by mixed results in recent clinical trials.➢ The future of OA management lies in precision molecular orthopaedics: matching patients to targeted therapies on the basis of their predominant disease endotype.

title: Music-based emotional regulation and nutrition strategies for mental health support among medical student-athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medical student-athletes face combined academic, clinical, and competitive training demands that may disrupt sleep, dietary routines, emotional regulation, recovery, and cognitive functioning.
OBJECTIVE: To examine associations between naturally occurring music-based emotional regulation, self-selected nutrition routines, psychophysiological recovery, and mental health-related markers using a non-interventional multimodal digital phenotyping framework.
METHODS: Over 8 weeks, 120 medical student-athletes were monitored without prescribed music, diet, therapy, or behavioral intervention. Data included wearable-derived nocturnal heart-rate variability, resting heart rate, sleep-wake rhythm, activity and training load, participant-recorded music use, meal timing, hydration routines, food-photo logs, and brief emotional reflections. Three indices were constructed: The Music Regulation Pattern Index, Nutrition Rhythm Stability Index, and Psychophysiological Recovery Balance Index.
RESULTS: Monitoring feasibility was high and index reliability was acceptable. Music-regulation patterns were more strongly associated with emotional balance and focus-related language, whereas nutrition-rhythm stability was more closely associated with sleep regularity, heart-rate variability stability, and recovery balance.
CONCLUSION: Naturally occurring music-use and nutrition-rhythm behaviors showed distinct associations with emotional and physiological recovery markers. Multimodal digital phenotyping may help identify potentially protective lifestyle patterns in medical student-athletes while preserving an observational, non-causal interpretation and avoiding unsupported treatment claims.

title: The effect of positive emotions on psychophysiological recovery and performance in athletes - investigating the undoing-hypothesis.
abstract: Athletes have to cope with psychosocial and physiological stressors, requiring recovery to ensure subsequent performance. According to the undoing-hypothesis, positive emotions (PE) may enhance psychophysiological recovery. The present two studies investigated the undoing hypothesis and its benefits for athletes' cognitive (Study 1; n = 60) and motor (Study 2; n = 30) performance. After a combined psychosocial-physiological stressor, participants either completed a five-minute PE induction (music; imagination exercise) or were assigned to a resting condition. Emotions, perceived stress-recovery, and physiological parameters (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, cortisol) were assessed. In Study 1, inhibition and cognitive flexibility were measured once. In Study 2, hand force and jump height were measured using a pre-posttest design. Due to the lack of psychological stress responses and successful PE induction, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the undoing hypothesis. Nevertheless, the present study provides valuable methodological insights into the challenges of testing the undoing hypothesis in athletes. These insights can inform the design and implementation of future studies and thereby contribute to advancing research on the undoing hypothesis in athletic populations.

title: Micro-recovery dosing in elite sport: an initiative-taking, organization-wide recovery framework.
abstract: Recovery in elite professional sport is now widely understood as a multidimensional process spanning physiological, psychological, cognitive, and social domains, yet recovery models applied in professional clubs and sporting organisations have been slow to reflect this. Most remain reactive and athlete-centred, leaving the full complexity of competitive fatigue inadequately addressed and the equivalent recovery demands on coaching and performance staff entirely unrecognised. No structural framework currently places initiative-taking, calendar-embedded multidimensional recovery as a deliberate component of seasonal planning. Main body. We introduce micro-recovery dosing (MRD): proactively planned, pre-scheduled 36-hour multidimensional recovery periods embedded within the competitive season as a proposed starting point at five to eight instances per year, extending to all members of the high-performance organisation. Drawing on neuromuscular recovery kinetics, autonomic science, sleep architecture research, occupational recovery psychology, and complex systems theory, we construct a convergent theoretical rationale for the proposed parameters and distinguish MRD from related constructs. We present a role-differentiated implementation framework with supporting evidence and a discussion of emerging AI-driven monitoring tools. Conclusions. Taken together, the four-domain convergent rationale and the complex systems perspective provide a theoretically coherent basis for MRD's proposed structure. We argue for a specific organisational transformation: the shift from recovery as an incidental gap between performance demands to an intentionally designed recovery architecture that encompasses athletes and staff alike. The article identifies the active ingredient problem as the central scientific challenge and sets out a structured empirical agenda.

title: Quantitative Muscle MRI Fat Fraction as a Biomarker of Disease Severity in Mitochondrial Myopathies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Quantitative muscle MRI is increasingly used to assess structural muscle damage in inherited myopathies, but its application in primary mitochondrial myopathies (PMM) has not been systematically evaluated in large cohorts. Because PMM are clinically and genetically heterogeneous, objective imaging biomarkers are needed to quantify skeletal-muscle involvement and define meaningful subgroups. We assessed whether MRI-derived proton density fat fraction (PDFF) captures genotype- and phenotype-specific patterns of fatty replacement and reflects disease severity using motor function outcomes and circulating biomarkers.
METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional analysis of 49 adults with genetically confirmed PMM enrolled in a prospective natural history study. Participants underwent standardised lower-limb MRI, including T1-weighted sequences and mDIXON-QUANT fat fraction imaging. Muscle involvement was assessed semi-quantitatively with the modified Mercuri scale and quantitatively by PDFF measurement in selected pelvic girdle and thigh muscles. A total fat fraction score (FF sum) was calculated. PDFF was compared across genotypes and phenotypes and against MRC score, NSAA, 6-min walk test, 100-m run test, CK, serum creatinine, GDF15 and disease duration.
RESULTS: Mean age at onset was 26.3 ± 15.1 years, mean age at MRI was 50.0 ± 12.3 years, and median disease duration was 23 years (IQR 15-31). Genetic diagnoses included mtDNA variants in 29 patients (59.1%; single large-scale deletions, n = 19; point mutations, n = 10), nuclear variants in POLG (n = 8), TK2 (n = 8) and TWNK (n = 4). Phenotypes were exercise intolerance without overt weakness (n = 7), isolated progressive external ophthalmoplegia (PEO; n = 16), PEO-plus (n = 16) and progressive myopathy (n = 8). Highest median PDFF values were observed in tensor fasciae latae (31%), gluteus maximus (30%), sartorius (25%) and gracilis (20%). FF sum correlated with MRC score (r = -0.567, p < 0.0001), NSAA (r = -0.731, p < 0.0001), 100-m run test time (r = 0.629, p < 0.0001), 6-min walk distance (r = -0.311, p = 0.0476) and serum creatinine (r = -0.715, p < 0.0001), but not with CK or GDF15. TK2 deficiency showed the highest fat replacement, particularly in gluteus maximus and gracilis (p < 0.001). Progressive myopathy showed greater fatty replacement than other phenotypes (p < 0.001), while exercise intolerance showed higher fat fraction than isolated PEO (p = 0.033).
CONCLUSIONS: Quantitative muscle MRI provides objective and clinically meaningful measures of muscle involvement in PMM. MRI-derived fat fraction reflects disease severity, discriminates between genotypes and phenotypes, and detects subclinical muscle damage. These cross-sectional findings support PDFF as a candidate imaging biomarker for patient stratification and disease characterisation; prospective longitudinal studies will be required to establish its sensitivity to change and its validity as an outcome measure for therapeutic trials.

title: Traumatic Proximal Rectus Femoris Avulsion With Recurrent Intramuscular Hematoma in a Competitive Martial Arts Athlete: A Case Report.
abstract: Proximal avulsion of the rectus femoris tendon is an uncommon injury in athletes and is rarely associated with direct trauma and extensive hematoma. We describe a 25-year-old competitive taekwondo athlete who developed acute hip flexor weakness and thigh swelling after a direct anterior thigh kick. Bedside musculoskeletal ultrasound demonstrated disruption of rectus femoris architecture with intramuscular hematoma, and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed complete avulsion of both proximal heads of the rectus femoris with tendon retraction and a large associated hematoma. The patient had sustained a recent prior quadriceps injury with hematoma. Recurrent hematoma development warranted hematologic testing, which revealed an isolated Factor VIII deficiency. Given his high functional demands, he underwent open surgical repair. This case highlights the importance of early imaging and consideration of operative management in high-level athletes presenting with trauma-related rectus femoris avulsion. It also highlights the importance of hematologic workups in athletes presenting with unexplained recurrent hematomas to effectively risk-stratify surgery and return to sport.

title: Examining the Impact of Supramaximal Eccentric and Long-Lever Isometric Training Protocols on Isometric Hamstring Strength, Nordic Hamstring Performance, and Sprint Speed.
abstract: The aim of this study was to compare the effects of a 6-week higher-volume eccentric training protocol with a combined lower-volume eccentric and long-lever isometric protocol on posterior chain strength and sprint performance. Thirty-three NCAA Division II soccer players (men: n = 17, age = 19.7 ± 1.2 years, height = 178.9 ± 6.6 cm, body mass 79.8 ± 8.1 kg; women: n = 16, age = 20.1 ± 0.9 years, height = 166.7 ± 5.2 cm, body mass = 67.0 ± 12.1 kg) were allocated to either group via exhaustive minimization. Nordic hamstring exercise break-point angle (NBPA), rapid isometric hamstring strength (LLB), 20m sprint performance, and continuous angular knee extension velocity waveforms were assessed pre- and post-intervention, and following a 2-week detraining period. A significant main effect of time was observed for sprint, NBPA, and rapid isometric strength (p < 0.05); however, Bonferroni-corrected within-group comparisons reached significance only for sprint performance in both groups, with no significant between-group differences for any outcome. Equivalence testing supported comparable sprint adaptations between protocols but could not be established for eccentric or isometric hamstring strength. All discrete outcome measures were largely maintained or continued to develop following the detraining period though range-specific eccentric strength appeared more sensitive to the training cessation. A combined low-volume eccentric and isometric training approach may represent a viable alternative to higher-volume eccentric programming for hamstring strength and speed development, although this should be approached cautiously to preserve neuromuscular qualities relevant to hamstring injury risk mitigation.

title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise.
abstract: The duration of the repeated-bout effect following eccentric knee-extensor exercise remains undefined, despite its widespread use in muscle damage research and training. The present study examined how long this protective effect persists in the knee extensors. Forty-eight young men performed two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 × 15 repetitions at 60°/s). Four independent groups performed the second bout 3, 6, 9, or 12 weeks after the first. Isometric torque, range of motion (ROM), delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), muscle thickness, echo intensity, creatine kinase (CK), and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) were assessed before and 2 and 4 days after each bout. Baseline-adjusted linear mixed-effects models were used to compare responses between bouts, complemented by equivalence testing at 12 weeks. The repeated-bout effect was evident at 3 and 6 weeks across most outcomes and remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers. At 12 weeks, no significant differences between bouts were observed at either day 2 or day 4 for any outcome. Exploratory equivalence analyses further indicated that the effect was no longer meaningfully present at these time points for isometric torque, ROM, DOMS, muscle thickness, and echo intensity, whereas the findings for CK and hs-CRP remained inconclusive. Overall, the repeated-bout effect may persist for some outcomes for up to 9 weeks, whereas by 12 weeks no meaningful effect was detectable at the assessed post-exercise time points. This time course can guide the design of muscle damage studies and the scheduling of eccentric training sessions.

title: Jiawei Duhuo Jisheng Mixture Attenuates H2O2-induced Oxidative Injury and Osteogenic Dysfunction in Primary Osteoblasts: An Integrated Target Analysis and Experimental Validation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Oxidative stress-induced osteoblast dysfunction is an important event in osteoporosis (OP). Jiawei Duhuo Jisheng Mixture (JDJM) is clinically used for bone-related disorders, but its molecular basis in OP remains unclear. This study explored OP-related candidate targets of JDJM and evaluated its cytoprotective effects in a hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-induced primary osteoblast injury model.
METHODS: Candidate JDJM targets were predicted from its identified constituents and intersected with OP-related genes. The study integrated network-based and enrichment analyses with single-cell mapping, followed by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation. An H2O2-induced primary osteoblast injury model was used for experimental validation.
RESULTS: A total of 210 shared targets were identified. Network pharmacology and enrichment analyses implicated JDJM in the regulation of oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, extracellular matrix remodelling, osteogenesis and apoptosis, primarily through the MAPK, JAK-STAT and PI3K-Akt signalling pathways. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis further localized these candidate targets to osteogenic, stromal, vascular, and inflammatory cell populations. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations predicted stable interactions between representative JDJM-derived compounds and selected protein targets. In H2O2-injured primary osteoblasts, JDJM significantly reduced mean DCF fluorescence intensity, increased the alkaline phosphatase (ALP)-positive area and Alizarin Red S absorbance, and partially restored osteocalcin/bone Gla protein (OCN/BGP) protein and Bglap mRNA expression.JDJM was also associated with decreased total JAK1, STAT3, MAPK3, MMP9, and Bad expression and partial restoration of ESR1 expression.
DISCUSSION: JDJM attenuated H2O2-induced oxidative injury and osteogenic dysfunction in primary osteoblasts, accompanied by changes in JAK1, STAT3, MAPK3, MMP9, ESR1, and Bad expression. These results support a multi-target cytoprotective effect of JDJM under oxidative-stress conditions, although direct regulation of the corresponding signaling pathways remains to be confirmed.
CONCLUSION: JDJM attenuated H2O2-induced oxidative injury and partially restored osteogenic function in primary osteoblasts, accompanied by coordinated expression changes in JAK1, STAT3, MAPK3, MMP9, ESR1, and Bad. These findings support a multi-target protective effect of JDJM against oxidative stress-related osteoblast dysfunction.

title: The Influence of Menstrual Cycle Phase and Cramp Severity on Psychological Responses and Exercise Capacity in Physically Active Eumenorrheic Women.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The scientific literature is characterized by a historical underrepresentation of the female population in sports science. A critical issue in the current literature is the inconsistency between objectively measured (e.g., time to exhaustion) and subjectively perceived performance across the menstrual cycle. This inconsistency is often attributed to methodological limitations (e.g., absence of hormonal assessments and ovulation kits) and to the lack of consideration of menstrual-related symptoms and psychological variables.
PURPOSE: The primary objective of the study was to compare graded exercise test (GXT) performance outcomes across menstrual cycle phases. A secondary objective was to investigate whether cramp severity was associated with GXT performance during menses. A final objective was to examine the effects of menstrual cycle phase on psychological responses to exercise.
METHODS: Nineteen physically active eumenorrheic women (age 24 ± 4 years, V̇O2peak 38.4 ± 3.1 mL·kg -1·min -1) completed five GXTs: two for familiarization and three performed during experimental sessions scheduled in three specific phases of the menstrual cycle (menses, follicular, and luteal). Variables of interest included estradiol and progesterone levels, affective valence, arousal, anxiety, heart rate, rating of perceived exertion, mood disturbance, and motivation. Exercise capacity was operationalized as GXT performance outcomes (peak power output [Wpeak] and time to exhaustion). Cramp severity was measured only during menses.
RESULTS: No statistically significant differences in Wpeak or time to exhaustion were detected across menstrual cycle phases (p > 0.05). Secondary and exploratory regression analyses indicated that each one-point increase in menstrual cramp severity during menses was associated with lower GXT performance (Wpeak: -1.50 W; time to exhaustion: 2.72 s; p = 0.04; R 2 = ~0.35). Higher affective valence scores were associated with improved Wpeak (+4.27 W) and time to exhaustion (-8.51 s; p = 0.02; R 2 = ~0.36), whereas higher arousal scores were associated with lower Wpeak (-11.40 W) and higher time to exhaustion (6.47 s; p = 0.01; R 2 = ~0.46) across the menstrual cycle. Motivation was lower during menses than during the follicular phase (p = 0.04).
CONCLUSIONS: No statistically significant differences in GXT performance were detected across menstrual cycle phases. However, secondary and exploratory analyses suggest that greater menstrual cramp severity during menses was associated with lower time to exhaustion and Wpeak. These findings provide preliminary evidence that menstrual-related symptoms and psychological factors may contribute to variability in GXT performance outcomes and warrant further investigation in larger cohorts.
journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

title: Using High-Field Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy to Measure Muscle Glycogen in Patients With McArdle Disease.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION/AIMS: Patients with McArdle disease demonstrate exercise intolerance with muscle contractures and episodic rhabdomyolysis. Additionally, some patients show progressive fat replacement of paraspinal and shoulder muscles with aging. The cause of fat replacement in older McArdle patients is unknown but could relate to a higher glycogen accumulation in these muscles in line with what is found in Pompe disease. The aim of the study was to investigate if this is also the case in McArdle disease, which could imply that excess levels of glycogen accumulation are a potential driver of fat replacement of muscle.
METHODS: Using 7 Tesla 13C magnetic resonance spectroscopy, we measured glycogen noninvasively in lumbar, thigh, and calf muscles in 14 patients with McArdle disease and 19 healthy controls.
RESULTS: Patients with McArdle disease showed increased levels of glycogen in all muscles compared to controls; calf (3.2 times normal, p < 0.005), hamstrings (2.7 times normal, p < 0.005), anterior thigh compartment (2.7 times normal, p < 0.005), and lumbar muscle (2.1 times normal, p < 0.005). Glycogen was evenly distributed among muscle groups in both patients with McArdle disease and healthy controls.
DISCUSSION: Our results are in line with previous studies showing two to three times increased glycogen compared to control in muscle biopsies. We found no variability in glycogen concentration among muscles that could indicate glycogen as a predictor of muscle injury in McArdle disease.

title: Anti-inflammatory and Early Osteogenic Potential of a 96% Ethanol Extract of Drynaria bonii.
abstract:
ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Drynaria bonii H. Christ rhizome is traditionally used in Vietnamese medicine for fractures and musculoskeletal disorders. However, the effects of extraction solvent on chemical composition and biological activities relevant to the inflammatory and early mineralization phases of bone repair remain insufficiently defined.
AIM OF THE STUDY: This study compared 30%, 70%, and 96% ethanol extracts of D. bonii (DB30, DB70, and DB96, respectively) to identify a lead extract for further fracture-healing-oriented investigation.
METHODS: Rhizome extracts prepared with 30%, 70%, and 96% ethanol were profiled by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-QTOF-MS/MS). TNF-α inhibition was evaluated in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; acute anti-inflammatory activity was assessed in carrageenan-induced mouse paw edema; and calcium-associated staining was evaluated in canine mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) cultures using Alizarin Red S (ARS). Acute oral toxicity was assessed at 5000 mg/kg, and selected constituents were isolated from DB96. The four NMR-characterized constituents were subsequently evaluated by molecular docking against IκB kinase β (IKKβ).
RESULTS: The extracts showed distinct qualitative LC-MS/MS profiles, with DB70 displaying a broader curated phenolic/flavonoid profile and DB96 showing a different compositional pattern. DB96 produced the strongest TNF-α inhibition (IC50 = 32.05 μg/mL), compared with DB70 (63.73 μg/mL), whereas DB30 did not reach 50% inhibition at 100 μg/mL. DB96 also showed the largest numerical paw-edema inhibition among the extract groups at 1 and 24 h; however, statistical comparisons were performed only against the disease-control group and not among active treatment groups. In canine MSC cultures, DB96 at 50 μg/mL showed the highest descriptive normalized ARS-positive area among the extracts (12.0 ± 2.1%), although staining remained weak relative to the positive control and did not establish complete osteogenic differentiation. Betulin, ursolic acid, rutin, and kaempferol were isolated from DB96 and independently identified by NMR from a preparative DB96 batch. Among these constituents, ursolic acid and betulin showed the most favorable predicted IKKβ docking profiles, with binding energies of -8.52 and -8.41 kcal/mol, respectively. No mortality or overt acute toxicity was observed for any of the three extracts after a single oral dose of 5000 mg/kg.
CONCLUSION: The findings support DB96 as the lead extract among the three preparations for subsequent mechanistic and bone-repair-oriented investigation. Docking provided complementary mechanistic support for possible interactions of selected DB96 constituents with IKKβ, but did not establish direct target inhibition. Direct fracture-healing efficacy, definitive osteogenic differentiation, quantitative constituent enrichment, and repeated-dose safety remain to be established.

title: Radial pressure wave treatment accelerates recovery from immobilization-induced soleus muscle atrophy and improves ankle range of motion in mice.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Disuse muscle atrophy following immobilization is characterized by decreased muscle mass and reduced joint range of motion (ROM). Radial pressure wave (RPW) treatment is a non-invasive modality that delivers mechanical energy to musculoskeletal tissues, but its efficacy in skeletal muscle recovery from disuse atrophy remains largely unknown. We examined whether RPW treatment accelerates soleus muscle structural recovery and passive ankle dorsiflexion ROM following immobilization-induced atrophy in mice. Furthermore, we investigated the underlying molecular signaling cascades and gene expression profiles associated with RPW-mediated recovery.
METHODS: Male C57BL/6 J mice ([Formula: see text] per group) underwent 14 days of unilateral hindlimb immobilization, followed by a 7-day recovery period with or without RPW treatment (1 bar, 10 Hz, 2,000 pulses, three sessions on alternate days). Candidate genes identified as differentially expressed by exploratory RNA-sequencing in one mouse per group ([Formula: see text]) were subsequently evaluated by quantitative PCR and immunoblotting across all animals in the full cohort ([Formula: see text] per group).
RESULTS: RPW treatment increased fiber CSA to [Formula: see text] (vs. [Formula: see text] in the sham group) and improved ankle dorsiflexion ROM to [Formula: see text] (vs. [Formula: see text]). Gene set enrichment analysis revealed suppression of the forkhead box O (FoxO) signaling pathway and enrichment of the extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling pathway. Igf1 expression was higher in the RPW group ([Formula: see text]-fold vs. sham: [Formula: see text]-fold), accompanied by elevated Akt phosphorylation. Col3a1 was uniquely upregulated in the RPW group ([Formula: see text]-fold vs. [Formula: see text]-fold).

title: The associations among athlete status, sleep, and well-being in a large national sample of college students.
abstract: Objective: College students, specifically student athletes, experience environments that can support and create barriers to flourishing, a form of well-being reflecting positive functioning in relationships, self-esteem, purpose, and optimism. Sleep is one factor that can have implications for student athletes' flourishing. This study explored whether sleep characteristics, including duration, quality, and napping, accounted for part of the association between athlete status and flourishing, as measured using the eight-item Flourishing Scale. Participants: Using the Fall 2022 National College Health Assessment (N = 28,608), structural equation models assessed these associations. Results: Compared with non-athletes, athletes reported better sleep quality, smaller weekday-weekend differences in sleep duration, and longer sleep duration. Athletes also reported more frequent and longer naps. These sleep factors were associated with flourishing although indirect associations were small (β < .06). Conculsion: Overall, athletes reported several favorable sleep characteristics relative to non-athletes, alongside more frequent and longer naps. Sleep remains important in understanding student athletes' flourishing.

title: Advances in disease management and treatment outcomes for obesity and knee osteoarthritis in primary care practice.
abstract: The lifetime risk of developing knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is approximately doubled in people with obesity compared with those without obesity. Many patients with KOA are treated by primary care physicians in the community setting. We performed a targeted literature search on PubMed to identify relevant literature describing the impact of weight loss in patients with obesity and KOA. A strong body of evidence supports the use of weight loss through lifestyle interventions, including caloric restriction in combination with exercise, as a primary intervention in patients with KOA and obesity. Studies show that these interventions are associated with improvements in pain, physical function, and quality of life; however, adherence to lifestyle interventions can be challenging, even with individually tailored programs. Obesity medications, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, are emerging as a new addition to weight management approaches in KOA, with a recent phase 3 clinical study demonstrating the benefits of semaglutide for weight loss in adults with KOA and high body mass index. Although initial data are promising, further clinical evidence is required, and perceived barriers to use need to be addressed before obesity medications can be widely adopted into clinical practice for patients with KOA. Specifically, further data are required to guide decisions regarding optimal treatment duration with obesity medications and to establish their tolerability profile associated with longer-term use. The importance of preserving functional muscle mass in patients with KOA and mitigation of weight regain after obesity medication treatment withdrawal are also identified as areas warranting further research. In this narrative review, we provide practical recommendations to primary care physicians on integrating obesity medications into weight-loss programs, including patient screening, risk stratification, communication, use of guidelines, and the benefits of a multidisciplinary approach.

title: Cartilage-targeting engineered probiotic bacterial extracellular vesicles treat osteoarthritis through modulation of matrix homeostasis.
abstract: Reversing extracellular matrix (ECM) metabolic dysregulation to facilitate cartilage repair represents a key therapeutic strategy for osteoarthritis (OA) treatment. Owing to the avascular nature of joint structures, intra-articular injection is a commonly used clinical administration route. However, the current drug retention time is insufficient to effectively reverse OA progression. In this study, we demonstrated that natural bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) are capable of repairing cartilage damage. We modified Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)-derived BEVs with a chondrocyte-targeting peptide to prolong their therapeutic efficacy. Engineered BEVs, as a drug delivery system, are capable of continuously transporting endogenous miRNAs. Cartilage-targeting LGG-EVs (W-LGG-EVs) penetrate deeply into cartilage tissue and promote extracellular matrix secretion by chondrocytes. Furthermore, W-LGG-EVs were shown to restore cartilage homeostasis and ultimately alleviate stress-related OA. BEVs, as a novel and safe therapeutic agent, hold clinical feasibility.

title: Beyond a mechanical cushion: the paracrine secretome of the infrapatellar fat pad in knee homeostasis and osteoarthritis.
abstract: The Infrapatellar Fat Pad (IFP), traditionally regarded as a passive adipose structure providing mechanical support within the knee, is increasingly recognized as an immunometabolic organ that shapes the intra-articular microenvironment through its paracrine secretome. Understanding these interactions may clarify Osteoarthritis (OA) pathophysiology and inform new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. This narrative review examined current evidence on the paracrine role of the IFP in knee OA. We focused on its anatomy and cellular composition; cytokines, adipokines, growth factors, matrix-remodeling mediators, and extracellular vesicles; and interactions with cartilage, synovium, subchondral bone, and resident immune cells. Current evidence indicates that the IFP regulates the joint microenvironment through a network of paracrine mediators. Under physiological conditions, its secretome supports tissue homeostasis, repair, and immune regulation. In OA, secretome dysregulation promotes chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix degradation, fibrosis, angiogenesis, and pain sensitization. Emerging findings also suggest that the IFP may provide biomarkers and therapeutic targets for regenerative and disease-modifying strategies. The IFP should be regarded as a biologically active immunometabolic organ involved in knee OA initiation and progression. Better characterization of its secretome may refine OA phenotyping, support biomarker discovery and patient stratification, and guide precision-medicine and disease-modifying approaches.

title: Estrogen and Lysyl Oxidase: How Crosslink Changes Increase Biological Female Athlete ACL Injury Risk.
abstract: Across sports that involve cutting, pivoting, and single-leg jump landings, biological female athletes sustain anterior cruciate ligament injuries at 2- to 9-fold greater rates than males. The mechanical resilience of the anterior cruciate ligament depends on extracellular matrix stabilization. Crosslinking, primarily mediated by lysyl oxidase, is essential to extracellular matrix maturation, to resisting the tensile and shear forces encountered during athletic activity, and to long-term anterior cruciate ligament health. Estrogen-mediated lysyl oxidase modulation may weaken the extracellular matrix, reducing its capacity to withstand mechanical loads. This narrative review explores how estrogen influences lysyl oxidase function, particularly in the context of collagen crosslinking and connective tissue health. Special emphasis is placed on biological female anterior cruciate ligament injury risk, a highly relevant example of clinical estrogen-associated extracellular matrix vulnerability. By integrating epidemiologic evidence with emerging molecular and mechanistic data, clinicians are provided with a contemporary biologically informed perspective on sex-specific anterior cruciate ligament injury risk. Future research and prevention strategies are discussed.

title: Optimising Pre-race Physical Preparation for Sprint Events at Major Championships Under New Rule Changes and Competition Formats.
abstract: Championship sprint outcomes are often decided by margins as small as hundredths or even thousandths of a second, placing great importance on optimising every aspect of race-day preparation. At major championships, the interval between warm-up and race start includes time in a designated Call Room and can exceed 50 min, long enough to compromise the physiological benefits of the warm-up. Whilst this delay is not new, recent World Athletics technology regulations prohibit heated garments in the Call Room, and athletes must now enter the track wearing only their race kit, making muscle temperature and neuromuscular readiness harder to maintain. The addition of mixed relay events further increases exposure to repeated pre-race transition periods. This leading article therefore reviews the determinants of sprint performance most sensitive to the pre-race period and evaluates acute strategies that may help preserve or restore readiness on the day of competition. Particular attention is given to evidence-informed strategies that complement the main warm-up and can be implemented within current competition regulations. Passive heat maintenance and plyometric conditioning activities appear to offer the greatest practical relevance within current Call Room constraints, with maintenance of muscle temperature an important consideration for preserving sprint and power performance. While there is relevant supporting research, no study has simulated the exact demands of a major championship sprint event, and recommendations therefore rest on mechanistic rationale and applied practice as well as direct evidence. These include a same-day priming session ~ 4-6 h before competition, passive insulation to attenuate muscle temperature decline during the transition period, and a brief plyometric or short acceleration stimulus 8-16 min before race start, with athletes encouraged to establish their individual responses in training and simulated competition.

title: Intensity-dependent microcurrent stimulation enhances BMSC-derived cartilage microtissue formation under defined culture conditions.
abstract: Engineering phenotypically favorable cartilage-like tissue from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) remains challenging because chondrogenic differentiation can be accompanied by insufficient cartilage-associated extracellular matrix accumulation and unfavorable hypertrophic and catabolic responses. Here, we established a microcurrent-assisted culture system for scaffold-free BMSC-derived cartilage microtissues (CMTs) and investigated the intensity-dependent effects of continuous unidirectional direct-current stimulation at 0, 50, 100, 150, 250, or 500 μA under a defined electrical and culture configuration. Among the tested conditions, 150 μA (nominal electrode current density, 3 μA/mm2) showed the most consistently favorable overall response, with enhanced cartilage-associated gene and protein expression, greater type II collagen- and glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix accumulation, improved CMT morphology, and higher apparent mechanical properties. In contrast, 250 and 500 μA were associated with reduced cartilage-associated matrix formation and increased fibrotic, hypertrophic, catabolic, inflammatory, and apoptosis-related markers. The 150 μA condition was also associated with a distinct intracellular Ca2+ response pattern and increased NFATc1 nuclear localization; verapamil, BAPTA-AM, and cyclosporin A attenuated NFATc1 nuclear localization, supporting involvement of Ca2+/calcineurin/NFAT-related signaling without establishing a unique causal mechanism. After 2 weeks of xenogeneic subcutaneous implantation in nude mice, CMTs preconditioned at 150 μA exhibited greater cartilage-like matrix accumulation and higher apparent compressive properties than those preconditioned at 0 or 500 μA. These findings identify 150 μA as the best-performing tested condition under the present electrical configuration and provide short-term ectopic proof-of-concept evidence, while longer-term orthotopic studies are required to evaluate phenotypic stability, tissue integration, and functional outcomes in cartilage-defect models.

title: Flowable and microporous granular grafts made from decellularized extracellular matrix microgels for tissue repair.
abstract: Decellularized extracellular matrix (dECM) scaffolds are widely used in tissue engineering, primarily due to their inherent bioactivity and cell-instructive properties. ECM scaffolds are conventionally prepared as monolithic and rigid sheet-like constructs and while these form factors are generally sutured at the defect site, it can be challenging to achieve even filling of the defect volume, where flowable scaffolds may be beneficial. Although infusible and injectable dECM formulations have been developed, optimizing for high mechanical strength and a porous microstructure that permits integration with host tissue remains difficult. Here, we report the fabrication of granular dECMs, which are flowable and microporous biomaterials that are assembled through the packing of crosslinked dECM microgels. A feature of these dECM microgels is their crosslinking through dityrosine photochemistry, which circumvents the need for chemical modification of the dECM with synthetic functional groups. Granular dECMs show tunable porosity through optimization of microgel packing, and shear-responsive rheological behaviors that impart extrudability from syringe needles. When tested in a mouse model of volumetric muscle loss and compared against no treatment negative controls, bioinert granular controls made with poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate, and bulk dECM implants, granular dECMs showed improved wound healing properties and support robust angiogenesis and myogenesis at a structural level. Data from longitudinal muscle force measurements carried out over 12 weeks showed comparable levels of functional recovery across all groups. Collectively, these results showcase the potential promise of dityrosine crosslinked granular dECMs as acellular injectable grafts for reconstructive surgery and wound healing applications. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Acellular biomaterial grafts made with decellularized tissues are commercially available and clinically used for reconstructive and wound healing applications. Their rigid design and low malleability has motivated the development of injectable and infusible dECM hydrogels. However, it has remained challenging to co-optimize their mechanical properties and microporosity for tissue repair applications. This work presents a granular dECM graft technology that uses light-activated crosslinking of tyrosine groups naturally present in protein-rich tissues to fabricate dECM microgels that are then assembled into microporous scaffolds that flow under strain and can be extruded via syringe into irregularly shaped tissue defects. Using a clinically relevant mouse model of muscle injury, we highlight the regenerative potential of granular dECM grafts in supporting rapid vascularization and myogenesis at the defect site. This advanced design of injectable and flowable dECM biomaterials is likely to find broad utility in reconstructive surgery and tissue engineering applications.

title: Precision Diagnostics in Bone Disease: The Potential of Circulating and Stem Cell-Associated miRNAs as Minimally Invasive Biomarkers.
abstract: Stem cell-associated microRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as pivotal regulators of osteogenesis, influencing lineage commitment, differentiation, and skeletal tissue homeostasis. Their dysregulation has been increasingly linked to a spectrum of osteogenic disorders, including osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and impaired fracture healing. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the diagnostic potential of stem cell-associated miRNAs in bone-related pathologies. We highlight their roles in modulating osteoblast and osteoclast activity, maintaining mesenchymal stem cell fate, and orchestrating signaling pathways such as Wnt/β-catenin, bone morphogenetic protein, and Notch. Particular emphasis is placed on circulating miRNAs as minimally invasive biomarkers, offering prospects for early detection, disease stratification, and monitoring therapeutic response. Furthermore, we discuss methodological advances in miRNA profiling, challenges in clinical translation, and the need for standardized validation frameworks. By integrating molecular insights with translational perspectives, this review underscores the promise of stem cell-associated miRNAs as diagnostic tools in osteogenic disorders, while identifying critical gaps that must be addressed to enable their incorporation into precision medicine strategies.

title: Muscle satellite cell dysfunction in critical illness: niche biology, regenerative failure, and implications for recovery.
abstract: Adult skeletal muscle can regenerate. After muscle injury, muscle stem cells (satellite cells) can generate new muscle fibers. Under normal conditions, satellite cells are mitotically quiescent and located beneath the basal lamina of muscle fibers. In response to regenerative stimuli, satellite cells activate and proliferate as myogenic precursor cells. After several rounds of cell division, these precursor cells differentiate and fuse to form new muscle fibers. A subset of proliferating myogenic precursor cells returns to a quiescent state to replenish the satellite cell pool through self-renewal. Intensive care unit-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) affects many critically ill patients partly due to acute muscle loss. It is a major physical component of post-intensive care syndrome. Current explanations of ICU-AW focus on rapid protein breakdown and impaired energy metabolism during the early catabolic phase, but these mechanisms do not fully explain why some survivors fail to rebuild muscle once the initial catabolic stress has subsided. In this review, we argue that persistent weakness may also reflect defective muscle regeneration, with satellite cell dysfunction and niche abnormalities as plausible contributors. Recent serial-biopsy studies suggest that dysfunction can occur without stem-cell depletion: satellite cell number can be preserved even when differentiation or later proliferative capacity is impaired in culture. We first review the normal satellite cell niche, including the parent fiber, microvasculature and perivascular cells, extracellular matrix, resident immune and interstitial cells, and systemic signals, with separate consideration of the diaphragm. We then examine how critical illness affects these compartments and how cell-intrinsic defects may additionally impair regeneration. We use this evidence to develop three working hypotheses (niche-detached activation, abortive myogenesis, and niche locking) and treat them as testable models rather than recognized mechanisms. Finally, we consider how future studies might measure, target, and test these processes.
journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

title: Therapeutic Limb Hypothermia Preserves Neurophysiologic Function and Reduces Tissue Injury in a Novel Porcine Survival Model of Acute Hindlimb Ischemia.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute limb ischemia carries high morbidity and risk of limb loss. Prior animal models were limited to non-survival designs and biochemical endpoints, precluding assessment of long-term outcomes. We developed a porcine survival model of ischemia-reperfusion injury to evaluate therapeutic limb hypothermia with functional, neurophysiologic, and histopathologic endpoints.
METHODS: Ten female Yorkshire pigs underwent unilateral hindlimb ischemia via balloon occlusion of the ipsilateral external and internal iliac arteries for six hours, confirmed by angiography, and were randomized to hypothermia (5°C) or normothermia, with the contralateral limb as control. Hypothermia was applied via a closed-loop limb-cooling device to achieve goal muscle temperature. Animals were monitored for 7 days with daily Tarlov assessment and underwent terminal neurophysiologic testing and muscle/nerve biopsy on day 7.
RESULTS: Hypothermia-treated limbs showed significantly preserved sensory and motor nerve conduction at POD7 versus marked loss in controls (p = 0.008 for both SNAP and CMAP preservation), and markedly reduced histologic muscle injury across degeneration, necrosis, inflammation, and regeneration (cumulative score, p < 0.001). Nerve histologic injury did not differ significantly between groups (p = 0.45), and gait recovery showed a favorable but non-significant trend versus controls (p = 0.34).
CONCLUSION: Localized limb hypothermia preserves neurophysiologic function and reduces tissue injury after acute limb ischemia (p ≤ 0.008 for both), with a favorable but non-significant trend in functional recovery. This novel large-animal model is relevant for studying human acute limb ischemia and reperfusion injury in traumatic or embolic settings.

title: Bioengineered skeletal muscle construct using a cell-seeded decellularized diaphragm muscle scaffolding system for pelvic muscle regeneration.
abstract: Pelvic floor muscle injury often leads to dysfunction of the entire pelvic urogenital system, negatively impacting the patient's quality of life. Current treatment options include autologous muscle transfer and biomaterial-based meshes and slings; however, adequately restoring muscle function remains a significant challenge. With advances in skeletal muscle tissue engineering, bioengineered skeletal muscle constructs have emerged as promising therapeutic solutions for treating various types of muscle injuries. Recently, these strategies have been expanded to address injuries involving pelvic musculature. In this study, we developed a bioengineered skeletal muscle construct by seeding human muscle progenitor cells (hMPCs) onto a decellularized skeletal muscle scaffold to regenerate damaged pelvic muscle tissues. Allogeneic decellularized diaphragm muscle tissue was employed as a biological scaffold due to its structural and mechanical similarities to native pelvic muscle tissues. We demonstrated that the decellularized diaphragm retained aligned skeletal muscle matrix microstructures and preserved mechanical properties. hMPCs seeded on the decellularized scaffold remained viable and differentiated into aligned muscle fibers. The feasibility of the bioengineered muscle construct was investigated in a rat model of extensive pelvic muscle injury. Our in vivo results demonstrated that the implanted construct supported the formation of new skeletal muscle tissue with vascular and neural integration and improved recovery of muscle weight and function. To our knowledge, this is the first approach using decellularized diaphragm muscle tissue matrices as a biologic scaffold for pelvic muscle repair. With further advances, this approach may offer an alternative strategy for repairing pelvic muscle injuries. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Pelvic floor muscle injury significantly impairs quality of life, yet current mesh- and sling-based treatments are limited by poor structural and biological integration. Here, we developed a bioengineered skeletal muscle construct using human muscle progenitor cells seeded onto a decellularized diaphragm scaffold, given its biomimetic architecture and mechanical properties that closely resemble native pelvic floor muscle. In a rat model of pelvic floor injury, this construct promoted muscle regeneration, vascularization, and neural integration while improving muscle mass and function. To our knowledge, this is the first use of decellularized diaphragm tissue for pelvic muscle reconstruction. This approach may provide a promising strategy for supporting structural and functional muscle repair.

title: Osteogenic priming of canine perivascular mesenchymal stromal cells enhances extracellular vesicle yield and in vitro activity for bone regeneration.
abstract: The therapeutic efficacy of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) is intrinsically linked to their response to the host microenvironment by the interplay with resident cells. While MSC-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) offer a promising cell-free alternative, optimizing their production and cargo for specific clinical applications remains a challenge. We investigated the impact of in vitro osteogenic priming on the yield, molecular profile, and functional activity of EVs derived from canine umbilical cord perivascular MSCs (cPMSCs). The EVs secreted by osteogenic primed and naïve cPMSC were isolated by ultracentrifugation and characterized by nanoparticle tracking analysis, western blotting, and electronic transmission microscopy. In vitro functional assays of cellular uptake, proliferation, migration, and mineralization were performed. MicroRNAs known to participate in osteogenesis (cfa-miR-21, cfa-miR26a, cfa-miR-27a and cfa-miR-29a) were evaluated in EV samples of both groups through RT-qPCR. Notably, osteogenic priming led to a 1.5-fold increase in vesicle yield (5.6 ± 0.5 ×1010 particles/ml) compared to naïve MSCs (3.7 ± 0.7 ×1010 particles/ml), without altering vesicle distribution nor TSG101 expression (similar expression for both groups). Functional assays revealed that while both EV populations were efficiently internalized, osteogenic priming significantly improved extracellular matrix mineralization (P=0.0003) and enhanced EV-mediated cell migration (P=0.005). Molecular analysis confirmed the enrichment of key osteogenic microRNAs, including cfa-miR-21, cfa-miR-26a, cfa-miR-27a, and cfa-miR-29a, in both groups. These findings demonstrate that osteogenic priming is a robust strategy to improve EV production efficiency and migratory potential, providing a molecularly characterized foundation for advanced cell-free orthopedic therapies in veterinary medicine.

title: Aerobic Exercise Ameliorates Osteoarthritic Chondrocyte Degradation in Osteoarthritis via Regulating E2F8/NLRP14 Signaling Pathway.
abstract: Although physical activity is known to mitigate disease risks, its protective molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. E2F8, a regulator of cell cycle and metabolism, showed significant differential expression between osteoarthritis (OA) and exercise models, suggesting it may link mechanical activity to OA alleviation. In vitro, Interleukin-1 Beta (IL-1β) simulated inflammation. In vivo, OA was induced in rats via Monosodium iodoacetate (MIA) injection. The effects of E2F8 and mechanical stress were assessed using moderate treadmill exercise, histology, and joint observation. Bioinformatic analysis, cyclic tensile strain, Western blot, immunofluorescence, and gene knockdown were used to investigate mechanisms. In OA rats, E2F8 was downregulated in cartilage while NLRP14 increased. Exercise reversed E2F8 downregulation, alleviated cartilage degeneration, restored anabolic activity, and reduced inflammatory catabolism linked to senescence. In vitro, mechanical stress reversed the IL-1β-induced anabolic/catabolic imbalance by regulating the E2F8/NLRP14, mitigating OA progression. Mechanical stress enhances E2F8 expression in osteoarthritic chondrocytes, which in turn protects cartilage by suppressing the expression of NLRP14. These findings underscore the role of E2F8 as a mechano-sensitive mediator and highlight the potential of exercise or exercise-mimetic therapies as effective strategies for preventing and treating OA.

title: A multifunctional MOF-mineralized conductive hydrogel coating on zinc implants orchestrates neuro-osteogenic coupling for enhanced bone defect repair.
abstract: Zinc (Zn)-based implants face critical challenges in clinical orthopedic applications due to rapid corrosion, localized Zn2+-induced cytotoxicity, and inadequate osteogenic activity. Herein, we report a metal-organic framework (MOF)-mediated mineralization strategy to engineer a multifunctional conductive hydrogel coating on pure zinc substrates, integrated with polypyrrole nanoparticles (Ppy NPs). This hierarchical coating design significantly enhances interfacial adhesion and reduces the in vitro corrosion volume ratio of zinc substrates by approximately 53.23% after 14 days of immersion, effectively mitigating excessive degradation-associated ion release. The MOF- mediated mineralized layer provides controlled Zn2+/Cu2+ release and stabilizes the implant interface, while Ppy NPs establish an intrinsic electroactive microenvironment. These synergistic ionic and electrical cues promote Schwann cell functional activity, enhance neurotrophic factor secretion, and subsequently facilitate mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) osteogenic differentiation through neuro-osteogenic communication. Notably, co-culture of MSCs with Schwann cells on the Zn/H@MP coating surface results in a 257% increase in alkaline phosphatase activity and a 222% enhancement in mineralized nodule formation compared to MSC mono-culture, accompanied by significant upregulation of key osteogenic markers, demonstrating the neuro-osteogenic coupling effect. In vivo evaluation in a rat bone defect model reveals that the coated implants achieve 79.46% new bone volume fraction at 8 weeks post-implantation, with accelerated osseointegration, mature bone formation, and enhanced peri-implant innervation. By integrating corrosion regulation, bioactive ion delivery, and electroactive neuro-osteogenic modulation, this multifunctional coating provides a promising strategy for next-generation biodegradable orthopedic implants.
